contentText: Syllabus — Theories of the State: Liberal, Neo-liberal, Marxist, Pluralist, Post-colonial and Feminist. (UPSC PSIR Paper-1A, Unit 2) Unit Snapshot What this unit covers:  the concept & elements of the state; theories of sovereignty (monistic/Austin vs pluralist) and the impact of globalization on sovereignty; and the six theories of the state — Liberal (negative, positive, neo-liberal), Marxist (instrumentalist & structuralist), Pluralist, Post-colonial and Feminist — plus the Fascist, Gandhian and legitimacy-crisis conceptions and the crisis of the modern nation-state. Must-know thinkers:  Hobbes, Locke, Austin, Laski, MacIver, Krabbe, Marx, Engels, Lenin, Miliband, Poulantzas, Gramsci, Robert Dahl, C. Wright Mills, Kenichi Ohmae, David Held, Edward Said, Hamza Alavi, A.G. Frank, Wallerstein, Gunnar Myrdal, F.W. Riggs, Catherine MacKinnon, Carole Pateman, Mussolini, Gandhi, Habermas. PYQ trend:  the heaviest-scoring unit. Neo-liberal state (2016/17/18), Feminist (2021), Post-colonial (2020), Pluralist (2019), Marxist & materialism (2013/14), sovereignty & globalization (2015), Gandhi (2015), Fascism (2014/18), legitimacy crisis (2015), Hobbesian obligation (2017). Master Questions Q — Trace the evolution of the liberal theory of the state through its negative, positive and neo-liberal phases, and critically examine the neo-liberal conception of the state and its link with globalization. (UPSC 2016/2017/2018) What it’s asking:  Tell the story of liberalism in three phases → then judge neo-liberalism and its marriage with globalization. Gist — the spine to recall 1. Core idea  — a neutral, limited state resting on consent;  Paine’s  ‘necessary evil’.  (The state is the referee, not a player — it enforces the rules of the market but never picks the winner.) 2. Negative phase  —  Smith, Bentham, Spencer :  laissez-faire  and ‘negative liberty’, i.e. the simple absence of interference.  (The state keeps law and order and enforces contracts — nothing more.) 3. Positive phase  —  J.S. Mill, Green, Hobhouse : the state becomes an  agency of common good  creating the conditions of self-development.  (Free speech is empty for a hungry illiterate — hence MGNREGA and the Right to Education.) 4. Neo-liberal phase  —  Hayek, Friedman, Nozick  roll the welfare ‘nanny state’ back to a  night-watchman state ; ‘social justice is a mirage’.  (India’s 1991 LPG reforms — the licence raj dismantled, PSUs disinvested.) 5. Globalization link  — neo-liberalism became globalization’s ideology via  Thatcher, Reagan , the  Washington Consensus  and the WTO.  (IMF loans carried structural-adjustment conditions — as with India in 1991.) 6. Critique & conclusion  — widening inequality breeds a  legitimacy crisis ;  Sen  and  Stiglitz  push back.  (The 2008 bailouts brought the state straight back.) Model Answer 1. Core idea.  The liberal theory sees the state as a  neutral, limited instrument  that exists to protect individual rights and freedom and rests on the  consent of the people . It is a referee rather than a player: it lays down and enforces the rules within which individuals pursue their own ends, but does not prescribe those ends.  Thomas Paine  caught the ambivalence in calling it a ‘necessary evil’ — evil because every law restricts freedom, necessary because freedom cannot be safeguarded without it. From this single premise the doctrine evolved through three phases. 2. Negative phase.  Classical or negative liberalism ( Adam Smith, Bentham, James Mill, Herbert Spencer ) begins from the rational individual possessing inalienable rights to life, liberty and property. The state must therefore follow  laissez-faire , confining itself to defence, law and order and the enforcement of contracts, since the market coordinates society better than any minister can. Liberty here is  negative  — the mere absence of external interference — so that the less the state does, the freer the citizen is held to be. 3. Positive phase.  By the late nineteenth century laissez-faire had produced liberty without equality, and welfare liberals ( J.S. Mill, T.H. Green, Hobhouse ) recast the state as an  agency of the common good . Liberty became  positive  — not being left alone but possessing the actual capacity for self-development — which requires education, health and a floor of income. Freedom of speech means little to a hungry illiterate; hence the welfare state, and in India measures such as MGNREGA and the Right to Education, are read as enabling rather than restricting freedom. 4. Neo-liberal phase.  Neo-liberalism or libertarianism ( Hayek, Friedman, Nozick ) is a reaction against this interventionist ‘nanny state’, which it charges with inefficiency, dependence and creeping serfdom. It restores the  night-watchman state , gives priority to economic liberty — “economic freedom is a precondition of political freedom” ( Friedman ) — and rejects redistribution outright,  Hayek  declaring that “social justice is a mirage” because market outcomes are unintended and so cannot be called unjust. India’s 1991 liberalisation, dismantling the licence raj and disinvesting public undertakings, is the clearest domestic instance. 5. Globalization link.  Neo-liberalism became the ruling ideology of globalization. Adopted by  Thatcher  and  Reagan , it was exported through ‘shock therapy’, structural adjustment and the  Washington Consensus  — deregulation, privatisation and ‘trade not aid’ — with the  WTO  as its institutional high point. Loans carried conditionalities obliging borrowing states to shrink themselves, as India experienced in 1991; hence the examiner’s proposition that “the political ideology of globalization is neo-liberalism.” 6. Critique and conclusion.  By overestimating the individual and underestimating the state, liberalism builds a capitalist order that can serve exploitative ends, and neo-liberalism’s widening inequality has produced a  legitimacy crisis  for it.  Amartya Sen , for whom development is the expansion of capabilities, and  Joseph Stiglitz , who exposes the asymmetries of globalization, therefore argue for a balanced, welfare-oriented state — a case vindicated by the post-2008 return of massive state intervention. Q — Examine the Marxist theory of the state — its origin, its instrumentalist and relative-autonomy (structuralist) variants, and its materialist basis. (UPSC 2013/2014) What it’s asking:  Show why the state is a class weapon → prove the materialist basis → contrast the two Marxist variants → end with withering away. Gist — the spine to recall 1. Core claim  — the state is not neutral but a  class institution  born of force, not contract ( Engels ).  (The colonial state’s law protected the planter, never the tenant.) 2. Materialist basis  — the economic  base  (who owns the means of production) determines the political  superstructure .  (Whoever owns the factory shapes who writes the factory law.) 3. Instrumentalist variant  —  Marx, Lenin, Miliband : the state is the ‘executive committee of the bourgeoisie’.  (Even the welfare state left wealth concentrated and the bureaucracy elitist.) 4. Structuralist variant  —  Poulantzas, Althusser :  relative autonomy  means the state may act against individual capitalists to save capitalism itself.  (It legislates a minimum wage in calm times, but bails out the banks in a crash — 2008.) 5. Hegemony & withering away  —  Gramsci : rule works by consent, not coercion alone, and the state lasts only as long as classes do.  (Schools and the press make the ruler’s worldview feel like common sense.) 6. Critique & conclusion  —  Dahl : not all conflict is class conflict; yet no theory exposes the state’s hidden class bias better. Model Answer 1. Core claim.  Marxism is above all a critique of the liberal-capitalist state. Against the liberal claim of neutrality it argues that the state is a  class institution  — an instrument of organised coercion serving whichever class owns the means of production. Its origin lies not in a social contract but in  force  and in the splitting of society into contending classes: for  Engels , in  The Origin of the Family, Private Property and the State , the state arises precisely when class antagonism becomes unmanageable — as the colonial state’s codes protected the planter and never the tenant. 2. Materialist basis.  Marx’s understanding is materialistic because the state belongs to the  superstructure  — law, politics, religion and ideas — which is determined by the economic  base , that is, the mode of production and the class owning it. Whoever owns the factory ultimately shapes who writes the factory law. Political power is thus ‘the organised power of one class for oppressing another’, and ‘the ruling ideas of every age are the ideas of the ruling class’: the state cannot float free of the property relations that sustain it. 3. Instrumentalist variant.  On the instrumentalist reading ( Marx, Lenin, Ralph Miliband ) the state is a direct tool in the hands of the capitalists — “the executive committee of the bourgeoisie” ( Marx ), which “represents the irreconcilability of class antagonism” ( Lenin ).  Miliband , in  The State in Capitalist Society , showed empirically that even in the post-war welfare state wealth remained concentrated and the higher bureaucracy, judiciary and army were recruited from the propertied elite — exploding the myth of a ‘managerial revolution’. 4. Structuralist variant.  The structuralists ( Poulantzas, Althusser ), building on Marx’s  The 18th Brumaire , hold that the state enjoys  relative autonomy : it is not a puppet, and where no single class is dominant it can act as an ‘equilibrium-maker’ above classes, as under Bonapartism, thereby appearing neutral. It may even legislate against particular capitalists — a minimum wage, a factory safety law — in order to preserve capitalism as a whole. But the autonomy is only relative: in a genuine crisis it intervenes for the rich, as the 2008 bank bailouts amid ‘Occupy Wall Street’ revealed. 5. Hegemony and withering away.  Antonio Gramsci  enriched the theory by showing that class rule survives less through force than through  hegemony  — the manufacture of consent in civil society, so that schools, churches and newspapers make the ruling class’s worldview feel like plain common sense. The state is nevertheless historical, not eternal: it exists only as long as classes exist, and once the dictatorship of the proletariat has abolished private property it will  ‘wither away’  in a classless communist society. 6. Critique and conclusion.  Robert Dahl  and the pluralists object that the theory reduces all conflict to class conflict, ignoring the real competition of religious, linguistic, regional and professional groups, while twentieth-century experience suggests the state does not wither but hardens. Yet the Marxist theory remains the sharpest available exposure of the class bias concealed behind the state’s claim to neutrality. Q — Critically examine the pluralist theory of the state and sovereignty as an attack on the monistic (Austinian) theory. (UPSC 2019) What it’s asking:  State the monistic doctrine → mount the pluralist attack → grade the pluralists → weigh the charge of inconsistency. Gist — the spine to recall 1. The monistic theory  —  Hobbes, Austin : one  absolute, indivisible, inalienable  sovereign; ‘law is the command of the sovereign’.  (Sovereignty = the last word that no one may lawfully answer back.) 2. The pluralist attack  —  Laski, MacIver : the state is only  one association among many .  (A citizen’s life is ruled as much by her union, caste panchayat, temple and university.) 3. Laski’s formula  — “since society is federal, authority should also be federal”;  Krabbe : sovereignty must be ‘expunged from political theory’.  (India’s Seventh Schedule and the 73rd Amendment are federal authority in practice.) 4. Two grades of pluralism  — moderate ( Laski : the state is still ‘the keystone of the social architecture’) versus extreme ( MacIver : the ‘service state’ “commands because it serves”). 5. Critique  — charged with  inconsistency  (it attacks the state yet keeps it — ‘cake and eat it too’) and with ignoring group inequality ( C. Wright Mills ). 6. Conclusion  — inconsistency is not irrelevance: dispersed power fits an age of federalism, the UN and the EU better than war-prone monism. Model Answer 1. The monistic theory.  The  monistic or Austinian theory  holds that in every independent political society there must exist one determinate sovereign whose power is  absolute, universal, permanent, indivisible and inalienable .  John Austin  put it formally: if a determinate human superior, not habitually obeying any other superior, receives habitual obedience from the bulk of a given society, that superior is sovereign and ‘law is the command of the sovereign’. Sovereignty is thus the last word to which no one may lawfully answer back — a position echoed in  Weber’s  definition of the state by its monopoly of legitimate force, and rooted in  Hobbes’s  undivided Leviathan. 2. The pluralist attack.  Pluralists ( Laski, MacIver, Figgis, Barker ) deny that any single centre can absorb all authority. Human beings pursue many interests through many associations, so power should be  distributed  among them; the state is  one association among many , not their master, and cannot satisfy the whole of human need. A citizen’s conduct in India is in fact governed as much by her trade union, caste panchayat, religious body and university as by Parliament, and each of these commands a genuine loyalty of its own. 3. Laski’s formula.  Harold Laski  compressed the argument into a maxim: “since society is federal, authority should also be federal.” Sovereignty must be functionally divided among the groups that actually perform society’s work, and obedience must be earned rather than commanded.  Krabbe  went further, insisting that “the notion of sovereignty must be expunged from political theory” and replaced by the sovereignty of law and the community’s sense of right. The Indian Constitution’s distribution of powers in the Seventh Schedule and the devolution effected by the 73rd Amendment illustrate such federal authority in practice. 4. Two grades of pluralism.  Pluralists differ in degree.  Moderate pluralists  such as  Laski  still make the state ‘the keystone of the social architecture’, because it alone can resolve conflicts between associations and command the widest allegiance.  Extreme pluralists  such as  MacIver  allow it no primacy at all: the ‘service state’ “commands because it serves” and is ‘both the guardian and the child of law’, so its authority is derivative and conditional. 5. Critique.  The theory is charged with  inconsistency : it attacks the state’s supremacy yet, unlike anarchism, retains the state, so critics say ‘pluralists want to keep the cake and eat it too’. It also assumes associations compete on equal terms, whereas  C. Wright Mills  shows a ‘power elite’ of corporate, military and political leaders dominating the rest, a survival of the fittest among groups.  Henry Maine  adds that no historical state, Ranjit Singh’s Punjab included, ever matched Austin’s model either. 6. Conclusion.  Inconsistency, however, is not irrelevance. By dispersing power, dignifying associations and taking international law seriously, pluralism describes an age of federalism, the United Nations, the ICJ and the European Union far better than the monistic doctrine, and by denying any state an absolute will it is also the more conducive to peace. Q — Discuss the theories of sovereignty and examine the challenges posed by globalization to the sovereignty of the modern nation-state. (UPSC 2015) What it’s asking:  Define sovereignty and its rival theories → then test how far globalization and internal strains have hollowed it out. Gist — the spine to recall 1. What sovereignty is  — the supreme, final law-making power;  Hobbes  gave its first full theory.  (Only Parliament can bind every person within India’s territory.) 2. Rival theories  —  monistic  ( Austin : absolute and indivisible) versus  pluralist  ( Laski, MacIver : shared with associations). 3. Globalization’s challenge  — the state’s ‘hard shell’ turns  porous ;  Ohmae’s   Borderless World .  (A WTO ruling can unsettle a national farm subsidy; capital exits at a keystroke.) 4. Three perspectives  —  globalists  (sovereignty really diluted),  state-centric  (states still in control),  transformationalist  —  Held : ‘not a zero-sum game’. 5. Internal challenges  — stateless nations, multi-ethnic break-ups and nuclear insecurity.  (The Kurds; the collapse of the USSR and Yugoslavia.) 6. Conclusion  — sovereignty is not extinguished but  reconfigured .  (The EU pools it; climate and trade treaties make India accept limits it writes itself.) Model Answer 1. What sovereignty is.  Sovereignty — the supreme and final power to make and enforce law within a territory — is the defining attribute of the modern nation-state and, with population, territory and government, one of its four elements.  Hobbes  supplied its first complete theory in  Leviathan , where subjects surrender their right of self-government to a single undivided sovereign in exchange for security. In practical terms it means that only Parliament may bind every person within India’s territory, and that externally no other state may command it. 2. Rival theories.  Classically sovereignty is  absolute, universal, permanent, indivisible and inalienable  — the  monistic  view of  Austin , for whom law is simply the command of the sovereign backed by sanction. Against it the  pluralist  theory of  Laski  and  MacIver  insists that authority is shared with the many associations of a federal society, while  Krabbe  would abolish the concept altogether. The globalization debate is in effect the empirical continuation of this old theoretical quarrel. 3. Globalization’s challenge.  If the nation-state is a ‘billiard ball with a hard shell’, globalization has made that shell  porous . Information technology carries data and ideas past frontiers; market integration lets capital exit at a keystroke; international organisations and law bind states from above, so that a WTO ruling can unsettle a national farm subsidy; and a global civil society of NGOs and movements presses from below.  Kenichi Ohmae , in  The Borderless World , concludes that political boundaries are fading as ‘global citizens’ and transnational firms escape state control. 4. Three perspectives.  There is no consensus on how far this goes.  Globalists  ( Ohmae, McLuhan ) hold that sovereignty is genuinely diluted both internally and externally. The  state-centric  school ( Gilpin, Kapstein ) replies that the world remains state-centric and that globalization is itself a policy states chose and can reverse.  David Held’s  transformationalist  position mediates: globalization is ‘not a zero-sum game’ — in some domains the state loses, in others it gains new regulatory reach — while  Sorensen  notes that weak and strong states are affected very unequally. 5. Internal challenges.  The nation-state is strained from within as well. Stateless nations such as the  Kurds  deny the congruence of nation and state; multi-ethnic federations have broken up, as in the USSR and Yugoslavia; sub-nationalism and diaspora loyalties divide allegiance; and nuclear weapons mean no state can any longer guarantee the security that was sovereignty’s original justification — producing a ‘global village’ of shared risks, from pandemics to climate change. 6. Conclusion.  Sovereignty is therefore not extinguished but  reconfigured : because global problems demand collective solutions, states now accept self-imposed adjustments to their own authority, as the European Union’s pooling of sovereignty and India’s climate and trade commitments show.  Susan Strange  rightly urges that economics and politics be studied together to grasp this shift of authority from states to markets. Q — Analyse the post-colonial theory of the state through the modernization and Marxist (dependency/structuralist) perspectives. (UPSC 2020) What it’s asking:  Say what makes the post-colonial state distinctive → then read it twice over, once through modernization and once through Marxism. Gist — the spine to recall 1. What it studies  — newly independent ‘third world’ states still shaped by colonialism;  Nkrumah’s   neo-colonialism .  (Flag independence, while the economy still ships raw material to the old metropolis.) 2. The twin task  —  nation-building  (one shared identity) plus  state-building  (effective authority).  (India integrating 500-odd princely states while forging one identity across language, caste and religion.) 3. Modernization view  —  Riggs’   prismatic society  (formalism: the law on paper differs from the law in the village) and  Myrdal’s   soft state .  (Land-ceiling laws passed everywhere, enforced almost nowhere.) 4. Marxist dependency  —  Frank, Amin, Wallerstein : a rich  core  and a dependent  periphery  in unequal exchange — the ‘development of underdevelopment’; escape lies in  de-linking . 5. Structuralist view  —  Alavi’s   overdeveloped state : an imported apparatus towering over a traditional base.  (Pakistan as a military-bureaucratic oligarchy; India’s ‘inspector raj’.) 6. Conclusion  — caught between an imported form and inherited economic dependence, its nation- and state-building remain unfinished. Model Answer 1. What it studies.  Post-colonial theory is not a fresh general theory of the state but an attempt to analyse the  newly independent ‘third world’ states  whose politics remains shaped by their colonial past. Formal independence coexists with continuing economic and cultural domination — a  neo-colonialism , the term coined by  Kwame Nkrumah , in which a country flies its own flag while still exporting raw material to its former metropolis.  Edward Said  (in  Orientalism ) and  Gayatri Spivak  stress how deeply this legacy penetrates knowledge and identity themselves. 2. The twin task.  Such states confront a  twin task  the Western state never faced simultaneously.  Nation-building  means transferring loyalty from tribe, caste, sect and village to a single central political community;  state-building  means creating an effective centre capable of maintaining law and order, extracting revenue and delivering welfare. India had to integrate over five hundred princely states while simultaneously forging one civic identity across many languages, castes and religions — attempting in decades what Europe took centuries to do. 3. Modernization view.  Western and World Bank scholars argue these societies will prosper only by modernising and integrating with the world economy.  F.W. Riggs  describes them as  ‘prismatic societies’  caught between the traditional and the modern, marked by  formalism  — a wide gap between the law as written and the law as practised — along with poly-communalism, overlapping functions and the ‘bazaar-canteen’ and ‘sala’ models.  Gunnar Myrdal , in  Asian Drama , calls India a  ‘soft state’ : one that legislates ambitiously but cannot enforce, so that land-ceiling laws were passed everywhere and implemented almost nowhere, defeating even Nehru. 4. Marxist dependency perspective.  The  dependency  or instrumentalist approach ( A.G. Frank, Samir Amin, Immanuel Wallerstein ) locates the cause of backwardness outside these societies altogether. The capitalist ‘world system’ is divided into a rich  core  and a dependent  periphery  locked into unequal exchange, whereby the periphery exports cheap primary goods and imports costly manufactures — a relation Frank called the  ‘development of underdevelopment’ . The state in the periphery serves this external interest, and the prescribed escape is  de-linking  from the world market. 5. Structuralist view.  The  structuralist  approach of  Hamza Alavi  calls the post-colonial state  ‘overdeveloped’ . Because the modern state was an  imported institution  grafted by colonial rulers onto a traditional agrarian base, its bureaucracy and military were built to subordinate a whole society and now tower over weak indigenous classes — Pakistan becoming a ‘military-bureaucratic oligarchy’ and India acquiring its ‘inspector raj’. Such a state is relatively autonomous, mediating between the metropolitan bourgeoisie, the native bourgeoisie and the landed classes rather than serving any one of them. 6. Conclusion.  Read together, the two perspectives show the post-colonial state as doubly constrained — by an imported modern form that sits uneasily on a traditional society, and by an inherited economic dependence it did not choose. That is why nation-building and state-building, rather than the classic Western question of how to limit the state, remain its central and unfinished projects. Q — Critically examine the feminist critique of the state. (UPSC 2021) What it’s asking:  Show why feminists deny the state is neutral → lay out the rival feminist streams → assess the remedies they propose. Gist — the spine to recall 1. Core claim  — the state is not neutral but patriarchal;  MacKinnon : “when I look at the state, it appears male to me.” 2. ‘The personal is political’  — the public/private divide conceals subordination inside the family.  (Unpaid domestic work and violence at home were long treated as ‘private’ and left outside law.) 3. Liberal feminists  — the state is a potential ally from which women were wrongly excluded; the cure is inclusion.  (One-third of panchayat seats reserved for women by the 73rd Amendment.) 4. Marxist-feminists  — the welfare state’s benevolence is the cheap way of  reproducing labour power .  (Benefits presume a male breadwinner and fix the woman as carer.) 5. Radical critique  —  Pateman’s   The Sexual Contract ,  Millett’s  sexual politics,  Okin : no neutral state without dismantling the patriarchal family. 6. Remedies & conclusion  — the male state rests on military power;  Young’s   differentiated citizenship  and a  feminist foreign policy  answer its false neutrality. Model Answer 1. Core claim.  Feminists reject the central liberal assumption that the state is a  neutral  arbiter standing above social divisions.  Catherine MacKinnon , in  Towards a Feminist Theory of the State , writes that “when I look at the state, it appears male to me”: its law adopts the male point of view as the objective standpoint, so that what counts as consent, provocation or reasonableness is defined from men’s experience. Neutrality of form thus conceals partiality of substance. 2. ‘The personal is political’.  The critique rests on this slogan. Liberalism confines politics to the public sphere and treats the household as a private realm beyond regulation; feminists reply that the family is precisely where power, labour and violence are most unequally distributed. Unpaid domestic work is excluded from national income accounting, and violence and coercion within marriage were long left outside the criminal law as ‘private’ matters. The public/private divide is therefore not innocent — it is the mechanism by which women’s subordination is placed beyond political challenge. 3. Liberal feminists.  Liberal feminists  ( Wollstonecraft, Betty Friedan ) regard the state as a potentially neutral ally from which women were historically and wrongly excluded, and whose remedy is therefore inclusion: the vote, equal legal personality, equal opportunity and representation. India’s reservation of one-third of panchayat seats for women under the 73rd Amendment exemplifies this strategy of using state power to correct exclusion rather than abandoning the state as irredeemable. 4. Marxist-feminists.  Marxist-feminists  are sceptical of that faith. They argue that the welfare state’s apparently benign provision is the cheapest available means of  reproducing labour power  — someone must feed, nurse and raise the next generation of workers, and unpaid female domestic labour does so at no cost to capital. Welfare policy consequently reinforces the woman’s domestic role and her dependence on a male breadwinner, while extending state surveillance over reproduction and child-rearing. 5. Radical critique.  The critique deepens with  Carole Pateman , whose  The Sexual Contract  argues that the celebrated social contract was preceded by a sexual contract establishing men’s political right over women, so the masculinist bias lies at the very foundation of modern political theory.  Kate Millett’s   sexual politics  shows patriarchy operating as a system of power in every relationship between the sexes, and  Susanne Moller Okin  draws the conclusion that “without destroying the patriarchal family we cannot get the neutral state.” 6. Remedies and conclusion.  Because women are excluded from its making, the state builds its strength on  military power , generating inter-state tension rather than cooperation and neglecting nature and care.  Iris Marion Young  answers this false neutrality with  differentiated citizenship , which recognises group difference instead of assuming a uniform citizen, while others argue for a more humane  feminist foreign policy . The streams differ on whether to enter, reform or bypass the state; their common and lasting insight is that genuine neutrality is impossible while patriarchy structures both family and public life. Q — Compare the conceptions of the state in Fascism and Marxism, and discuss the Gandhian view and the ‘crisis of legitimacy’ in capitalist societies. (UPSC 2014/2015/2018) What it’s asking:  Set Fascism against Marxism → draw the contrast sharply → add Gandhi’s moral rejection → close with the legitimacy crisis of the capitalist state. Gist — the spine to recall 1. Fascist state  — an  absolute, totalitarian end  in itself;  Mussolini : “nothing against the State, nothing over it, nothing beyond it.”  (The individual exists for the state, never the reverse.) 2. Marxist state  — a  temporary class instrument , the ‘executive committee of the bourgeoisie’, destined to  wither away  once classes end. 3. The contrast  — exact opposites in destination (state-worship versus statelessness), yet twins in rejecting liberal democracy and individual autonomy. 4. Gandhi’s view  — the state is a ‘soulless machine’ resting on coercion and violating  Ahimsa ; the ideal is  enlightened anarchy  and Ramrajya of ‘oceanic circles’.  (Ambedkar disagreed — for him the state is the Dalit’s shield.) 5. Crisis of legitimacy  —  Habermas : democratic welfare demands outrun what capital accumulation can fund.  (Subsidies and loan waivers promised faster than revenue can be raised.) 6. Conclusion  — from worshipped absolute to doomed class tool to coercive machine — and even the liberal state struggles to reconcile democracy with capitalism. Model Answer 1. Fascist state.  Fascism  glorifies the state as an  absolute, totalitarian end  in itself, in which the individual finds meaning only as a part.  Mussolini  declared: “nothing against the State, nothing over it, nothing beyond it.” Drawing on  Hegel  — for whom the state is ‘the march of God on earth’ — it builds a corporate, single-party dictatorship with a cult of the leader, autarky at home and expansion abroad.  Laski  dismissed it as an ‘unsystematic doctrine’, while Marxists read it as capitalism in decay defending itself by force. 2. Marxist state.  Marxism, by contrast, treats the state as a  temporary class instrument  — the ‘executive committee of the bourgeoisie’ — which exists only because society is divided into classes. It has neither moral value nor permanence: once the dictatorship of the proletariat abolishes private property, the state loses its reason for being and  ‘withers away’ , the administration of things replacing government over persons. 3. The contrast.  The two doctrines are therefore  exact opposites  in destination: Fascism culminates in state-worship and permanent dictatorship, Marxism in an eventual stateless society. Fascism exalts nation and race, Marxism class and internationalism; Fascism retains private property under state direction, Marxism abolishes it. Yet they converge in method and enemy — both reject liberal democracy, parliamentary competition and individual autonomy, and both justify a monopoly party as the vehicle of a higher historical purpose. 4. Gandhi’s view.  For  Gandhi  the state is  ‘a soulless machine’  resting on coercion — police, courts and prisons — which stunts self-reliance and violates  Ahimsa , since it represents ‘violence in a concentrated and organised form’. Drawing on Thoreau and  Tolstoy , he would dissolve it through  Swaraj  understood as self-control into ‘enlightened anarchy’ and  Ramrajya , a moral order of self-governing village republics arranged in ‘oceanic circles’ rather than a pyramid.  Ambedkar  rejected this, insisting that for the Dalit the village is a den of oppression and the state the only instrument of emancipation. 5. Crisis of legitimacy.  Jurgen Habermas , in  Legitimation Crisis , argues that capitalist democracies face structural ‘crisis tendencies’: democratic politics continually generates demands for welfare and equality whose satisfaction requires taxation and spending that constrain private capital accumulation, so the state can be legitimate or profitable but struggles to be both.  Anthony King  calls the result ‘government overload’, and  Atul Kohli  diagnoses a  ‘crisis of governability’  in India, where subsidies and loan waivers are promised faster than revenue can be raised. 6. Conclusion.  Across these conceptions the state ranges from a worshipped absolute in Fascism, to a doomed class tool in Marxism, to a coercive machine to be morally transcended in Gandhi. The legitimacy-crisis debate completes the picture by showing that even the liberal-capitalist state, which claims to have escaped all three critiques, struggles to reconcile the promises of democracy with the requirements of capitalism. Revision Box — facts, keywords & quotes 4 elements of the state:  population, territory, government, sovereignty. Weber : the state has the ‘monopoly of the legitimate use of physical force within a territory’. Sovereignty (monistic):  absolute, universal, permanent, indivisible, inalienable; ‘law = command of the sovereign’ (Austin). Laski : ‘since society is federal, authority should also be federal’;  Krabbe : ‘sovereignty must be expunged from political theory’. Liberal state phases:  negative (Smith/Bentham) → positive (J.S. Mill/Green) → neo-liberal (Hayek/Friedman/Nozick). Paine : the state is a ‘necessary evil’;  Friedman : economic freedom precedes political freedom;  Hayek : ‘social justice is a mirage’. Neo-liberalism = ideology of globalization:  Thatcher, Reagan, WTO, Washington Consensus (‘trade not aid’); India’s 1991 LPG reforms. Marx : state = ‘executive committee of the bourgeoisie’;  Lenin : state = ‘irreconcilability of class antagonism’. Materialism:  economic base determines the political superstructure (the state); state ‘withers away’ in communism. Miliband  = instrumentalist;  Poulantzas / Althusser  = structuralist ‘relative autonomy’ (Bonapartism);  Gramsci  = hegemony (rule by consent, not force alone). K.C. Hsiao : the pluralist state has ‘no single source of authority… divisible in parts’;  C. Wright Mills : groups are unequal (‘survival of the fittest’). Ohmae : ‘borderless world’;  Held : globalization vs sovereignty is ‘not a zero-sum game’ (transformationalist). Post-colonial:  Nkrumah  (neo-colonialism);  Riggs  (prismatic society, formalism);  Myrdal  (soft state);  Frank/Wallerstein  (core-periphery);  Alavi  (overdeveloped state). MacKinnon : ‘the state appears male to me’;  Pateman :  The Sexual Contract ; ‘the personal is political’;  Young : differentiated citizenship. Mussolini : ‘nothing against/over/beyond the State’;  Gandhi : state = ‘soulless machine’ → ‘enlightened anarchy’;  Ambedkar : the state emancipates. Habermas :  Legitimation Crisis  in capitalist societies;  Anthony King : ‘government overload’;  Kohli : ‘crisis of governability’. Last-Minute Revision Sheet (1 page) Liberal (MQ1):  neutral/minimal ‘necessary evil’; negative → positive → neo-liberal; neo-liberalism = globalization’s ideology; critique = inequality + legitimacy crisis. Marxist (MQ2):  class instrument; materialist base→superstructure; instrumentalist (Marx/Lenin/Miliband) vs structuralist relative autonomy (Poulantzas); Gramscian hegemony; withers away. Pluralist (MQ3):  attacks monistic/Austinian sovereignty; power dispersed among associations (Laski/MacIver); moderate vs extreme; realistic but ‘inconsistent’. Sovereignty & globalization (MQ4):  Hobbes’ first full theory; porous ‘hard shell’; globalists vs state-centric vs transformationalist (Held); crisis of nation-state. Post-colonial (MQ5):  nation- + state-building; modernization (Riggs, Myrdal) vs Marxist dependency (Frank/Wallerstein) & Alavi’s overdeveloped state. Feminist (MQ6):  state is patriarchal (MacKinnon); ‘personal is political’; liberal vs Marxist-feminist vs radical (Pateman/Okin); differentiated citizenship (Young). Fascist/Gandhian/legitimacy (MQ7):  Fascism = state worship (Mussolini) vs Marxism = withering; Gandhi = soulless machine → enlightened anarchy; Habermas = legitimation crisis. Killer quotes:  Mussolini — ‘nothing beyond the State’; Marx — ‘executive committee of the bourgeoisie’; MacKinnon — ‘the state appears male’; Hayek — ‘social justice is a mirage’; Laski — ‘society is federal, so authority must be federal’. title: 03 - Justice

content.text: Syllabus — Justice: conceptions of justice with special reference to Rawls’ theory of justice and its communitarian critique. (UPSC PSIR Paper-1A, Unit 3)

justice as an architectonic and dynamic idea; classical (Plato, Aristotle) and modern theories; the types/dimensions of justice (distributive, procedural vs substantive, retributive); Rawls’ ‘justice as fairness’; and its critiques — Nozick (libertarian), Amartya Sen (methodological) and the communitarians (Sandel, Walzer, Taylor, MacIntyre), with Rawls’ reply in Political Liberalism.

Plato, Aristotle, Hume, David Miller, John Rawls, Robert Nozick, Amartya Sen, Ronald Dworkin, Michael Sandel, Michael Walzer, Charles Taylor, Alasdair MacIntyre, Carole Gilligan, Thomas Pogge, A.V. Dicey.

Rawls dominates — original position (2013), difference principle (2015), contractual & distributive (2017), justification of discrimination (2018), Rawls enriching liberalism (2021); plus Greek vs Rawlsian (2020), communitarian perspectives (2019) and distributive justice (2018).

Q — Explain Rawls’ ‘justice as fairness’ — the original position, veil of ignorance, primary goods, maximin, the two principles and lexical order, the difference principle and democratic equality. Is it both contractual and distributive? (UPSC 2013/2015/2017/2018/2021)
Lay out Rawls’ machinery step by step, then prove it is at once a social contract and a scheme of redistribution.
: no person may be sacrificed for the aggregate.
(Utilitarianism could justify displacing a tribal village for a dam because more people gain; Rawls forbids it.)
— a hypothetical ‘thought experiment’ in which rational, mutually disinterested people frame the rules before society exists.
(Like drafting the Constitution before knowing which caste, class or religion you will be born into.)
— stripped of knowledge of class, caste, sex and talent, risk-averse agents pick the option whose
(Not knowing whether you will be born a Delhi industrialist or a landless Dalit, you insure the bottom rung.)
— (1) equal basic liberty; (2) fair equality of opportunity + the difference principle.
= principle 1 must be fully satisfied before 2 is even considered.
(No amount of poverty relief may buy away the right to vote or to free speech.)
— inequality is legitimate only if it lifts the
(A surgeon may earn ten times a clerk if the higher pay is what staffs rural PHCs; reservation is defended on the same logic.)
— a hypothetical agreement (Locke, Rousseau, Kant) that also redistributes
, whom the text calls “the greatest political philosopher of the 20th century,” revived normative theory in
with ‘justice as fairness’. He writes against

, which permits the individual to be sacrificed for the ‘greatest happiness of the greatest number’ — as when a tribal village is displaced for a dam because the aggregate gain is larger. Reviving the
tradition of human dignity, his theory is
: “each person possesses an inviolability founded on justice that even the welfare of society as a whole cannot override.”

is a hypothetical, purely procedural ‘thought experiment’ — not a historical state of nature — in which rational, mutually disinterested agents choose the principles that will govern the basic structure of society. It is the equivalent of drafting a constitution before one knows which caste, class, religion or region one will be born into. Because the choosers are free and equal and the procedure is fair, whatever principles emerge are by definition just: this is the sense in which fairness generates justice.

deprives each chooser of knowledge of his class, caste, race, sex, natural talents and conception of the good — he knows only that he could turn out to be anyone. Not knowing whether he will be a Delhi industrialist or a landless Dalit, he becomes risk-averse and applies the
rule: choose the alternative whose worst possible outcome is the best among the worst outcomes. The society so designed is one you would accept even if ‘your enemy were to assign you your place’.
The chosen principles govern the distribution of
— liberty, rights, opportunity, income, wealth and the social bases of self-respect, which any rational person wants whatever else he wants. First, each person has an
equal right to the most extensive basic liberty
compatible with a like liberty for all. Second, social and economic inequalities must be attached to positions open under
greatest benefit of the least advantaged
: the first must be fully met before the second is entertained, so no measure of poverty relief may be traded against the right to vote or to free speech.

permits inequality only where it improves the position of the worst-off — a surgeon may earn many times a clerk if that differential is what staffs rural health centres, and reservation is defended on exactly this logic. Since the natural distribution of talents is ‘neither just nor unjust’ — what matters is how institutions respond to it — Rawls ‘democratises’ equality, and the advantaged accept the arrangement as rational social insurance taken out behind the veil. It is thus ‘the best possible utilisation of inequality’, distinct from socialism’s ‘equal poverty’.
in form — a hypothetical agreement reviving Locke, Rousseau and Kant — and

in substance, since its second principle redistributes primary goods to secure the least advantaged. Wedding liberty to social equality is precisely how Rawls enriched liberalism, converting it from a doctrine of non-interference into one of positive obligation. As
conceded, political philosophers must now “either work within Rawls’ theory or explain why not.”
Q — Make a comparative assessment of the Greek (Plato and Aristotle) perspective of justice with the Rawlsian concept of justice. (UPSC 2020)
Set out the Greek conception, then the Rawlsian, and judge where they diverge and where they quietly converge.
and the basis of a stable order, but fill it with opposite content.
: “each doing his own task, doing it well and doing it only.”
(A varna-like division — rulers rule, soldiers guard, producers produce; injustice is meddling in another’s station.)
(Distributive, corrective and commutative justice — offices go by merit, not by lot.)
— Plato’s ‘myth of the metals’ and Aristotle’s natural slave; women and slaves stand outside the Polis.
: free and equal individuals choose behind the
, so inequality survives only if it lifts the worst-off.
(You cannot defend caste hierarchy if you may yourself be born at its bottom.)

— Greek justice is teleological and community-centred, Rawlsian justice individualist and egalitarian; yet Indian affirmative action echoes both Aristotle’s ‘unequals unequally’ and the difference principle.
Both traditions treat justice as ‘the first virtue of social institutions’ and as the condition of a stable political order, and both make it the organising question of political philosophy —
opens with the same claim. They diverge entirely on content: the Greeks derive justice from an objective natural order, Rawls from a fair procedure of choice among equals.

defines justice as “each element in society doing its appropriate task, doing it well and doing it only” — every person remaining ‘at the station allotted by nature’, so that reason rules through the philosopher-kings, spirit guards through the auxiliaries and appetite produces. The scheme is varna-like: injustice is meddling in another class’s function. Justice is thus a virtue of the soul writ large upon the city, not a rule of distribution among rights-bearing individuals.
: “treating equals equally and unequals unequally in proportion to their inequalities.” He divides it into
justice (honours and offices allotted according to merit or desert, not by lot),
justice (the judge restoring what a wrong has disturbed) and
justice (fairness in voluntary exchange). Justice for him is a mean, and ‘complete virtue in relation to another’.
‘myth of the metals’ fixes classes by an alleged natural endowment of gold, silver and bronze;

defends slavery as natural and excludes women, slaves and labourers from citizenship of the Polis. Justice for them conserves an ordered hierarchy of function and desert: each is given his ‘due’, but the due is fixed by nature rather than chosen by the persons concerned.
begins instead from the free and equal individual. Justice is not a pre-given natural order but
— whatever rational choosers would agree upon behind the

, ignorant of their caste, class, sex and talents. Because you might be born at the bottom of the hierarchy, no defence of caste or of natural slavery can survive the test. The outcome is equal basic liberty for all, with inequality permitted only where it works to the greatest benefit of the

The Greek view is teleological and community-centred, justice consisting in fitting into a natural whole; the Rawlsian view is individualist and egalitarian, justice consisting in protecting each person’s inviolable rights. Yet both hold that a stable society must rest on justice, and both allow differential treatment: Indian affirmative action, which treats unequals unequally in order to raise the worst-off, draws simultaneously on
difference principle — proving the two traditions are not wholly opposed.
Q — Examine the communitarian critique of Rawls and assess his response in Political Liberalism. (UPSC 2019)
Two halves — first what the communitarians attack in Rawls, then whether his later political turn answers them.
: the person is not an unencumbered chooser but is
(An Indian is born into a language, caste, faith and family before he ever ‘chooses’ anything — ‘we always wear the glasses of community’.)
— strip away a person’s roles, ties and desires behind the veil and “is anything left of the person?” The Rawlsian self is ‘woefully impoverished’.
: different goods must be distributed by different criteria in separate ‘spheres’.
(Money should buy a car but not a medical seat, a verdict or an election ticket.)
— the ‘atomistic’ individual is a fiction; people ‘flourish only within socially established cooperative activity’, so justice cannot be universal.
(“What is rational in the USA may not be rational in Afghanistan.”)
, not metaphysical, claims and rests stability on an
(Hindu, Muslim and secular Indians endorse the same Constitution for their own different reasons.)
— the critique exposes the thinness of the abstract self, but the political turn lets liberalism live with diversity.
Communitarianism is a reaction against liberalism’s stress on the
— the individual conceived as prior to, and independent of, his ends. Its central claim is that the real person is a

: “we never look at reality with naked eyes; we always wear the glasses of community.” An Indian is born into a language, a caste, a faith and a family long before he chooses anything; the self is therefore not prior to its ends but
Liberalism and the Limits of Justice

, attacks Rawls’ ‘conception of the self’ rather than his principles. If the veil of ignorance strips a person of his desires, roles, attachments and conception of the good, “is anything left of the person?” The chooser in the original position is ‘woefully impoverished’ — a ghost with preferences but no identity — and principles chosen by such a phantom cannot bind real, historically located people.
, denies that one formula can govern all goods: “different goods ought to be distributed differently, for different reasons, by different agents.” His

holds that each social good has its own sphere with its own criterion — money may rightly buy a car but must not buy a medical seat, a judicial verdict or an election ticket. Injustice is ‘dominance’, the invasion of one sphere by the currency of another; hence justice is ‘not the science of homogenisation but the art of differentiation’.
faults Rawls’ ‘atomistic’ individual, insisting that the individual’s well-being presupposes the good of the community which makes autonomy possible in the first place;

, holds that people ‘flourish only within socially established cooperative activity’ and that moral reasoning is intelligible only inside a tradition. The shared conclusion is that there is no universal justice — “what is rational in the USA may not be rational in Afghanistan.”
Rawls accommodates the critique without surrendering his principles. He
limits their scope to the basic political institutions
, offering a ‘political, not metaphysical’ conception of justice that takes no position on the good life and therefore presupposes no thin metaphysical self. Stability is then grounded in an

: citizens holding rival comprehensive doctrines — Hindu, Muslim, Christian, secular-liberal — can endorse the same political principles for their own distinct reasons, which makes the agreement moral and durable rather than a merely prudential Hobbesian
. It rests on public reason, reciprocity and the ‘burdens of judgement’ that make reasonable disagreement permanent.

The communitarians rightly expose the thinness of the abstract self and the plurality of social goods, and their influence is visible in multiculturalism and in Indian debates on personal law and group rights. But Rawls’ political turn shows that liberalism can coexist with cultural diversity: justice as fairness survives as the shared political framework of a plural society, even if it can no longer claim to be a universal metaphysics.
Q — Critically examine Nozick’s libertarian entitlement theory of justice as a critique of Rawls.
Explain how Nozick shifts justice from the pattern of holdings to their history, and then weigh the cost of that shift.

(A lopsided income chart is not unjust in itself if every rupee arrived by fair means.)

(Tendulkar is rich because millions freely bought tickets — perfectly just.)

exception where a life-threatening monopoly justifies intervention.

(Nothing in it corrects inherited caste disability or landlessness.)

Any patterned principle — to each according to need, merit or the difference principle — must be continuously enforced against people’s voluntary choices; hence Rawls “compromises liberty for the sake of equality” and violates human dignity.

It follows that the state may not take from A to give to B: “progressive taxation is like bonded labour,” since taxing earnings appropriates hours of a person’s life without consent. Echoing

The only justifiable state is the

The theory ‘makes the welfare of the poor dependent on the justice of the rich’, reducing relief to charity, and in practice defends existing oppression in the name of justice. It ignores that ‘what a person possesses is not due to talent alone’ but to accidents of birth, inheritance and social structure — nothing in the three principles corrects inherited caste disability or landlessness, and rectification is practically unworkable across centuries. The text itself judges it “just a criticism of Rawls from a libertarian point of view — not a sound theory in comparison to Rawls.”

But by reducing the state to a guardian of holdings he leaves the disadvantaged at the mercy of the market, which is why his theory is read as an indispensable foil to Rawls rather than as a self-standing account of justice.
Q — Analyse Amartya Sen’s methodological critique of Rawls — social choice vs rational choice, Niti vs Nyaya, and the realization/capability approach.

Against Rawls’ claim that one unique set of principles would be chosen, Sen offers the parable of the

All three arguments are reasonable and none is decisive, so plural competing principles must be reconciled through public reasoning. In the

Justice means expanding these freedoms, ‘development as freedom’, and removing manifest injustice; the test is not the size of the transfer but whether a girl can actually reach school, read and choose. This reasoning underpins the Human Development Index.

Sen does not overthrow Rawls so much as reorient him — from ideal institutions to real lives, from arrangement to realisation, from the transcendental to the comparative. His critique makes justice practical and actionable, better suited to a diverse world in which perfectly just institutions may never be agreed upon but manifest injustices can still be identified and removed.
Q — Discuss the types and dimensions of justice — distributive (David Miller), procedural vs substantive, retributive, and social/political/economic/legal. (UPSC 2018)

Justice takes different forms depending on what is being distributed, corrected or enforced.

These dimensions interlock rather than compete: legal and political justice supply the framework within which claims can be pressed, while distributive and substantive justice supply the content of those claims. The Indian Preamble’s pledge of ‘justice — social, economic and political’ captures the combination, and the modern welfare state, guided by
