contentText: Syllabus — Justice: conceptions of justice with special reference to Rawls’ theory of justice and its communitarian critique. (UPSC PSIR Paper-1A, Unit 3) Unit Snapshot What this unit covers:  justice as an architectonic and dynamic idea; classical (Plato, Aristotle) and modern theories; the types/dimensions of justice (distributive, procedural vs substantive, retributive); Rawls’ ‘justice as fairness’; and its critiques — Nozick (libertarian), Amartya Sen (methodological) and the communitarians (Sandel, Walzer, Taylor, MacIntyre), with Rawls’ reply in Political Liberalism. Must-know thinkers:  Plato, Aristotle, Hume, David Miller, John Rawls, Robert Nozick, Amartya Sen, Ronald Dworkin, Michael Sandel, Michael Walzer, Charles Taylor, Alasdair MacIntyre, Carole Gilligan, Thomas Pogge, A.V. Dicey. PYQ trend:  Rawls dominates — original position (2013), difference principle (2015), contractual & distributive (2017), justification of discrimination (2018), Rawls enriching liberalism (2021); plus Greek vs Rawlsian (2020), communitarian perspectives (2019) and distributive justice (2018). Master Questions Q — Explain Rawls’ ‘justice as fairness’ — the original position, veil of ignorance, primary goods, maximin, the two principles and lexical order, the difference principle and democratic equality. Is it both contractual and distributive? (UPSC 2013/2015/2017/2018/2021) What it’s asking:  Lay out Rawls’ machinery step by step, then prove it is at once a social contract and a scheme of redistribution. Gist — the spine to recall 1. Premise  — anti-utilitarian, Kantian,  deontological : no person may be sacrificed for the aggregate.  (Utilitarianism could justify displacing a tribal village for a dam because more people gain; Rawls forbids it.) 2. Original position  — a hypothetical ‘thought experiment’ in which rational, mutually disinterested people frame the rules before society exists.  (Like drafting the Constitution before knowing which caste, class or religion you will be born into.) 3. Veil of ignorance + maximin  — stripped of knowledge of class, caste, sex and talent, risk-averse agents pick the option whose  worst  outcome is best.  (Not knowing whether you will be born a Delhi industrialist or a landless Dalit, you insure the bottom rung.) 4. Two principles in lexical order  — (1) equal basic liberty; (2) fair equality of opportunity + the difference principle.  Lexical order  = principle 1 must be fully satisfied before 2 is even considered.  (No amount of poverty relief may buy away the right to vote or to free speech.) 5. Difference principle & democratic equality  — inequality is legitimate only if it lifts the  worst-off .  (A surgeon may earn ten times a clerk if the higher pay is what staffs rural PHCs; reservation is defended on the same logic.) 6. Contractual and distributive  — a hypothetical agreement (Locke, Rousseau, Kant) that also redistributes  primary goods ; this is how Rawls ‘enriched’ liberalism. Model Answer 1. Premise.  John Rawls , whom the text calls “the greatest political philosopher of the 20th century,” revived normative theory in  A Theory of Justice (1971)  with ‘justice as fairness’. He writes against  utilitarianism , which permits the individual to be sacrificed for the ‘greatest happiness of the greatest number’ — as when a tribal village is displaced for a dam because the aggregate gain is larger. Reviving the  Kantian  tradition of human dignity, his theory is  deontological : “each person possesses an inviolability founded on justice that even the welfare of society as a whole cannot override.” 2. Original position.  The  original position  is a hypothetical, purely procedural ‘thought experiment’ — not a historical state of nature — in which rational, mutually disinterested agents choose the principles that will govern the basic structure of society. It is the equivalent of drafting a constitution before one knows which caste, class, religion or region one will be born into. Because the choosers are free and equal and the procedure is fair, whatever principles emerge are by definition just: this is the sense in which fairness generates justice. 3. Veil of ignorance and maximin.  Within the original position the  veil of ignorance  deprives each chooser of knowledge of his class, caste, race, sex, natural talents and conception of the good — he knows only that he could turn out to be anyone. Not knowing whether he will be a Delhi industrialist or a landless Dalit, he becomes risk-averse and applies the  maximin  rule: choose the alternative whose worst possible outcome is the best among the worst outcomes. The society so designed is one you would accept even if ‘your enemy were to assign you your place’. 4. Two principles in lexical order.  The chosen principles govern the distribution of  primary goods  — liberty, rights, opportunity, income, wealth and the social bases of self-respect, which any rational person wants whatever else he wants. First, each person has an  equal right to the most extensive basic liberty  compatible with a like liberty for all. Second, social and economic inequalities must be attached to positions open under  fair equality of opportunity  and arranged to the  greatest benefit of the least advantaged . They hold in  lexical (serial) order : the first must be fully met before the second is entertained, so no measure of poverty relief may be traded against the right to vote or to free speech. 5. Difference principle and democratic equality.  The  difference principle  permits inequality only where it improves the position of the worst-off — a surgeon may earn many times a clerk if that differential is what staffs rural health centres, and reservation is defended on exactly this logic. Since the natural distribution of talents is ‘neither just nor unjust’ — what matters is how institutions respond to it — Rawls ‘democratises’ equality, and the advantaged accept the arrangement as rational social insurance taken out behind the veil. It is thus ‘the best possible utilisation of inequality’, distinct from socialism’s ‘equal poverty’. 6. Contractual and distributive.  The theory is  contractual  in form — a hypothetical agreement reviving Locke, Rousseau and Kant — and  distributive  in substance, since its second principle redistributes primary goods to secure the least advantaged. Wedding liberty to social equality is precisely how Rawls enriched liberalism, converting it from a doctrine of non-interference into one of positive obligation. As  Nozick  conceded, political philosophers must now “either work within Rawls’ theory or explain why not.” Q — Make a comparative assessment of the Greek (Plato and Aristotle) perspective of justice with the Rawlsian concept of justice. (UPSC 2020) What it’s asking:  Set out the Greek conception, then the Rawlsian, and judge where they diverge and where they quietly converge. Gist — the spine to recall 1. Common ground  — both make justice the  first virtue of social institutions  and the basis of a stable order, but fill it with opposite content. 2. Plato — functional harmony : “each doing his own task, doing it well and doing it only.”  (A varna-like division — rulers rule, soldiers guard, producers produce; injustice is meddling in another’s station.) 3. Aristotle — proportional justice : “treat equals equally and unequals unequally.”  (Distributive, corrective and commutative justice — offices go by merit, not by lot.) 4. Both accept natural inequality  — Plato’s ‘myth of the metals’ and Aristotle’s natural slave; women and slaves stand outside the Polis. 5. Rawls — fairness, not station : free and equal individuals choose behind the  veil of ignorance , so inequality survives only if it lifts the worst-off.  (You cannot defend caste hierarchy if you may yourself be born at its bottom.) 6. Assessment  — Greek justice is teleological and community-centred, Rawlsian justice individualist and egalitarian; yet Indian affirmative action echoes both Aristotle’s ‘unequals unequally’ and the difference principle. Model Answer 1. Common ground.  Both traditions treat justice as ‘the first virtue of social institutions’ and as the condition of a stable political order, and both make it the organising question of political philosophy —  The Republic  is subtitled ‘concerning justice’ and  A Theory of Justice  opens with the same claim. They diverge entirely on content: the Greeks derive justice from an objective natural order, Rawls from a fair procedure of choice among equals. 2. Plato — functional harmony.  Plato  in  The Republic  defines justice as “each element in society doing its appropriate task, doing it well and doing it only” — every person remaining ‘at the station allotted by nature’, so that reason rules through the philosopher-kings, spirit guards through the auxiliaries and appetite produces. The scheme is varna-like: injustice is meddling in another class’s function. Justice is thus a virtue of the soul writ large upon the city, not a rule of distribution among rights-bearing individuals. 3. Aristotle — proportional justice.  Aristotle  makes justice  proportional : “treating equals equally and unequals unequally in proportion to their inequalities.” He divides it into  distributive  justice (honours and offices allotted according to merit or desert, not by lot),  corrective  justice (the judge restoring what a wrong has disturbed) and  commutative  justice (fairness in voluntary exchange). Justice for him is a mean, and ‘complete virtue in relation to another’. 4. Both accept natural inequality.  Neither Greek is an egalitarian.  Plato’s  ‘myth of the metals’ fixes classes by an alleged natural endowment of gold, silver and bronze;  Aristotle  defends slavery as natural and excludes women, slaves and labourers from citizenship of the Polis. Justice for them conserves an ordered hierarchy of function and desert: each is given his ‘due’, but the due is fixed by nature rather than chosen by the persons concerned. 5. Rawls — fairness, not station.  Rawls  begins instead from the free and equal individual. Justice is not a pre-given natural order but  fairness  — whatever rational choosers would agree upon behind the  veil of ignorance , ignorant of their caste, class, sex and talents. Because you might be born at the bottom of the hierarchy, no defence of caste or of natural slavery can survive the test. The outcome is equal basic liberty for all, with inequality permitted only where it works to the greatest benefit of the  least advantaged . 6. Assessment.  The Greek view is teleological and community-centred, justice consisting in fitting into a natural whole; the Rawlsian view is individualist and egalitarian, justice consisting in protecting each person’s inviolable rights. Yet both hold that a stable society must rest on justice, and both allow differential treatment: Indian affirmative action, which treats unequals unequally in order to raise the worst-off, draws simultaneously on  Aristotle’s  proportional justice and  Rawls’  difference principle — proving the two traditions are not wholly opposed. Q — Examine the communitarian critique of Rawls and assess his response in Political Liberalism. (UPSC 2019) What it’s asking:  Two halves — first what the communitarians attack in Rawls, then whether his later political turn answers them. Gist — the spine to recall 1. Core claim — the situated self : the person is not an unencumbered chooser but is  constituted  by community.  (An Indian is born into a language, caste, faith and family before he ever ‘chooses’ anything — ‘we always wear the glasses of community’.) 2. Sandel  — strip away a person’s roles, ties and desires behind the veil and “is anything left of the person?” The Rawlsian self is ‘woefully impoverished’. 3. Walzer — complex equality : different goods must be distributed by different criteria in separate ‘spheres’.  (Money should buy a car but not a medical seat, a verdict or an election ticket.) 4. Taylor & MacIntyre  — the ‘atomistic’ individual is a fiction; people ‘flourish only within socially established cooperative activity’, so justice cannot be universal.  (“What is rational in the USA may not be rational in Afghanistan.”) 5. Rawls’ reply  — in  Political Liberalism  he narrows the theory to  political , not metaphysical, claims and rests stability on an  overlapping consensus .  (Hindu, Muslim and secular Indians endorse the same Constitution for their own different reasons.) 6. Conclusion  — the critique exposes the thinness of the abstract self, but the political turn lets liberalism live with diversity. Model Answer 1. Core claim — the situated self.  Communitarianism is a reaction against liberalism’s stress on the  autonomous, unencumbered self  — the individual conceived as prior to, and independent of, his ends. Its central claim is that the real person is a  ‘situated (embedded) self’ : “we never look at reality with naked eyes; we always wear the glasses of community.” An Indian is born into a language, a caste, a faith and a family long before he chooses anything; the self is therefore not prior to its ends but  constituted by them . 2. Sandel.  Michael Sandel , in  Liberalism and the Limits of Justice , attacks Rawls’ ‘conception of the self’ rather than his principles. If the veil of ignorance strips a person of his desires, roles, attachments and conception of the good, “is anything left of the person?” The chooser in the original position is ‘woefully impoverished’ — a ghost with preferences but no identity — and principles chosen by such a phantom cannot bind real, historically located people. 3. Walzer — complex equality.  Michael Walzer , in  Spheres of Justice , denies that one formula can govern all goods: “different goods ought to be distributed differently, for different reasons, by different agents.” His  complex equality  holds that each social good has its own sphere with its own criterion — money may rightly buy a car but must not buy a medical seat, a judicial verdict or an election ticket. Injustice is ‘dominance’, the invasion of one sphere by the currency of another; hence justice is ‘not the science of homogenisation but the art of differentiation’. 4. Taylor and MacIntyre.  Charles Taylor  faults Rawls’ ‘atomistic’ individual, insisting that the individual’s well-being presupposes the good of the community which makes autonomy possible in the first place;  Alasdair MacIntyre , in  After Virtue , holds that people ‘flourish only within socially established cooperative activity’ and that moral reasoning is intelligible only inside a tradition. The shared conclusion is that there is no universal justice — “what is rational in the USA may not be rational in Afghanistan.” 5. Rawls’ reply.  In  Political Liberalism  Rawls accommodates the critique without surrendering his principles. He  limits their scope to the basic political institutions , offering a ‘political, not metaphysical’ conception of justice that takes no position on the good life and therefore presupposes no thin metaphysical self. Stability is then grounded in an  overlapping consensus : citizens holding rival comprehensive doctrines — Hindu, Muslim, Christian, secular-liberal — can endorse the same political principles for their own distinct reasons, which makes the agreement moral and durable rather than a merely prudential Hobbesian  modus vivendi . It rests on public reason, reciprocity and the ‘burdens of judgement’ that make reasonable disagreement permanent. 6. Conclusion.  The communitarians rightly expose the thinness of the abstract self and the plurality of social goods, and their influence is visible in multiculturalism and in Indian debates on personal law and group rights. But Rawls’ political turn shows that liberalism can coexist with cultural diversity: justice as fairness survives as the shared political framework of a plural society, even if it can no longer claim to be a universal metaphysics. Q — Critically examine Nozick’s libertarian entitlement theory of justice as a critique of Rawls. What it’s asking:  Explain how Nozick shifts justice from the pattern of holdings to their history, and then weigh the cost of that shift. Gist — the spine to recall 1. Historical, not patterned  — the  entitlement theory  judges  how  you got what you hold, not the shape of the final distribution.  (A lopsided income chart is not unjust in itself if every rupee arrived by fair means.) 2. Three principles  — just  acquisition , just  transfer  and  rectification  of past wrongs; pass all three and the title is absolute.  (Tendulkar is rich because millions freely bought tickets — perfectly just.) 3. Redistribution is illegitimate  — “progressive taxation is like bonded labour”; echoing  Hayek , ‘social justice is a mirage’, since only persons and not outcomes can be just. 4. Minimal state  — a ‘night-watchman’ confined to protection and contract enforcement, with the  single-well  exception where a life-threatening monopoly justifies intervention. 5. Critique  — it ‘makes the welfare of the poor depend on the justice of the rich’ and ignores that holdings owe as much to chance as to talent.  (Nothing in it corrects inherited caste disability or landlessness.) 6. Conclusion  — a powerful foil to Rawls rather than a self-standing theory of justice. Model Answer 1. Historical, not patterned.  Robert Nozick , in  Anarchy, State and Utopia (1974) , answers Rawls with the  entitlement theory . Justice is  historical , not  patterned : a distribution is just if it arose through a sequence of just steps, whatever shape it finally takes, so a lopsided income chart is not unjust in itself. Any patterned principle — to each according to need, merit or the difference principle — must be continuously enforced against people’s voluntary choices; hence Rawls “compromises liberty for the sake of equality” and violates human dignity. 2. Three principles.  Entitlement rests on three rules: (1)  just acquisition  — original appropriation from nature is legitimate so long as no one else is made worse off; (2)  just transfer  — voluntary exchange and gift, which treat the other as an end and never merely as a means, a Kantian premise Nozick shares with Rawls; and (3)  rectification  — correction of holdings tainted by past theft or conquest. If a holding survives all three tests the owner has an absolute right to it.  Sachin Tendulkar’s  wealth, arising because millions freely paid to watch him bat, is the model case of a just holding. 3. Redistribution is illegitimate.  It follows that the state may not take from A to give to B: “progressive taxation is like bonded labour,” since taxing earnings appropriates hours of a person’s life without consent. Echoing  F.A. Hayek , Nozick treats  ‘social justice as a mirage’  — only human actions, not impersonal market outcomes, can be called just or unjust, and no one designed the distribution that redistribution proposes to correct. 4. Minimal state.  The only justifiable state is the  minimal or ‘night-watchman’ state , limited to the protection of person and property, the enforcement of contracts and defence, with ‘no role in distributive justice’; anything more extensive violates rights. His single concession is the  single-well  case: where one person’s monopoly over the only source of water threatens life itself, intervention becomes permissible — an admission that even libertarian rights bend before survival. 5. Critique.  The theory ‘makes the welfare of the poor dependent on the justice of the rich’, reducing relief to charity, and in practice defends existing oppression in the name of justice. It ignores that ‘what a person possesses is not due to talent alone’ but to accidents of birth, inheritance and social structure — nothing in the three principles corrects inherited caste disability or landlessness, and rectification is practically unworkable across centuries. The text itself judges it “just a criticism of Rawls from a libertarian point of view — not a sound theory in comparison to Rawls.” 6. Conclusion.  Nozick powerfully defends liberty, property and the separateness of persons against Rawlsian redistribution, and forces liberalism to justify every coercive transfer. But by reducing the state to a guardian of holdings he leaves the disadvantaged at the mercy of the market, which is why his theory is read as an indispensable foil to Rawls rather than as a self-standing account of justice. Q — Analyse Amartya Sen’s methodological critique of Rawls — social choice vs rational choice, Niti vs Nyaya, and the realization/capability approach. What it’s asking:  Show that Sen attacks Rawls’ method rather than his goal, and set out what he puts in its place. Gist — the spine to recall 1. Nature of the quarrel  —  methodological , not about ends: Sen shares the egalitarian goal but denies that justice can be deduced from an imaginary bargain. 2. Social choice > rational choice  — ‘real persons negotiating in real-life situations’ replace ‘abstract individuals in abstract situations’.  (Ask actual Indian citizens about MGNREGA, not phantoms behind a veil.) 3. Niti vs Nyaya  —  Niti  is the perfect rulebook,  Nyaya  is justice as it actually turns out in people’s lives.  (A flawless Right to Education Act is Niti; children actually learning to read is Nyaya.) 4. No single formula  — the  three children and a flute : Carla (can play it), Bob (has no other toy), Ann (made it) — utilitarian, egalitarian and libertarian claims, all reasonable, none absolute. 5. Capability approach  — justice means expanding real freedoms, ‘development as freedom’, and removing manifest injustice.  (Not the size of the transfer but whether a girl can actually reach school and read.) 6. Conclusion  — Sen reorients Rawls from ideal institutions to real lives, making justice comparative rather than transcendental. Model Answer 1. Nature of the quarrel.  Amartya Sen’s  objection in  The Idea of Justice (2009)  is  methodological  rather than substantive: he accepts Rawls’ egalitarian purpose and calls him the outstanding political philosopher of the age, but denies that a workable theory of justice can be deduced from a hypothetical bargain among idealised agents. Rawls answers ‘what would perfectly just institutions look like?’; Sen holds that the urgent question is ‘how do we make this society less unjust than it is?’ 2. Social choice over rational choice.  Sen rejects Rawls’  rational choice  framework — ‘abstract individuals negotiating in abstract situations’ — in favour of the  social choice  tradition of Condorcet and Arrow: ‘real persons negotiating in real-life situations’, reasoning publicly and comparing feasible alternatives. Judgments on MGNREGA or on reservation must issue from actual public reasoning among affected citizens, not from phantoms behind a veil; and Sen adds the  ‘impartial spectator’  borrowed from Adam Smith to correct parochial bias without pretending to unanimity. 3. Niti versus Nyaya.  Sen recovers two Sanskrit terms.  Niti  denotes organisational propriety and behavioural correctness — the perfect rulebook, which is where Rawls’ ‘justice as fairness’ belongs, being procedural, institutional and  transcendental .  Nyaya  denotes justice as it is actually  realised  in the lives people are able to lead. A flawless Right to Education Act is Niti; whether children in a Bihar village can actually read is Nyaya. Since ‘substance is more important than procedure’, Sen’s approach is  consequentialist  where Rawls’ is deontological — matsyanyaya, the ‘justice of the fish’ in which the big devour the small, must be prevented in fact and not merely prohibited on paper. 4. No single formula.  Against Rawls’ claim that one unique set of principles would be chosen, Sen offers the parable of the  three children and a flute : Carla claims it because she alone can play it (the utilitarian or best-use claim), Bob because he is poorest and has no other toy (the egalitarian claim), and Ann because she made it with her own hands (the libertarian claim). All three arguments are reasonable and none is decisive, so plural competing principles must be reconciled through public reasoning. In the  Krishna–Arjuna  debate of the Gita he likewise finds Arjuna’s consequentialist anxiety — that countless lives would be destroyed — as compelling as Krishna’s deontological insistence on duty. 5. Capability approach.  Sen therefore substitutes a  realization-focused capability approach : what matters is not the bundle of primary goods a person holds but the  capabilities  — the real freedoms — he has to be and to do what he has reason to value, since equal income buys very unequal functioning for a disabled or a socially excluded person. Justice means expanding these freedoms, ‘development as freedom’, and removing manifest injustice; the test is not the size of the transfer but whether a girl can actually reach school, read and choose. This reasoning underpins the Human Development Index. 6. Conclusion.  Sen does not overthrow Rawls so much as reorient him — from ideal institutions to real lives, from arrangement to realisation, from the transcendental to the comparative. His critique makes justice practical and actionable, better suited to a diverse world in which perfectly just institutions may never be agreed upon but manifest injustices can still be identified and removed. Q — Discuss the types and dimensions of justice — distributive (David Miller), procedural vs substantive, retributive, and social/political/economic/legal. (UPSC 2018) What it’s asking:  Classify the forms justice takes and show how each answers a different question about sharing, procedure or punishment. Gist — the spine to recall 1. Distributive justice  — the fair sharing of resources and opportunities, the defining concern of the welfare state.  (Who gets the college seat, the subsidised grain, the reserved post?) 2. Miller’s three principles  — distribution by  rights  (hierarchical order, Hume), by  desert  (competitive market, Spencer) and by  need  (solidarity community, Kropotkin) — need being ‘the most appropriate’. 3. Procedural vs substantive  — fair rules versus a fair outcome.  (‘Procedure established by law’ vs ‘due process’ — Maneka Gandhi moved Article 21 from the first to the second.) 4. Retributive → restorative  — punishment proportioned to the crime (Aristotle, Kant, Hegel), criticised for ignoring the offender, yielding to reform and reconciliation.  (Juvenile boards and plea bargaining.) 5. Social / political / economic / legal  — equal access regardless of birth; power-sharing (suffrage, reservation); a dignified livelihood; and enforcement of law, which ‘may or may not’ be morally just.  (Untouchability and apartheid were legal but unjust.) 6. Conclusion  — the dimensions interlock; the modern welfare state, guided by Rawls and Sen, tilts from procedure toward substantive, need-based justice. Model Answer 1. Distributive justice.  Justice takes different forms depending on what is being distributed, corrected or enforced.  Distributive justice  concerns the fair allocation of resources, offices and opportunities — who gets the college seat, the subsidised grain, the reserved post — and is the defining concern of the modern welfare state. Schools differ sharply on its scope: classical liberals want minimal intervention,  Nozick  almost none,  Rawls  the difference principle, and  Sen  the building of capabilities. 2. Miller’s three principles.  David Miller , in  Social Justice , argues that each criterion of distribution belongs to a type of society: distribution by  rights  suits a hierarchical order and is associated with  Hume ; by  desert  suits a competitive market society and  Spencer ; and by  need  suits a solidarity community and  Kropotkin . Miller holds the last to be ‘the most appropriate’, which aligns social justice with welfare provision rather than with mere reward for merit. 3. Procedural versus substantive.  Procedural justice  operates ‘at the level of application’ — the letter of the law, equality before law, ‘procedure established by law’ — and inspires the minimal state, since it demands only that the rules be applied impartially.  Substantive justice  looks to the  outcome  — the spirit of the law, ‘due process’ — and encourages state intervention. The Indian illustration is decisive: in  Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978)  the Supreme Court read Article 21 as requiring a procedure that is ‘just, fair and reasonable’, shifting Indian constitutional law from procedural to substantive justice. 4. Retributive to restorative.  Retributive justice , rooted in  Aristotle ,  Kant  and  Hegel , fixes punishment in proportion to the crime and treats the penalty as the criminal’s own desert rather than as a mere instrument of deterrence. It is criticised for attending only to the act while ignoring the offender’s circumstances and the victim’s healing, and so gives way to  restorative and transformative justice , which aim at reform, reparation and reconciliation — the logic of juvenile justice boards, plea bargaining and truth commissions. 5. Social, political, economic and legal.  Social justice  means equal access to goods and opportunities irrespective of the circumstances of birth — caste, sex, religion or region.  Political justice  concerns the sharing of power: universal suffrage, free elections and reservation of seats.  Economic justice  demands equal opportunity to earn a dignified livelihood and freedom from exploitation.  Legal justice  is the impartial enforcement of established law, which ‘may or may not’ be morally just — untouchability in India and apartheid in South Africa were perfectly legal and wholly unjust — which is why legal justice must always be tested against social justice. 6. Conclusion.  These dimensions interlock rather than compete: legal and political justice supply the framework within which claims can be pressed, while distributive and substantive justice supply the content of those claims. The Indian Preamble’s pledge of ‘justice — social, economic and political’ captures the combination, and the modern welfare state, guided by  Rawls  and  Sen , tilts the balance decisively from mere procedure toward substantive, need-based justice. Q — “Justice is an architectonic and dynamic idea.” Discuss its importance in political philosophy and how conceptions of justice have evolved. What it’s asking:  Unpack the two adjectives — why justice is foundational, and why its content keeps moving. Gist — the spine to recall 1. Meaning  — from the Latin  jus  (a bond) and  jungere  (to bind): justice binds people into a fair order by giving each his due.  Rawls : ‘the first virtue of social institutions’. 2. Architectonic  — the master value that organises every other concept: liberty, equality and rights are all argued out as questions of justice.  ( The Republic  is subtitled ‘concerning justice’.) 3. Basis of obligation  — people obey institutions “only when they find them just”, so justice underwrites legitimacy and stability.  (From Champaran to today’s protest movements, resistance is framed as injustice, not illegality.) 4. Dynamic  — the ideal is fixed but our grasp of it is ‘a continuous process’ tracking social consciousness ( D.D. Raphael ).  (Slavery, untouchability and the subordination of women were once ‘just’; all are now condemned.) 5. Evolution  — Plato (natural station) → Aristotle (proportion) → Hobbes (the sovereign’s command) → utilitarians (hedonistic calculus) → Marx (ending class exploitation) → today ‘redistribution based on affirmative action’. 6. Conclusion  — architectonic as the foundation of legitimate order, dynamic as a moving frontier of moral progress. Model Answer 1. Meaning.  Derived from the Latin  jus  (a bond) and  jungere  (to bind), justice ‘binds people into a fair order of relationships by giving each their due’. Its classic formulation is  suum cuique  — to each his own — but the content of that ‘own’ is precisely what every theory disputes.  Rawls  states its standing definitively: “justice is the first virtue of social institutions, as truth is of systems of thought.” 2. Architectonic.  Justice is the  master or foundational value  around which the whole of Western political philosophy is organised: liberty, equality, rights, property and punishment are ultimately argued out as questions about what is just.  Plato’s   Republic  is subtitled ‘concerning justice’, and  Aristotle  makes it ‘complete virtue in relation to another’. It is architectonic in the builder’s sense — the design principle that determines how all the other values are fitted together. 3. Basis of obligation.  Its centrality is practical and not merely academic: people accept and obey institutions “only when they find them just”, so justice underpins political obligation, legitimacy and stability itself. Resistance is characteristically framed as a charge of injustice rather than of illegality — from Champaran and the Salt Satyagraha to contemporary farm and anti-corruption agitations — which is why an unjust order must rest on coercion where a just one rests on consent. 4. Dynamic.  Although justice embodies an ideal ‘akin to absolute truth’, our apprehension of it is ‘a continuous process’ that tracks changing  social consciousness .  D.D. Raphael  calls this ‘modern consciousness’: slavery and serfdom were once held just in Europe, untouchability in India, and the subordination of women almost everywhere — all are now condemned. A defensible conception of justice must therefore rest on  reason  read in the light of the prevailing social consciousness, which makes justice a moving rather than a settled standard. 5. Evolution.  Conceptions have accordingly shifted: from  Plato  (each at the station allotted by nature) and  Aristotle  (proportional equality), through  Hobbes  (justice is obedience to the sovereign’s command, there being no justice in the state of nature) and the  utilitarians  (the hedonistic calculus of the greatest happiness), to the  Marxists  (justice as the abolition of class exploitation) and, in our own time, to ‘redistribution based on affirmative action’ as elaborated by  Rawls  and  Sen . 6. Conclusion.  As an architectonic idea justice is the foundation of legitimate political order, the value from which all the others take their bearings; as a dynamic idea it is a moving frontier of moral progress that each generation must redraw. That is why every major work of political philosophy, from Plato to Rawls and Sen, turns out on inspection to be a theory of justice. Revision Box — facts, keywords & quotes Rawls : ‘justice is the first virtue of social institutions’; justice = fairness; deontological (Kantian). Original position  +  veil of ignorance  +  maximin  → choose fair principles not knowing your place. Two principles:  (1) equal basic liberty; (2) fair equality of opportunity + difference principle (help the least advantaged) — in lexical order. Primary goods:  liberty, rights, income, wealth, self-respect. Plato : justice = each doing his own duty (station by nature);  Aristotle : treat equals equally, unequals unequally. Nozick ,  Anarchy, State and Utopia : entitlement theory (acquisition/transfer/rectification); ‘tax = forced labour’; minimal state. ‘Social justice is a mirage’ = Hayek  (not Nozick — source typo). Amartya Sen : social choice > rational choice; Niti vs Nyaya (realization-focused); three children & a flute; capability approach. Communitarians  (Sandel, Walzer, Taylor, MacIntyre): the ‘situated self’; ‘justice is the art of differentiation, not homogenisation’. Sandel ,  Liberalism and the Limits of Justice ;  Walzer ,  Spheres of Justice  (complex equality). Rawls’ reply ,  Political Liberalism : political (not metaphysical) conception; overlapping consensus (vs modus vivendi). David Miller : 3 principles of distributive justice — rights (Hume), desert (Spencer), need (Kropotkin). Procedural  (procedure established by law) vs  substantive  (due process); Maneka Gandhi expanded Art.21. The Law of Peoples : Rawls does NOT extend the difference principle between societies; ‘decent peoples’. Carole Gilligan ,  In a Different Voice : ‘ethics of care’ — justice is masculinist. Last-Minute Revision Sheet (1 page) Rawls (M1):  original position + veil of ignorance + maximin → 2 principles (equal liberty; fair opportunity + difference principle) in lexical order; contractual + distributive; democratic equality. Greek vs Rawls (M2):  Plato (station by nature) & Aristotle (proportional) justify hierarchy; Rawls builds egalitarian, individual-rights justice. Communitarian critique (M3):  Sandel/Walzer/Taylor/MacIntyre — situated self, complex equality; Rawls’ reply = political conception + overlapping consensus. Nozick (M4):  entitlement theory (acquisition/transfer/rectification); minimal state; tax = forced labour; welfare of poor left to the rich. Sen (M5):  social choice > rational choice; Niti vs Nyaya; capability / ‘development as freedom’; three children & a flute. Dimensions (M6):  distributive (Miller: rights/desert/need), procedural vs substantive (Maneka Gandhi), retributive; social/political/economic/legal. Architectonic & dynamic (M7):  first virtue of institutions; evolves with social consciousness (Raphael); Plato→utilitarians→Marx→affirmative action. Killer quotes:  Rawls — ‘each person possesses an inviolability founded on justice’; Sandel — ‘is anything left of the person?’; Walzer — ‘different goods distributed differently’; Hayek — ‘social justice is a mirage’. Previous Year Questions — coverage map 2021 — How Rawls enriched the idea of justice in liberalism → M1. 2020 — Greek perspective vs Rawlsian concept of justice → M2. 2019 — Communitarian perspectives on justice → M3. 2018 — Distributive Justice → M6. 2018 — Rawls’ justification of discrimination → M1. 2017 — Rawls’ theory is contractual and distributive → M1. 2015 — ‘Difference principle’ → M1. 2013 — ‘Original Position’ → M1. Model Qs (Nozick vs communitarian self, procedural vs substantive) → M4 / M6.

title: 04 - Equality

content.text: Syllabus — Equality: social, political and economic; relationship between equality and freedom; affirmative action. (UPSC PSIR Paper-1A, Unit 4)

the meaning and evolution of equality (formal, of opportunity, of outcome); the views of Laski, Barker and Bryan Turner; the schools of thought (liberal — welfare/resources/capability, Marxist, communitarian, multiculturalist); the dimensions of equality (legal, political, economic, social); affirmative action; and the relation of equality with liberty and justice, including Berlin’s value pluralism.

Laski, Barker, Bryan Turner, Aristotle, Rousseau, Marx, Engels, Hayek, Ronald Dworkin, Amartya Sen, Martha Nussbaum, Michael Walzer, Will Kymlicka, Bhikhu Parekh, R.H. Tawney, Hobhouse, Isaiah Berlin, Rawls.
equality of outcome, Aristotle’s conception, affirmative action, the liberty–equality relationship, and Berlin’s value pluralism are the recurring themes.
Q — Trace the historical evolution and meaning of equality, and compare the views of Laski, Barker and Bryan Turner.
Three tasks — how equality became a political demand, what it actually means, and how the three thinkers define it.
— inequality of ‘race, ancestry, sex, religion, wealth or knowledge’ was long thought natural, until the
(Caste rank was defended as the divinely ordained order until the social reformers attacked it.)
the opportunity to develop one’s personality.
(Abolishing untouchability is the negative face; free schooling and mid-day meals the positive.)
— four elements: no special privilege, adequate opportunity (above all education), access to social benefits, no exploitation.
(Economic equality is ‘a problem of proportion’ — not identical incomes but a defensible spread.)
value, flowing from the development of personality.
(Whatever right is guaranteed to me must be guaranteed to you in the same measure.)
— four types: fundamental, opportunity, condition, outcome.
(Equal dignity → an open entrance exam → equal coaching before it → equal result after it.)
— equality matures from a negative demand (Laski) to a developmental ideal (Barker) to a graded modern typology (Turner).

Inequality — by ‘race, ancestry, sex, religion, wealth or knowledge’ — was for most of history treated as natural and therefore beyond criticism, as caste rank was defended in India as a divinely ordained order. The
— turned equality into a political demand, directed first against feudal and clerical privilege and then, in the nineteenth century, extended to
J.S. Mill, T.H. Green and Marx
The concept is defined twice over.
it is the end of special privileges, so that no one may claim advantage by birth — the logic of abolishing untouchability.

it is the availability to each person of the opportunity to develop his or her personality — the logic of free schooling and mid-day meals. Because the two faces pull in different directions, equality remains an
defines equality through four elements: (1) the
— ‘the will of one is equal to the will of any other’; (2)
for all, especially education, ‘for the power that counts is the power to use knowledge’; (3)
with no bar of birth; and (4) the
absence of economic and social exploitation
. On the economic side he concedes it is ‘largely a problem of proportion’, not of identical incomes.
treats equality not as an end in itself but as a

— ‘derivative from the supreme value of the development of personality’. Its operative rule is reciprocity: “whatever rights are guaranteed to me shall also, and in the same measure, be guaranteed to others.” Equality is thus justified instrumentally, by what it enables each personality to become.
) gives the most comprehensive modern account, distinguishing four types: (1)
of persons, that is equal human dignity and worth; (2)
, open access on merit and talent, as in a competitive entrance examination; (3)
, which equalises the starting points — the coaching, nutrition and schooling that precede the exam; and (4)

Read together, the three show equality maturing from a negative demand (Laski’s end of privilege) to a positive, developmental ideal (Barker’s personality) and finally to a graded modern typology (Turner) that sets up the central debate between opportunity and outcome.
Q — “Equality of outcome, though the most radical face of egalitarianism, threatens liberty.” Critically examine, distinguishing formal equality, equality of opportunity and equality of outcome.
Separate the three forms of equality, then judge whether the most radical of them — outcome — destroys liberty.
— ‘equality is always just; only inequalities need justification’, and the demand rises in three stages.
(Same law → same starting line → same finishing line.)
— ‘all men are created equal’: equality before law, but essentially
(An equal right to dine in an expensive restaurant is worthless if you cannot pay the bill; the queue rule ‘first come, first served’ is fair but blind to need.)
— ‘an equal chance to become unequal’: strip away social handicaps, accept natural difference.
(No child should start the race halfway down the track — hence free schooling and mid-day meals before the entrance exam.)
: ‘from each according to his ability, to each according to his needs’.
(Not an equal chance at the seat, but an equal share of the harvest.)
: people differ, so equal treatment must yield inequality; outcome equality needs coercive social engineering and kills incentive.
counters that treating unequals equally is itself unjust.
— formal equality is free but hollow, outcome equality deep but coercive;
difference principle is offered as the mean.

Egalitarianism rests on the presumption that ‘equality is always just; only inequalities need justification’ — the burden of proof lies on whoever defends a difference. On that premise equality has assumed three progressively radical forms, each demanding more of the state: the same law, then the same starting line, then the same finishing line.

Formal or legal equality asserts a common human essence — ‘all men are created equal’ (US Declaration), ‘men are born free and equal in rights’ (French Declaration) — and is expressed as equality before law, the cornerstone of the

: it grants an equal right to dine in an expensive restaurant while ignoring whether one has the money, and leaves ‘institutionalised’ discrimination untouched. In the queue, ‘first come, first served’ is impeccably fair and wholly insensitive to need.

and amounts to ‘an equal opportunity to become unequal’: natural inequality of talent and effort is accepted, while social inequality of poverty and poor schooling is removed, so that no one ‘starts the race halfway down the track’. It is the tenet of
, realised through education, health and housing — free schooling and mid-day meals precede the common entrance examination.
Equality of outcome is ‘the most radical and controversial face of egalitarianism’ — not an equal start but an equal finish, so that ‘all runners finish in line together’.
feared that inequality would enslave the poor and corrupt the rich, and
captured the ideal in ‘from each according to his ability, to each according to his needs’ — distribution keyed to need rather than to contribution or to chance.

objects that ‘people are very different, so to treat them equally must result in inequality — the only way to make them equal is to treat them differently’; equality of outcome therefore requires coercive ‘social engineering’, destroys incentive and ‘remains utopia’. The reply is

: ‘injustice arises not only when equals are treated unequally, but when unequals are treated equally’ — so a measure of differential treatment is the price of real equality, not an assault on freedom.

The three forms trade off against liberty differently: formal equality is fully compatible with liberty but hollow; equality of opportunity is the liberal mean; equality of outcome secures the deepest equality but at the cost of coercion — which is why
difference principle, permitting only those inequalities that benefit the least advantaged, is offered as the balance between the two extremes.
Q — Critically examine the schools of thought on equality — liberal (welfare, resources, capability), Marxist, communitarian and multiculturalist.
Compare four schools by asking each the same question — equality of WHAT, and among whom.
— liberals agree on equality but differ on what to equalise: welfare (utilitarians) or
(Equal cash to a healthy man and a dialysis patient is equal resources, not equal welfare.)
compensates what you did not choose, not what you did.
(Born with a disability = brute luck, compensated; losing money on a bet = option luck, not.)
: equalise ‘the ability to do what one wants’, since people convert resources differently.
(‘Fasting is a choice, hunger is a deprivation’ — same empty stomach, opposite freedoms.)
: ‘we want to abolish classes, and in this sense we are for equality’ — impossible without abolishing private ownership of the means of production.
blocks advantage in one sphere from buying another.
(Wealth may buy a car, it must not buy a medical seat or a verdict.)
— the schools move outward from the individual to the group, showing genuine equality is plural, not simple.
Liberals agree that persons must be treated as equals but divide over the ‘currency’ of equality.
, the utilitarian answer, equates welfare with pleasure and would transfer resources until satisfactions are level — which rewards expensive tastes.
, holding that ‘equality is more fundamental than liberty — liberty is hollow without it’.
holds people responsible only for choices made in
ones, and therefore insists on a
: his ‘envy test’ and his ambition- and endowment-sensitive auction distinguish
— the disability or the caste one is born into, which must be compensated — from
, the loss on a wager freely taken, which must not. The aim is a distribution that is ‘equitable, not merely equal’.

— ‘the ability to do what one wants to do’ — because individuals differ in converting identical resources into actual functionings: the same grain feeds a healthy adult and fails a parasite-ridden child. The approach is social-choice based and realization-focused, and its sharpest formulation is that ‘fasting is a choice, hunger is a deprivation’ — the outcome is identical, the freedom is not. Hence development is itself ‘freedom’.

makes the abolition of classes central — ‘we want to abolish classes, and in this sense we are for equality’ — which is impossible without abolishing private ownership of the means of production. Legal and political equality alone is a bourgeois form: so long as one class owns the productive apparatus, formal equality of rights merely legitimises substantive domination.

: ‘sometimes we equalise people by differentiating’, and each social good — money, office, health, honour — has its own distributive sphere, so that advantage in one must be blocked from buying advantage in another. Wealth may legitimately buy a car; it must not buy a medical seat or a favourable verdict.
) relocate equality in cultures and demand
, Kymlicka’s ‘luck egalitarianism’ treating birth into a minority culture as ‘bad brute luck’ deserving special protection.

The schools move outward from the individual to the group: liberals refine what each person should have (welfare → resources → capability), Marxists locate equality in the abolition of class, and communitarians and multiculturalists relocate it in spheres and cultures — together showing that genuine equality is plural, not simple.
Q — Discuss the dimensions of equality — legal, political, economic and social — and how they combine into formal and substantive equality.
List the four working dimensions of equality, then show which two make ‘formal’ equality and which two make ‘substantive’ equality.
— rule of law plus ‘equality before law’ and ‘equal protection of the laws’.
(Equal rights are useless without equal power to vindicate them — hence free legal aid.)
— ‘one person, one vote’ with no bar to office; yet
: ‘the many have always been governed by the few’.
(Every vote weighs the same, but money, birth and bureaucracy still weigh more.)
— a level playing field of access to wealth;
: it needs ‘the presence of abilities, not merely the absence of disabilities’.
(Progressive taxation funding schools and health — Laski’s ‘problem of proportion’.)
— ends discrimination by caste, creed, religion or sex, and is ‘enhanced by affirmative action’.
(Temple entry and common water sources, not merely an equal wage.)
(The queue: ‘first come, first served’ is formal; a separate line for the elderly and the disabled is substantive.)
— the welfare state’s task is to convert formal equality into substantive equality.
Legal equality grants equal legal status to all: the
, supplemented by ‘equality before law’ and ‘equal protection of the laws’.

regarded it as the primary mark of an equal society. Its limit is decisive: it is ‘meaningless without equal opportunity to get justice — all may possess equal rights but not equal power to vindicate them’, which is why free legal aid, not merely an open court, is required.
Political equality means equal political rights on a ‘one person, one vote’ basis, with no bar of birth or property to holding office.
nevertheless notes that the ‘many have always been governed by the few’: political inequality has rested successively on knowledge (
), birth (aristocracy), money (plutocracy) and race, and real power may still vest in the bureaucracy, police and army rather than in the electorate.
Economic equality seeks a ‘level playing field’ of access to wealth and the means of livelihood.
insists that ‘equality of opportunity is not simply legal equality — it depends on the presence of abilities, not merely the absence of disabilities’, so the state must actively build capacity.
adds that it is ‘a problem of proportion’, met through differential taxation and social expenditure rather than identical incomes.

Social equality ends discrimination on grounds of caste, creed, religion, sex and the like, attacking status hierarchy rather than income — the equal use of a temple, a well or a school matters as much as the equal wage. It is the dimension most resistant to legislation alone, which is why it is said to be ‘enhanced by affirmative action’.
; social and economic equality together form

.” The queue captures the difference exactly: ‘first come, first served’ applies one rule to everybody and is formal equality, while a separate line for the elderly or the differently-abled relaxes the rule according to need and marks the shift to substantive equality.

Formal equality supplies equal rules and equal votes; substantive equality supplies real, need-sensitive equality of condition — and the central task of the modern welfare state is to convert the former into the latter.
Q — “Affirmative action is indispensable to substantive equality yet deeply contested.” Examine the arguments for and against it, with the Indian reservation debate.
Define affirmative action, argue both sides, and settle the Indian reservation question with the courts’ test.
— ‘positive intervention by the state’ in favour of the historically disadvantaged.
(Reservation for SCs/STs in India, affirmative action for Blacks in the USA.)
— the unit of claim is the community, not the person.
(A poor Brahmin does not qualify, since his community suffered no historical disadvantage — he is helped by poverty schemes instead.)
— compensatory discrimination on ‘reasonable and relevant grounds’ that corrects unjust historical inequality; grounded in
(It is the engine that turns formal equality into substantive equality.)
, punish a generation ‘not responsible for past injustice’ and wound self-respect.
: ‘reservation makes us immoral’; the courts call it enabling and temporary —
— indispensable, but legitimate only while it stays targeted, time-bound and evidence-based.

Q — Is liberty a precondition for equality? Examine the relationship between liberty, equality and justice, and evaluate Berlin’s value pluralism.
Take the liberty–equality relation through three schools, then test whether Berlin’s pluralism allows any final ranking.

Liberty, equality and justice are interdependent yet ‘essentially contested’ values, and the practical form of the dispute is sharp: does a reserved seat or a redistributive tax enlarge the freedom of the excluded, or invade the freedom of the taxed? Three schools answer differently, according to whether they treat the two values as contradictory, as hierarchically ordered, or as mutually completing.

Socialists and Marxists reverse the order: equality trumps a merely ‘bourgeois’ liberty, because without material equality freedom is the privilege of the propertied — the right to own a newspaper means nothing to one who cannot buy one.

He rejects value monism, which assumes one true ranking, and equally value relativism, which denies that values are real: liberty and equality are both authentic goods that may irreducibly clash.

Q — “Aristotle supports proportionate, not absolute, equality.” Discuss his conception of equality and its relevance to modern substantive equality.
Explain what proportional equality means in Aristotle, note its limits in his own society, and show it is the logic of affirmative action today.

(Equal marks deserve equal grades; unequal need deserves unequal help.)

(One flight of stairs for everyone is equal treatment that excludes the wheelchair user.)

(Reservation under Articles 15–16, progressive taxation and a separate queue for the elderly all relax a uniform rule for the disadvantaged.)
— though framed in a hierarchical Greek polis, his proportionality is the enduring premise of the welfare state.

he defines just equality as “the treating of equals equally and of unequals unequally in proportion to their inequalities.” Equality is thus a ratio, not a quantity: what is owed to a person depends on the relevant respect in which he stands equal or unequal to others, so identical treatment is just only among genuine equals.

From this follows his most quoted proposition: ‘injustice arises not only when equals are treated unequally, but also when unequals are treated equally’. The second half is the radical half — a single flight of stairs applied to everyone alike is impeccably equal treatment which nonetheless excludes the person in a wheelchair. Uniformity, in other words, can itself be a form of injustice.
Equality therefore becomes a matter of

: in distributive justice, honours, office and wealth are to be shared according to relevant merit rather than divided identically, and the argument turns on which respects are relevant to which good. He accordingly rejects
as itself a source of injustice — the objection later pressed by
Aristotle also accepted a great deal of

: he distinguished citizens from slaves and men from women in ‘rational and civic capacity’, restricted participation in the Polis to citizens, and even held slavery to be ‘good for both master and slave’ — a reminder that proportionality is only as just as the criteria of relevance it employs. Yet he was acutely alert to inequality’s dangers: ‘inequality, real or imagined, is the main cause of revolution’.
His principle that ‘unequals be treated unequally’ is precisely the logic of modern

: reservation under Articles 15 and 16, progressive taxation, special provisions for the disabled and a separate queue for the elderly all relax a uniform rule in favour of the disadvantaged, treating unequals unequally so as to produce genuine rather than merely formal equality.

Aristotle’s proportional equality, though embedded in a hierarchical Greek society, supplies the enduring insight behind today’s welfare state — that real equality often requires differential, need-sensitive treatment rather than identical treatment for all.
