contentText: Syllabus — Equality: social, political and economic; relationship between equality and freedom; affirmative action. (UPSC PSIR Paper-1A, Unit 4) Unit Snapshot What this unit covers:  the meaning and evolution of equality (formal, of opportunity, of outcome); the views of Laski, Barker and Bryan Turner; the schools of thought (liberal — welfare/resources/capability, Marxist, communitarian, multiculturalist); the dimensions of equality (legal, political, economic, social); affirmative action; and the relation of equality with liberty and justice, including Berlin’s value pluralism. Must-know thinkers:  Laski, Barker, Bryan Turner, Aristotle, Rousseau, Marx, Engels, Hayek, Ronald Dworkin, Amartya Sen, Martha Nussbaum, Michael Walzer, Will Kymlicka, Bhikhu Parekh, R.H. Tawney, Hobhouse, Isaiah Berlin, Rawls. PYQ trend:  equality of outcome, Aristotle’s conception, affirmative action, the liberty–equality relationship, and Berlin’s value pluralism are the recurring themes. Master Questions Q — Trace the historical evolution and meaning of equality, and compare the views of Laski, Barker and Bryan Turner. What it’s asking:  Three tasks — how equality became a political demand, what it actually means, and how the three thinkers define it. Gist — the spine to recall 1. Evolution  — inequality of ‘race, ancestry, sex, religion, wealth or knowledge’ was long thought natural, until the  Renaissance, Reformation and natural-rights theory  made equality a demand.  (Caste rank was defended as the divinely ordained order until the social reformers attacked it.) 2. Meaning  —  negatively  the end of special privilege,  positively  the opportunity to develop one’s personality.  (Abolishing untouchability is the negative face; free schooling and mid-day meals the positive.) 3. Laski  — four elements: no special privilege, adequate opportunity (above all education), access to social benefits, no exploitation.  (Economic equality is ‘a problem of proportion’ — not identical incomes but a defensible spread.) 4. Barker  — equality is a  derivative  value, flowing from the development of personality.  (Whatever right is guaranteed to me must be guaranteed to you in the same measure.) 5. Turner  — four types: fundamental, opportunity, condition, outcome.  (Equal dignity → an open entrance exam → equal coaching before it → equal result after it.) 6. Conclusion  — equality matures from a negative demand (Laski) to a developmental ideal (Barker) to a graded modern typology (Turner). Model Answer 1. Evolution.  Inequality — by ‘race, ancestry, sex, religion, wealth or knowledge’ — was for most of history treated as natural and therefore beyond criticism, as caste rank was defended in India as a divinely ordained order. The  Renaissance, Reformation and natural-rights theory  — pre-eminently  Locke  — turned equality into a political demand, directed first against feudal and clerical privilege and then, in the nineteenth century, extended to  economic and social equality  by  J.S. Mill, T.H. Green and Marx . 2. Meaning.  The concept is defined twice over.  Negatively  it is the end of special privileges, so that no one may claim advantage by birth — the logic of abolishing untouchability.  Positively  it is the availability to each person of the opportunity to develop his or her personality — the logic of free schooling and mid-day meals. Because the two faces pull in different directions, equality remains an  ‘essentially contested concept’ . 3. Laski.  Harold Laski  defines equality through four elements: (1) the  absence of special privilege  — ‘the will of one is equal to the will of any other’; (2)  adequate opportunity  for all, especially education, ‘for the power that counts is the power to use knowledge’; (3)  access to social benefits  with no bar of birth; and (4) the  absence of economic and social exploitation . On the economic side he concedes it is ‘largely a problem of proportion’, not of identical incomes. 4. Barker.  Ernest Barker  treats equality not as an end in itself but as a  derivative value  — ‘derivative from the supreme value of the development of personality’. Its operative rule is reciprocity: “whatever rights are guaranteed to me shall also, and in the same measure, be guaranteed to others.” Equality is thus justified instrumentally, by what it enables each personality to become. 5. Turner.  Bryan Turner  (in  Equality ) gives the most comprehensive modern account, distinguishing four types: (1)  fundamental equality  of persons, that is equal human dignity and worth; (2)  equality of opportunity , open access on merit and talent, as in a competitive entrance examination; (3)  equality of condition , which equalises the starting points — the coaching, nutrition and schooling that precede the exam; and (4)  equality of outcome or result , which equalises end-states through law. 6. Conclusion.  Read together, the three show equality maturing from a negative demand (Laski’s end of privilege) to a positive, developmental ideal (Barker’s personality) and finally to a graded modern typology (Turner) that sets up the central debate between opportunity and outcome. Q — “Equality of outcome, though the most radical face of egalitarianism, threatens liberty.” Critically examine, distinguishing formal equality, equality of opportunity and equality of outcome. What it’s asking:  Separate the three forms of equality, then judge whether the most radical of them — outcome — destroys liberty. Gist — the spine to recall 1. Egalitarian premise  — ‘equality is always just; only inequalities need justification’, and the demand rises in three stages.  (Same law → same starting line → same finishing line.) 2. Formal equality  — ‘all men are created equal’: equality before law, but essentially  negative .  (An equal right to dine in an expensive restaurant is worthless if you cannot pay the bill; the queue rule ‘first come, first served’ is fair but blind to need.) 3. Equality of opportunity  — ‘an equal chance to become unequal’: strip away social handicaps, accept natural difference.  (No child should start the race halfway down the track — hence free schooling and mid-day meals before the entrance exam.) 4. Equality of outcome  — ‘all runners finish in line together’;  Marx : ‘from each according to his ability, to each according to his needs’.  (Not an equal chance at the seat, but an equal share of the harvest.) 5. Threat to liberty  —  Hayek : people differ, so equal treatment must yield inequality; outcome equality needs coercive social engineering and kills incentive.  Aristotle  counters that treating unequals equally is itself unjust. 6. Conclusion  — formal equality is free but hollow, outcome equality deep but coercive;  Rawls’  difference principle is offered as the mean. Model Answer 1. Egalitarian premise.  Egalitarianism rests on the presumption that ‘equality is always just; only inequalities need justification’ — the burden of proof lies on whoever defends a difference. On that premise equality has assumed three progressively radical forms, each demanding more of the state: the same law, then the same starting line, then the same finishing line. 2. Formal equality.  Formal or legal equality asserts a common human essence — ‘all men are created equal’ (US Declaration), ‘men are born free and equal in rights’ (French Declaration) — and is expressed as equality before law, the cornerstone of the  rule of law . Yet it is  essentially negative : it grants an equal right to dine in an expensive restaurant while ignoring whether one has the money, and leaves ‘institutionalised’ discrimination untouched. In the queue, ‘first come, first served’ is impeccably fair and wholly insensitive to need. 3. Equality of opportunity.  Proportional equality, traceable to  Plato , concerns  starting conditions  and amounts to ‘an equal opportunity to become unequal’: natural inequality of talent and effort is accepted, while social inequality of poverty and poor schooling is removed, so that no one ‘starts the race halfway down the track’. It is the tenet of  social liberalism , realised through education, health and housing — free schooling and mid-day meals precede the common entrance examination. 4. Equality of outcome.  Equality of outcome is ‘the most radical and controversial face of egalitarianism’ — not an equal start but an equal finish, so that ‘all runners finish in line together’.  Rousseau  feared that inequality would enslave the poor and corrupt the rich, and  Marx  captured the ideal in ‘from each according to his ability, to each according to his needs’ — distribution keyed to need rather than to contribution or to chance. 5. Threat to liberty.  Hayek  objects that ‘people are very different, so to treat them equally must result in inequality — the only way to make them equal is to treat them differently’; equality of outcome therefore requires coercive ‘social engineering’, destroys incentive and ‘remains utopia’. The reply is  Aristotle’s : ‘injustice arises not only when equals are treated unequally, but when unequals are treated equally’ — so a measure of differential treatment is the price of real equality, not an assault on freedom. 6. Conclusion.  The three forms trade off against liberty differently: formal equality is fully compatible with liberty but hollow; equality of opportunity is the liberal mean; equality of outcome secures the deepest equality but at the cost of coercion — which is why  Rawls’  difference principle, permitting only those inequalities that benefit the least advantaged, is offered as the balance between the two extremes. Q — Critically examine the schools of thought on equality — liberal (welfare, resources, capability), Marxist, communitarian and multiculturalist. What it’s asking:  Compare four schools by asking each the same question — equality of WHAT, and among whom. Gist — the spine to recall 1. The currency question  — liberals agree on equality but differ on what to equalise: welfare (utilitarians) or  resources  ( Dworkin ,  Sovereign Virtue ).  (Equal cash to a healthy man and a dialysis patient is equal resources, not equal welfare.) 2. Brute luck vs option luck  —  Dworkin  compensates what you did not choose, not what you did.  (Born with a disability = brute luck, compensated; losing money on a bet = option luck, not.) 3. Capability  —  Sen  and  Nussbaum : equalise ‘the ability to do what one wants’, since people convert resources differently.  (‘Fasting is a choice, hunger is a deprivation’ — same empty stomach, opposite freedoms.) 4. Marxist  —  Marx : ‘we want to abolish classes, and in this sense we are for equality’ — impossible without abolishing private ownership of the means of production. 5. Communitarian & multiculturalist  —  Walzer’s   complex equality  blocks advantage in one sphere from buying another.  (Wealth may buy a car, it must not buy a medical seat or a verdict.)   Kymlicka  and  Parekh  demand group rights. 6. Conclusion  — the schools move outward from the individual to the group, showing genuine equality is plural, not simple. Model Answer 1. The currency question.  Liberals agree that persons must be treated as equals but divide over the ‘currency’ of equality.  Equality of welfare , the utilitarian answer, equates welfare with pleasure and would transfer resources until satisfactions are level — which rewards expensive tastes.  Ronald Dworkin , in  Sovereign Virtue , rejects this for  equality of resources , holding that ‘equality is more fundamental than liberty — liberty is hollow without it’. 2. Brute luck versus option luck.  Dworkin  holds people responsible only for choices made in  chosen  circumstances, not  unchosen  ones, and therefore insists on a  just initial distribution : his ‘envy test’ and his ambition- and endowment-sensitive auction distinguish  brute luck  — the disability or the caste one is born into, which must be compensated — from  option luck , the loss on a wager freely taken, which must not. The aim is a distribution that is ‘equitable, not merely equal’. 3. Capability.  Amartya Sen , refined by  Martha Nussbaum , urges  equality of capability  — ‘the ability to do what one wants to do’ — because individuals differ in converting identical resources into actual functionings: the same grain feeds a healthy adult and fails a parasite-ridden child. The approach is social-choice based and realization-focused, and its sharpest formulation is that ‘fasting is a choice, hunger is a deprivation’ — the outcome is identical, the freedom is not. Hence development is itself ‘freedom’. 4. Marxist.  Marx  makes the abolition of classes central — ‘we want to abolish classes, and in this sense we are for equality’ — which is impossible without abolishing private ownership of the means of production. Legal and political equality alone is a bourgeois form: so long as one class owns the productive apparatus, formal equality of rights merely legitimises substantive domination. 5. Communitarian and multiculturalist.  Communitarians  such as  Michael Walzer  argue for  complex equality : ‘sometimes we equalise people by differentiating’, and each social good — money, office, health, honour — has its own distributive sphere, so that advantage in one must be blocked from buying advantage in another. Wealth may legitimately buy a car; it must not buy a medical seat or a favourable verdict.  Multiculturalists  ( Will Kymlicka ,  Bhikhu Parekh ) relocate equality in cultures and demand  group rights , Kymlicka’s ‘luck egalitarianism’ treating birth into a minority culture as ‘bad brute luck’ deserving special protection. 6. Conclusion.  The schools move outward from the individual to the group: liberals refine what each person should have (welfare → resources → capability), Marxists locate equality in the abolition of class, and communitarians and multiculturalists relocate it in spheres and cultures — together showing that genuine equality is plural, not simple. Q — Discuss the dimensions of equality — legal, political, economic and social — and how they combine into formal and substantive equality. What it’s asking:  List the four working dimensions of equality, then show which two make ‘formal’ equality and which two make ‘substantive’ equality. Gist — the spine to recall 1. Legal equality  — rule of law plus ‘equality before law’ and ‘equal protection of the laws’.  (Equal rights are useless without equal power to vindicate them — hence free legal aid.) 2. Political equality  — ‘one person, one vote’ with no bar to office; yet  Lipson : ‘the many have always been governed by the few’.  (Every vote weighs the same, but money, birth and bureaucracy still weigh more.) 3. Economic equality  — a level playing field of access to wealth;  Tawney : it needs ‘the presence of abilities, not merely the absence of disabilities’.  (Progressive taxation funding schools and health — Laski’s ‘problem of proportion’.) 4. Social equality  — ends discrimination by caste, creed, religion or sex, and is ‘enhanced by affirmative action’.  (Temple entry and common water sources, not merely an equal wage.) 5. Formal vs substantive  — legal + political =  formal ; social + economic =  substantive .  (The queue: ‘first come, first served’ is formal; a separate line for the elderly and the disabled is substantive.) 6. Conclusion  — the welfare state’s task is to convert formal equality into substantive equality. Model Answer 1. Legal equality.  Legal equality grants equal legal status to all: the  rule of law , supplemented by ‘equality before law’ and ‘equal protection of the laws’.  Rousseau  regarded it as the primary mark of an equal society. Its limit is decisive: it is ‘meaningless without equal opportunity to get justice — all may possess equal rights but not equal power to vindicate them’, which is why free legal aid, not merely an open court, is required. 2. Political equality.  Political equality means equal political rights on a ‘one person, one vote’ basis, with no bar of birth or property to holding office.  Lipson  nevertheless notes that the ‘many have always been governed by the few’: political inequality has rested successively on knowledge ( Plato ), birth (aristocracy), money (plutocracy) and race, and real power may still vest in the bureaucracy, police and army rather than in the electorate. 3. Economic equality.  Economic equality seeks a ‘level playing field’ of access to wealth and the means of livelihood.  R.H. Tawney  insists that ‘equality of opportunity is not simply legal equality — it depends on the presence of abilities, not merely the absence of disabilities’, so the state must actively build capacity.  Laski  adds that it is ‘a problem of proportion’, met through differential taxation and social expenditure rather than identical incomes. 4. Social equality.  Social equality ends discrimination on grounds of caste, creed, religion, sex and the like, attacking status hierarchy rather than income — the equal use of a temple, a well or a school matters as much as the equal wage. It is the dimension most resistant to legislation alone, which is why it is said to be ‘enhanced by affirmative action’. 5. Formal versus substantive.  “Legal and political equality together form  formal equality ; social and economic equality together form  substantive equality .” The queue captures the difference exactly: ‘first come, first served’ applies one rule to everybody and is formal equality, while a separate line for the elderly or the differently-abled relaxes the rule according to need and marks the shift to substantive equality. 6. Conclusion.  Formal equality supplies equal rules and equal votes; substantive equality supplies real, need-sensitive equality of condition — and the central task of the modern welfare state is to convert the former into the latter. Q — “Affirmative action is indispensable to substantive equality yet deeply contested.” Examine the arguments for and against it, with the Indian reservation debate. What it’s asking:  Define affirmative action, argue both sides, and settle the Indian reservation question with the courts’ test. Gist — the spine to recall 1. What it is  — ‘positive intervention by the state’ in favour of the historically disadvantaged.  (Reservation for SCs/STs in India, affirmative action for Blacks in the USA.) 2. Group-based, not individual  — the unit of claim is the community, not the person.  (A poor Brahmin does not qualify, since his community suffered no historical disadvantage — he is helped by poverty schemes instead.) 3. Arguments for  — compensatory discrimination on ‘reasonable and relevant grounds’ that corrects unjust historical inequality; grounded in  Articles 15 and 16 .  (It is the engine that turns formal equality into substantive equality.) 4. Arguments against  —  neo-conservatives : quotas ‘erode respect for merit’, offend  procedural justice , punish a generation ‘not responsible for past injustice’ and wound self-respect. 5. The Indian debate  —  Guha : it ‘generates more heat than light’;  Mehta : ‘reservation makes us immoral’; the courts call it enabling and temporary —  Ashok Kumar : ‘the medicine, not the daily bread’. 6. Conclusion  — indispensable, but legitimate only while it stays targeted, time-bound and evidence-based. Model Answer 1. What it is.  Affirmative action is ‘positive intervention by the state — welfare policies in favour of the disadvantaged’. It targets the  historically disadvantaged  — Dalits and Adivasis in India, Blacks in the United States — and works by relaxing a uniform rule (reserved seats, relaxed cut-offs, preferential appointment) so that those excluded for centuries can in fact enter. It must be distinguished from a mere  preferential policy  secured by already dominant groups, such as the Jat and Maratha agitations. 2. Group-based, not individual.  Its unit of claim is the  class or community, not the individual . A poor Brahmin does not qualify, because his community suffered no historical disadvantage — his poverty is addressed instead by income-based poverty-alleviation schemes. This is what distinguishes affirmative action from welfare simpliciter: it remedies a status injury inflicted on a group, not a shortfall of income suffered by a person. 3. Arguments for.  It is compensatory or positive discrimination on ‘reasonable and relevant grounds’, correcting  unjust historical inequalities  and enabling the deprived to ‘escape tough competition’ in which their starting handicap would be decisive. In India it is constitutionally grounded in  Articles 15 and 16 , which permit special provision for socially and educationally backward classes — the engine by which formal equality is converted into substantive equality. 4. Arguments against.  Neo-conservatives  hold that equality means only equality of opportunity, and that quotas ‘erode respect for merit’. It is said to be ‘inimical to  procedural justice ’, since already advantaged members of a beneficiary group may edge out poorer members of the majority; that the present generation is ‘not responsible for past injustice’, so the burden is misplaced; and that it injures  self-respect , breeding a ‘feeling of inferiority’ in those it is meant to lift. 5. The Indian debate.  Ramachandra Guha  observes that reservation debates ‘generate more heat than light’, and  Pratap Bhanu Mehta  charges that ‘reservation makes us immoral’. The courts have accordingly framed it as  enabling and temporary : in the  Ram Singh (Jat)  case the government was directed to keep identifying genuinely vulnerable classes on fresh evidence rather than political pressure, and in  Ashok Kumar  it was held that reservation is ‘the medicine, not the daily bread’ — a remedy for a diagnosed disability, not a permanent diet. 6. Conclusion.  Affirmative action is indispensable for converting formal into substantive equality, and is simply  Aristotle’s  rule that unequals be treated unequally. Its legitimacy, however, depends on its remaining  targeted, time-bound and evidence-based  — correcting a historical wrong without hardening into a permanent entitlement. Q — Is liberty a precondition for equality? Examine the relationship between liberty, equality and justice, and evaluate Berlin’s value pluralism. What it’s asking:  Take the liberty–equality relation through three schools, then test whether Berlin’s pluralism allows any final ranking. Gist — the spine to recall 1. The question  — liberty, equality and justice are interdependent yet ‘essentially contested’, and three schools read the relation differently.  (Does a quota that opens a college seat enlarge freedom or invade it?) 2. Libertarian  —  Hayek, Nozick : the two are contradictory, so liberty comes first and equality stops at law and opportunity.  (Redistribution means taxing one man to fund another.) 3. Socialist  — equality first, since ‘bourgeois’ liberty is a privilege of the propertied;  Hobhouse : ‘liberty without equality is a name of noble sound and squalid results’. 4. Socio-liberal  —  Rawls  (lexical order),  Dworkin  (endowment-sensitive distribution),  Sen  (development as freedom) deny any necessary conflict.  (A literate voter is a freer voter.) 5. Berlin’s value pluralism  — values are ‘plural, conflicting and incommensurable’, with no objective ordering.  (The goods of the nun’s life and the married woman’s are both real and cannot both be had.) 6. Conclusion  — liberty is a precondition only for  substantive  equality — ‘treating people as equals’; justice remains the balancing value. Model Answer 1. The question.  Liberty, equality and justice are interdependent yet ‘essentially contested’ values, and the practical form of the dispute is sharp: does a reserved seat or a redistributive tax enlarge the freedom of the excluded, or invade the freedom of the taxed? Three schools answer differently, according to whether they treat the two values as contradictory, as hierarchically ordered, or as mutually completing. 2. Libertarian.  Libertarians and classical liberals ( Locke, Smith, Bentham, Nozick, Hayek ) hold liberty and equality to be  contradictory , give liberty priority, and confine equality to legal equality and equality of opportunity, since redistribution means coercing one person for another’s benefit.  Hayek : ‘people are very different, so treating them equally must produce inequality; equality before law leads to material inequality’ — a result he accepts as the price of freedom. 3. Socialist.  Socialists and Marxists reverse the order: equality trumps a merely ‘bourgeois’ liberty, because without material equality freedom is the privilege of the propertied — the right to own a newspaper means nothing to one who cannot buy one.  Hobhouse  states the point decisively: ‘liberty without equality is a name of noble sound and squalid results’. 4. Socio-liberal.  Socio-liberals and egalitarians ( Rawls, Sen, Dworkin ) deny any necessary conflict.  Rawls  reconciles them in  lexical order , the equal basic liberties ranking first and the difference principle governing what remains;  Dworkin  does so through endowment- and ambition-sensitive distribution;  Sen  through ‘development as freedom’, since literacy, health and nutrition are what make a formal right usable. On this view liberty, properly understood, is a precondition of a meaningful equal life, not its enemy. 5. Berlin’s value pluralism.  Isaiah Berlin  argues that fundamental values are ‘universal, plural, conflicting and incommensurable’ — ‘there is no objective criterion to determine their ordering’, as the goods realised in the life of a nun and in that of a married woman are both genuine and cannot both be possessed. He rejects value monism, which assumes one true ranking, and equally value relativism, which denies that values are real: liberty and equality are both authentic goods that may irreducibly clash. 6. Conclusion.  Liberty is a precondition for equality only when equality is understood  substantively  — as ‘treating people as equals’ with equal concern and respect, rather than treating them identically.  Berlin’s  pluralism warns that no single formula can always harmonise them, which is precisely why justice, as the balancing value, remains the central task of political theory. Q — “Aristotle supports proportionate, not absolute, equality.” Discuss his conception of equality and its relevance to modern substantive equality. What it’s asking:  Explain what proportional equality means in Aristotle, note its limits in his own society, and show it is the logic of affirmative action today. Gist — the spine to recall 1. Proportional, not arithmetical  —  Politics : ‘the treating of equals equally and of unequals unequally in proportion to their inequalities’.  (Equal marks deserve equal grades; unequal need deserves unequal help.) 2. Injustice runs both ways  — ‘injustice arises not only when equals are treated unequally, but also when unequals are treated equally’.  (One flight of stairs for everyone is equal treatment that excludes the wheelchair user.) 3. Desert and proportion  — in distributive justice, honours and wealth go by relevant merit, not identical division; hence  absolute or mechanical equality  is rejected. 4. Its limits  — he accepted  natural inequality , ranking citizens above slaves and men above women in ‘rational and civic capacity’, yet warned that ‘inequality, real or imagined, is the main cause of revolution’. 5. Relevance  — ‘unequals treated unequally’ is the very logic of  substantive equality .  (Reservation under Articles 15–16, progressive taxation and a separate queue for the elderly all relax a uniform rule for the disadvantaged.) 6. Conclusion  — though framed in a hierarchical Greek polis, his proportionality is the enduring premise of the welfare state. Model Answer 1. Proportional, not arithmetical.  Aristotle’s  conception of equality is  proportional, not arithmetical . In the  Politics  he defines just equality as “the treating of equals equally and of unequals unequally in proportion to their inequalities.” Equality is thus a ratio, not a quantity: what is owed to a person depends on the relevant respect in which he stands equal or unequal to others, so identical treatment is just only among genuine equals. 2. Injustice runs both ways.  From this follows his most quoted proposition: ‘injustice arises not only when equals are treated unequally, but also when unequals are treated equally’. The second half is the radical half — a single flight of stairs applied to everyone alike is impeccably equal treatment which nonetheless excludes the person in a wheelchair. Uniformity, in other words, can itself be a form of injustice. 3. Desert and proportion.  Equality therefore becomes a matter of  desert and proportion : in distributive justice, honours, office and wealth are to be shared according to relevant merit rather than divided identically, and the argument turns on which respects are relevant to which good. He accordingly rejects  absolute or mechanical equality  as itself a source of injustice — the objection later pressed by  Hayek  against equality of outcome. 4. Its limits.  Aristotle also accepted a great deal of  natural inequality : he distinguished citizens from slaves and men from women in ‘rational and civic capacity’, restricted participation in the Polis to citizens, and even held slavery to be ‘good for both master and slave’ — a reminder that proportionality is only as just as the criteria of relevance it employs. Yet he was acutely alert to inequality’s dangers: ‘inequality, real or imagined, is the main cause of revolution’. 5. Relevance.  His principle that ‘unequals be treated unequally’ is precisely the logic of modern  substantive equality  and  affirmative action : reservation under Articles 15 and 16, progressive taxation, special provisions for the disabled and a separate queue for the elderly all relax a uniform rule in favour of the disadvantaged, treating unequals unequally so as to produce genuine rather than merely formal equality. 6. Conclusion.  Aristotle’s proportional equality, though embedded in a hierarchical Greek society, supplies the enduring insight behind today’s welfare state — that real equality often requires differential, need-sensitive treatment rather than identical treatment for all. Revision Box — facts, keywords & quotes Meaning:  negative = end of privileges; positive = opportunity to develop personality; ‘essentially contested’. Laski : equality = no privilege + adequate opportunity + access to social benefits + no exploitation; economic equality = ‘problem of proportion’. Barker : equality is a ‘derivative value’ from the development of personality. Bryan Turner ,  Equality : 4 types — fundamental, opportunity, condition, outcome. Three forms:  formal (‘all men created equal’) → opportunity (‘equal chance to become unequal’) → outcome (all finish together). Marx : ‘from each according to ability, to each according to needs’; ‘abolish classes’. Hayek : treating different people equally must yield inequality; outcome equality needs coercion. Liberal currencies:  welfare (utilitarians) / resources (Dworkin) / capability (Sen). Dworkin ,  Sovereign Virtue : brute vs option luck; envy test; just initial distribution. Sen : capability = ‘ability to do what one wants’; ‘fasting is a choice, hunger is deprivation’; development as freedom. Walzer : complex equality — ‘block the exchanges’ across spheres;  Kymlicka : group rights, ‘luck egalitarianism’. Dimensions:  legal + political = formal equality; social + economic = substantive equality. R.H. Tawney : opportunity depends on ‘presence of abilities, not just absence of disabilities’. Affirmative action:  group-based, historically disadvantaged; Arts.15 & 16; Ashok Kumar — ‘medicine, not daily bread’. Hobhouse : ‘liberty without equality is a name of noble sound and squalid results’. Isaiah Berlin : value pluralism — values are ‘plural, conflicting and incommensurable’; no objective ordering. Aristotle : treat equals equally, unequals unequally; inequality = main cause of revolution. Last-Minute Revision Sheet (1 page) Meaning & thinkers (MQ1):  negative/positive meaning; Laski (4 elements), Barker (derivative value), Turner (4 types). Three forms (MQ2):  formal (negative, legal) → opportunity (‘equal chance to become unequal’) → outcome (radical, socialist; Hayek’s liberty critique). Schools (MQ3):  liberal currencies welfare/resources(Dworkin)/capability(Sen); Marxist (abolish classes); communitarian (Walzer complex equality); multiculturalist (Kymlicka group rights). Dimensions (MQ4):  legal + political = formal; social + economic = substantive; queue example. Affirmative action (MQ5):  group-based; for = corrects historical wrong (Arts.15/16); against = merit/reverse discrimination/self-respect; enabling & temporary. Liberty-equality-justice (MQ6):  libertarian (clash) vs socialist (equality first) vs socio-liberal (balance: Rawls/Sen/Dworkin); Berlin’s value pluralism. Aristotle (MQ7):  proportional not absolute equality; ‘unequals treated unequally’ → logic of modern affirmative action. Killer quotes:  Hobhouse — ‘noble sound, squalid results’; Hayek — ‘treat them equally → inequality’; Marx — ‘to each according to needs’; Aristotle — ‘unequals treated equally = injustice’. Previous Year Questions — coverage map Equality of outcome as a political idea → MQ2. Affirmative Action / Explain equality → MQ5 (+ MQ4). Aristotle’s conception of Equality → MQ7. Liberty as a precondition for equality; equality–liberty relationship → MQ6. Berlin’s notion of value pluralism → MQ6. (Foundational: meaning & thinkers, schools, dimensions → MQ1/MQ3/MQ4.)

title: 05 - Rights

content.text: Syllabus — Rights: meaning and theories; different kinds of rights; concept of Human Rights. (UPSC PSIR Paper-1A, Unit 5)

the meaning, nature and theories of rights (natural, legal, moral, conservative/historical, social-welfare, Marxist, and contemporary — libertarian, communitarian, multicultural); types of rights and the negative/positive distinction; the doctrine of ‘rights as trumps’; and human rights — the three generations, the ‘Asian values’ critique, and the universalism vs cultural-relativism debate.
Laski, Locke, Paine, Bentham, Burke, T.H. Green, Kant, Dworkin, Joseph Raz, Nozick, Walzer, Kymlicka, Bhikhu Parekh, Karel Vasak, Lee Kuan Yew, Isaiah Berlin, Susan Moller Okin, Amartya Sen.
universal conception of human rights (2021), right to property (2020), rights as trumps (2019), three generations (2018), implementation/changing conduct of states (2016), natural rights (2015).
Q — Critically examine the theories of rights — natural, legal, moral, conservative/historical, social-welfare and Marxist. ‘Idea of natural rights.’ Comment. (UPSC 2015)
Define a right → run through the rival theories of where rights come from → judge which account survives.
— a right is a condition of social life needed to be one’s best self, and it is originally
(A child without schooling can never develop her powers — hence Art 21A.)
the state, so the state only recognises them.
(The 1776 American Declaration’s ‘self-evident’ life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness — no legislature conferred them.)
— only the state creates rights; natural rights are
(You may vote at 18 only because the Constitution’s 61st Amendment says so — not because nature says so.)
— rights from reason and moral personality (
(But custom also sanctioned sati and untouchability — which is why India abolished them by law.)
— rights are justified by the common good (
(A bonded labourer has a legal right to freedom yet no means to use it.)
social-democratic synthesis: ‘every state is known by the rights it maintains’.

defines rights as “those conditions of social life without which no man can seek, in general, to be himself at his best” — a child denied schooling can never develop her powers, which is why India made elementary education a fundamental right under Article 21A. A right is thus a claim recognised by society, and historically a
concept that replaced the divine right of kings by limiting the power of state and society. The rival theories differ chiefly on the
The 17th–18th century doctrine treats rights as a corollary of
— inherent in human nature, held before and independently of the state, which merely recognises them.
(life, liberty and property) is its champion, and

gives it a teleological basis. Its power is visible in the ‘self-evident truths’ of the American Declaration (1776) and the French Declaration (1789), and in modern courts reading unenumerated rights into constitutional texts. Its weakness is that ‘nature’ supplies no agreed list and no enforcement.
is the real source, for ‘real laws give birth to real rights’, and rights claimed against the law are
and ‘anarchical fallacies’. The point is concrete: an Indian citizen votes at eighteen only because the 61st Amendment lowered the age, not because nature ordained it.

refines the position — a legal right is ‘an interest recognised and protected by the rule of law’, enforceable by a determinate authority. The criticism is that a purely legal theory leaves the citizen defenceless against an unjust law.

) derives rights from the dictates of reason and moral personality — persons must be treated ‘as ends, never merely as means’ — so a right exists wherever it is a condition of moral self-realisation, even if unenforced. The
grounds rights instead in a long process of

and prescription; he condemned the French Revolution’s ‘metaphysical abstractions’ in favour of ‘the rights of Englishmen’. The standing reply is Indian: custom equally sanctioned sati and untouchability, abolished only by deliberate legislation and Articles 17 and 15.
theory — Bentham’s utilitarian legacy carried forward by
— holds that rights are justified only in so far as they serve the ‘greatest happiness’ and the common good; critics find the standard vague and majoritarian. The

view is sharper: rights are a ‘bourgeois concept’, class law lodged in the superstructure, conferring formal liberty without substantive power — the bonded labourer holds a legal right to freedom yet lacks the means to exercise it, so genuine rights require the abolition of class division.

social-democratic synthesis best reconciles the traditions: rights are rooted in social good yet must secure both individual liberty and social justice, uniting the moral force of natural rights with the enforceability of legal rights. His maxim that ‘every state is known by the rights it maintains’ remains the working test of any regime.
Q — Discuss the doctrine of ‘rights as trumps’ (Dworkin) and its critics. Can the right to privacy trump state interest? (UPSC 2019)
Explain what ‘trumps’ means → apply it to privacy → test it against Dworkin’s own exceptions and his critics.
that beat collective goals, as a trump card beats any other suit.
(Privacy cannot be overridden merely because a database is administratively convenient.)
between a right and a policy benefit; rights are not state gifts.
(Majority welfare cannot license torturing one suspect.)
— a right sets the limit policy must respect.
(Puttaswamy, 2017: nine judges read privacy into Art 21, so surveillance must clear legality, necessity and proportionality — not mere ‘security’ assertion.)
— only where the right is at stake in an
— utilitarians deny the priority of rights over aggregate welfare;
— rights are near-absolute, not absolute: a via media between rigid absolutism and utilitarian expediency.
argues that individual rights function as

— as a trump card defeats any card of another suit, a right defeats the collective goals of the community or state. Rights are not what the state chooses to grant; on the contrary ‘the sole purpose of the state is the maintenance of rights’. Hence privacy cannot be overridden merely because a centralised database would be administratively convenient.
The doctrine is directed against the
view that a person is entitled only to what the state confers, and that any right may be balanced away once aggregate welfare rises. On the trumps model there is

: a genuine right cannot be defeated simply because its violation maximises utility, which is why majority benefit cannot license torturing a single suspect. Rights, for Dworkin, express the government’s duty of ‘equal concern and respect’ for each person.
cannot ordinarily be trumped by a bare appeal to national security or efficiency; the right fixes the boundary within which policy must operate. India supplies the sharpest illustration: in
K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017)

a nine-judge Bench held privacy intrinsic to the right to life under Article 21, so state intrusion must satisfy legality, necessity and proportionality. That test is the trumps doctrine in institutional form — the state must justify the intrusion, not the citizen the right.
Dworkin concedes that a right may be compromised in two narrow cases: first, where the value the right protects is at stake only in some
of honouring it is grossly disproportionate to its benefit — as with limited disclosure of movement data during an epidemic.

reasons similarly that even human dignity, though it normally prevails, may be ‘partially defeated’ in unavoidable circumstances. The exceptions are principled limits, not a general balancing licence.
Utilitarians reject any lexical priority of rights over aggregate welfare, arguing that Dworkin smuggles in an unargued moral hierarchy.
, holds that law is ‘autonomous’ — there is no necessary continuity between legal rights and morality — while communitarians such as
object that the rights-bearing individual is abstracted from the community that gives rights their meaning.

‘Rights as trumps’ remains the strongest defence of the individual against majoritarian and executive overreach, and it has shaped judicial review far beyond the Anglo-American world. Its qualified exceptions show that even Dworkin treats rights as near-absolute rather than wholly absolute — a via media between rigid absolutism and utilitarian expediency.
Q — Can there be a universal conception of human rights? Examine the debate between universalism and cultural relativism. (UPSC 2021)
State what human rights claim → give the case for universality → present the relativist attack → arrive at a defensible middle position.
— post-1945 claims held by all persons simply as human, codified in the
(UDHR 1948, drafted in reaction to Nazi atrocities, plus the two 1966 Covenants.)
(Echoed in the Indian Preamble’s promise of ‘dignity of the individual’.)
— a common humanity gives an equal, inalienable claim, and it has abolished manifestly inhuman practices.
(Sati, banned in 1829 after Raja Ram Mohan Roy; female foeticide; genital mutilation — no culture may plead custom.)
(The 1993 Bangkok Declaration’s plea for ‘national and regional peculiarities’; the ‘Asian values’ school.)
, so no culture may rank another’s.
(Liberty and equality both matter, yet more of one costs the other.)
‘dialogue among civilisations’, not imposed at gunpoint.

Human rights are claims held by every person ‘just because they are human’, irrespective of state, race or creed. They emerged after the Second World War in reaction to the Nazi atrocities and were codified in the

together with the two 1966 Covenants on Civil and Political and on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights. Their novelty lies in piercing sovereignty: how a state treats its own citizens becomes a matter of international concern.
natural rights — the ‘self-evident truths’ that survive the transfer to civil society — to
, by which every person is an end in himself and never merely a means. From this follows their defining and most contested attribute,
: rights are equal, inalienable and permanent. The Indian Preamble’s pledge to secure ‘the dignity of the individual’ shows how deeply the Kantian premise travelled into post-colonial constitutions.

If humanity is one, a claim grounded in humanity alone cannot stop at borders. The practical vindication is that universal standards have delivered where local custom would not: sati, defended as tradition, was banned in 1829 after the campaign of

; female foeticide and genital mutilation are today indefensible on cultural grounds; and the corpus keeps expanding, as with the United Nations’ recognition of a human right to water. Without a universal core, the victims of majoritarian custom would have no vocabulary of appeal.
— the concept descends from the anthropologist
— hold that every culture is rational on its own terms and that no hierarchy of cultures exists.
add that the self is ‘situated’ and constituted by community, so an abstract rights-bearer is a fiction. Together they charge that ‘universal’ rights are in fact
, stressing ‘national and regional peculiarities’, gave the objection diplomatic form.
deepens the difficulty: values are genuinely

— liberty and equality are both authentic goods, yet more of one is bought at the cost of the other, and there is ‘no objective criterion’ for ranking them. The West is therefore not entitled to impose its own ordering. Yet Berlin does not collapse into relativism: he retains certain ‘generic values’ common to humanity and prizes
— Voltaire’s ‘I detest what you say, yet will defend your right to say it’.
A universal conception is defensible, but only as a
of human dignity — against torture, slavery, genocide and arbitrary killing — whose content is enlarged through
‘dialogue among civilisations’ rather than imposed ‘at gunpoint’. Human rights should thus be universal in their core and plural in their expression.
Q — What do you understand by the three generations of human rights? (UPSC 2018)
Explain Vasak’s classification generation by generation, and bring out the negative/positive distinction that underlies it.
(1979, Strasbourg) classified human rights on the French Revolution’s
(The state may not censor a newspaper — Art 19(1)(a); ICCPR 1966.)
: the state MUST act and spend.
(The state must provide free schooling to every 6–14 year-old — Art 21A and the RTE Act, 2009; ICESCR 1966.)
(A healthy environment, development, peace — as in the climate-finance claims of the Global South.)
— negative vs positive rights; welfare states combine both.
(India: enforceable Part III rights beside non-justiciable Part IV directives, later judicially fused through Art 21.)
— the generations chart a widening of rights, but the sequence metaphor wrongly implies the later ones are less urgent.
The ‘three generations’ framework was proposed in

at the International Institute of Human Rights, Strasbourg. He classified the growing corpus of human rights along the lines of the French Revolution’s slogan ‘liberty, equality, fraternity’, each generation corresponding to a historical phase in which a new kind of claim was pressed and a different demand was made upon the state.
2. First generation — civil and political rights.
, these are the liberal rights of life, liberty, property, equality before law, freedom of expression, conscience and the vote, recognised in the 1966 Covenant on Civil and Political Rights. They are
in form: they succeed by the state’s

, not its exertion — the state must NOT censor a newspaper, arrest without warrant or bar a person from a public office. Article 19(1)(a) of the Indian Constitution is enforceable precisely because it demands abstention, which costs the treasury nothing.
3. Second generation — socio-economic and cultural rights.
and championed by socialist states, these cover work, fair wages, social security, health and education, and were recognised in the 1966 Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights. They are

: they require the state to build, employ and spend. India’s Article 21A read with the Right to Education Act, 2009 obliges the state to provide free and compulsory schooling to every child aged six to fourteen — a duty of provision, not of restraint. Both the first and second generations remain

claims ‘exercised in solidarity’ — self-determination, peace, development, a healthy environment, humanitarian assistance and a share in the common heritage of mankind. Their bearer is a people rather than a person, and their duty-holder is the international community: the Global South’s demand for climate finance and technology transfer, resting on common but differentiated responsibility, is a third-generation claim in action.
Cutting across the generations is the

between freedom from interference and freedom to realise oneself. Negative rights are cheap, judicially enforceable and immediate; positive rights are costly, progressive and politically contested. The modern welfare state combines both, and India illustrates the fusion — justiciable fundamental rights in Part III alongside non-justiciable Directive Principles in Part IV, which the Supreme Court has progressively read into Article 21 as rights to livelihood, health and a clean environment.
The generations map the historical widening of rights: from the individual
the state, to the individual’s welfare

the state, to humanity’s shared claims beyond the state. The metaphor must not be pressed too far, however — treating them as a sequence wrongly implies the later generations are derivative or less urgent, whereas the Vienna Declaration (1993) affirms that all human rights are indivisible and interdependent.
Q — Critically examine the ‘Asian values’ critique of human rights and the challenges to their implementation. (UPSC 2016)
Set out what the Asian-values school claims → explain why enforcement is hard → assess how far the critique holds.
— a 1990s East Asian assertion rooted in
, which prizes harmony and duty over individual claim.
— rights are not universal; society is

pressed ‘national and regional peculiarities’ before the Vienna World Conference.
— post-colonial thinkers see universal rights as

yet states are their only guardians, so enforcement means
(UN bodies can name and shame, but cannot enter a sovereign jurisdiction.)
: Asia is too diverse for one ‘Asian value’, and freedom is not un-Asian (

The ‘Asian values’ critique arose in the 1990s, after the collapse of the USSR left liberal rights apparently unchallenged and the rise of East Asia supplied a rival model of development. Its principal proponents,
of Malaysia, traced their position to

, which prizes social harmony, hierarchy and duty to the group above the assertion of individual claims — Singapore’s combination of high prosperity with tightly limited dissent being offered as proof of concept.
The school advances four propositions: first, human rights are
and cannot be globalised, since they grew from a specific Western history; second, Asian societies are centred on the
rather than the atomised individual; third,
— food, housing, employment — rank above political rights for poor societies, so ‘feed the people first, elections later’; and fourth,
includes domestic jurisdiction over one’s human-rights record, so other nations should not interfere.
These claims were not merely academic. At the regional meeting preceding the Vienna World Conference on Human Rights, the

affirmed the universality of human rights in principle while insisting that their implementation ‘must bear in mind the significance of national and regional peculiarities and various historical, cultural and religious backgrounds’ — an attempt to convert cultural relativism into a norm of international law.
Post-colonial and cultural-relativist thinkers reinforce the critique, reading the universal human-rights regime as

— the successor to the civilising mission, now deployed selectively against weaker states. The Western rejoinder is that Asian values amount to ‘soft authoritarianism’: a doctrine articulated by ruling elites rather than by peoples, and used to justify episodes such as the suppression at Tiananmen in 1989 or the silencing of opposition media.
The deeper difficulty is structural. Human rights are inherently
— they are claims against power — yet states remain their principal guardians, so governments offer ‘moral guarantees’ that they routinely fail to honour. Enforcement therefore becomes ‘a matter of

’, which sovereignty, the non-interference claim and the absence of coercive machinery all resist. International bodies can monitor, report and shame; beyond that, compliance depends on domestic courts, a free press and civil society.
offers the decisive rebuttal: Asia contains sixty per cent of humanity and an immense diversity of traditions, so there is no single ‘Asian value’; and freedom is not un-Asian — in
he cites Ashoka’s edicts on toleration and Akbar’s

as indigenous roots of liberty. The critique rightly warns against ethnocentric imposition, but hardens into a shield for authoritarian denial; the way forward is a negotiated basic minimum, monitored internationally yet advanced through dialogue rather than coercion.
Q — Discuss multiculturalism and minority rights, with special reference to Kymlicka and Bhikhu Parekh.
Explain why equal treatment may require unequal rights → give Kymlicka’s and Parekh’s schemes → weigh the feminist and liberal objections.
— grew out of the liberal–communitarian debate: identity is culturally embedded, so identical treatment can entrench disadvantage.
(A uniform dress code silently excludes a turbaned Sikh.)
— a secure culture is the precondition of
; being born a minority is ‘bad brute luck’ deserving rectification (
Arts 29–30: minorities may run their own schools
the Fifth and Sixth Schedules’ autonomous tribal councils
— multiculturalism is the ‘creative interplay’ of embeddedness and plurality; universal norms must emerge through
(personal laws can shield unequal maintenance or inheritance)
— accommodate difference, but bound it by a basic minimum of individual rights.

. Its premise is that culture is constitutive of identity and of the range of options from which a person chooses, so a formally neutral rule may in practice impose the majority’s culture — a uniform dress code or a Sunday holiday silently excludes the turbaned Sikh or the observant minority worker. Treating people as equals may therefore require not identical but
, argues that liberalism itself requires the protection of minority cultures, because a secure ‘societal culture’ is the context within which meaningful choice, and hence
, is possible. Being born into a vulnerable minority culture is ‘bad brute luck’ rather than a chosen disadvantage, and on his
premise the state owes its rectification. Multiculturalism is thus a completion of liberalism, not a departure from it.

protect distinctive religious and cultural practice — Articles 29 and 30 of the Indian Constitution permit minorities to conserve their script and to establish and administer their own educational institutions.
secure a political voice, as with reserved seats for Scheduled Castes and Tribes under Articles 330 and 332.

grant territorial autonomy, exemplified by the Fifth and Sixth Schedules with their autonomous district councils in the North-East. Crucially, he reserves the last for ‘national minorities’ incorporated involuntarily, not for voluntary immigrants.

, takes a post-colonial position: multiculturalism is the ‘creative interplay’ of cultural embeddedness and human plurality, and no culture is complete in itself. He finds no logic in denying special rights to non-citizen minorities, applies a
to test contested cultural practices rather than banning them wholesale, and insists that universal principles must be constructed through
, anchored in the shared value of
Feminists warn that protecting cultures can entrench patriarchy:

‘multiculturalism is bad for women’ argues that group rights typically empower male elders, and India’s personal-law debates over maintenance and inheritance illustrate the risk of internal minorities being sacrificed to external protection. Liberals such as
fear ‘ghettoisation’ and ‘plural monoculturalism’ — communities living side by side rather than together — with a corresponding weakening of shared citizenship.

Multiculturalism corrects the blindness of abstract equal treatment and is indispensable in deeply diverse societies such as India. But it must be bounded: group rights are legitimate as external protections against majority pressure, not as internal restrictions on dissenting members, so cultural accommodation must stop at the basic minimum of individual human rights.
Q — Assess the significance of the right to property in political theory. (UPSC 2020)
Trace why property is the most contested right — the liberal defence, the socialist attack, the social-liberal balance — and what its Indian career proves.
— property sits at the crossroads of
: securing one man’s freedom can entrench another’s subordination.
(Zamindari: title for one, tenancy for millions.)
saw it as corrupting (communism of the guardians),
: men ‘sooner forget the death of a father than the loss of patrimony’.
earned by mixing labour with nature;
: the engine of incentive and progress.
— private (productive) property is the basis of
and must serve the common good (
deleted Art 31 and demoted property from a
right (Art 300A) so land reform could proceed — property is conditional, not absolute.
Few rights have divided political theory as sharply as the right to property, precisely because it stands at the crossroads of

. As a bulwark of independence it shields the individual from the state; as an accumulation of power it reproduces inequality across generations. Colonial India furnishes the illustration: the permanent settlement created secure proprietary title for the zamindar and precarious tenancy for millions, so the same right simultaneously guaranteed freedom and entrenched subordination.
regarded property as a source of corruption and faction, and abolished it for the guardian class so that rulers might have no private interest distinct from the city’s.
replied that private ownership is a school of virtue — it teaches prudence, liberality and responsibility, and what is common to all is cared for by none.
added the political observation that men ‘sooner forget the death of their father than the loss of their patrimony’, warning princes never to touch their subjects’ possessions.

antecedent to government: by mixing his labour with nature a man makes a thing his own, and the protection of ‘lives, liberties and estates’ is the very end for which the state is instituted — the core of what
defended it on utilitarian grounds as the indispensable engine of incentive, security and social progress, an argument echoed today in evidence that secure land titling raises investment.
, private property in the means of production is the very

, generating exploitation through surplus value and the alienation of the worker from his product, his labour and himself; they carefully distinguish personal from productive property, abolishing only the latter.
aphorism ‘property is theft’ compresses the charge, and
had already traced civil inequality to the first man who enclosed a plot and said ‘this is mine’.
, treats property as an instrument of the
rather than an absolute claim, while
