contentText: Syllabus — Democracy: classical and contemporary theories; different models of democracy — representative, participatory and deliberative. (UPSC PSIR Paper-1A, Unit 6) Unit Snapshot What this unit covers:  the meaning and evolution of democracy; the democracy-development debate (Lee Kuan Yew vs Amartya Sen); classical/normative vs modern/empirical theories (elitist and pluralist — the ‘Dahl-Schumpeter axis’); Macpherson’s radical/substantive theory; procedural vs substantive democracy; the models — representative, participative and deliberative; and why democracy survived in India. Must-know thinkers:  Herodotus, Plato, Aristotle, J.S. Mill, Schumpeter, Robert Dahl, Macpherson, Pareto, Mosca, Michels, Rousseau, Edmund Burke, Habermas, Joshua Cohen, Nancy Fraser, Hannah Arendt, Carole Pateman, Lee Kuan Yew, Amartya Sen, David Held, Larry Diamond, Huntington. PYQ trend:  deliberative democracy (2019), Macpherson (2018), deliberation vs participation (2017), representative democracy (2016), and the democracy–development / Asian-values debate. Master Questions Q — Critically examine the classical (normative) versus modern (empirical) theories of democracy, and evaluate the elitist-pluralist ‘Dahl-Schumpeter axis’. What it’s asking:  Set the two families of democratic theory against each other, then judge whether the elitist-pluralist account of democracy is adequate. Gist — the spine to recall 1. The divide  — classical theory asks what democracy OUGHT to be, modern theory describes what it IS.  (Ought: has the vote improved the Dalit voter’s life? Is: which party won the seat, and by what margin?) 2. Classical / normative  — the  protective  model ( Locke, Bentham ) and the  developmental  model ( J.S. Mill, Green, Laski ).  (Protective: the vote as a shield against arbitrary power; developmental: the vote as a school of citizenship) 3. Elitist realism  —  Pareto’s  circulation of elites and  Michels’   iron law of oligarchy .  (Even a party founded to end elite rule ends up run by a tiny high command that picks every candidate — ‘who says organisation says oligarchy’) 4. Schumpeter  — democracy is only a  ‘competitive struggle for the people’s vote’ .  (Elections as a market: parties are firms, manifestos are advertising, votes are the currency and the citizen merely a buyer between sale seasons) 5. Dahl’s polyarchy  — not rule by ‘the people’ but dispersed bargaining among many groups.  (India: multiple parties, a free press, an independent EC, farmer lobbies and trade unions all pulling — an ‘approximate’, never ideal, democracy) 6. Macpherson’s verdict  — the  ‘Dahl-Schumpeter axis’  reduces democracy to a market equilibrium; the empirical is realistic but hollow, the classical noble but impractical. Model Answer 1. The divide.  C.B. Macpherson  splits democratic theory into a  classical (normative)  and a  modern (empirical)  family. The first is prescriptive, asking what democracy ought to achieve — whether the vote has actually improved the life of the Dalit or the landless labourer. The second is descriptive, recording only how democratic machinery in fact operates — who won which seat, by what margin, on what turnout. The quarrel between them is the quarrel between  substantive  and  procedural  conceptions of democracy. 2. Classical / normative.  Rooted in the Greek  polis , these theories locate democracy’s worth in its purpose. The  protective  model of  Locke  and  Bentham  prizes democracy as a shield — the vote protects life, liberty and property against arbitrary power. The  developmental  model of  J.S. Mill ,  T.H. Green  and  Laski  prizes it as a school — participation itself develops human personality, which is why Mill wanted the citizen to be an active, not a passive, being. Their weakness is that they stand ‘divorced from real-world dynamics’. 3. Elitist realism.  The modern reply begins with the elitists.  Pareto  and  Mosca  hold that a minority always rules, power passing by a ‘circulation of elites’ from lions to foxes.  Robert Michels , in  Political Parties , states the  iron law of oligarchy : organisation itself breeds rule by the few. The illustration is exact — a party founded to end elite domination soon becomes a small high command that selects every candidate and dictates the whip, the mass membership being reduced to applause. 4. Schumpeter.  Joseph Schumpeter , in  Capitalism, Socialism and Democracy , converts this realism into a definition: democracy is “an institutional arrangement in which individuals acquire the power to decide by means of a  competitive struggle for the people’s vote ”. The analogy is frankly commercial — parties are firms, manifestos advertising, votes the currency, and the citizen a buyer whose sovereignty lasts only until polling day. Democracy thus becomes a  method  of choosing rulers, not a form of self-rule. 5. Dahl’s polyarchy.  Robert Dahl , in  A Preface to Democratic Theory , answers the elitists with  polyarchy  — an ‘approximate democracy’ in which no single elite rules because power is dispersed through decentralised bargaining among many relatively autonomous groups, secured by rights, a free press, party competition and fair elections. India illustrates it: multiple parties, an independent Election Commission, farmer lobbies and trade unions all bargaining. Yet Dahl later conceded  ‘pluralist stagnation’  — organised groups produce ‘government overload’ and the unorganised go unheard. 6. Macpherson’s verdict.  Macpherson  collapses both into a single  ‘Dahl-Schumpeter axis’ : whether one speaks of elite competition or group bargaining, democracy is reduced from a humanist aspiration to a  market equilibrium system  in which demand meets supply and nothing more is asked. The empirical theories are therefore realistic but hollow, the classical noble but impractical — which is precisely why Macpherson seeks to recover democracy’s substantive promise without discarding its liberal institutions. Q — “Democracy is a humanist aspiration, not a market equilibrium system.” Critically examine Macpherson’s radical/substantive theory of democracy. (UPSC 2018) What it’s asking:  Explain what Macpherson is attacking, what he puts in its place, and whether it stands up to criticism. Gist — the spine to recall 1. The target  — the  Dahl-Schumpeter axis  treats democracy as a  market equilibrium system .  (Politics as shopping: parties supply promises, voters spend votes, and the transaction ends at the polling booth) 2. The humanist vision  — democracy exists for the  empowerment of the masses  and each person’s creative freedom.  (Not merely counting a slum-dweller’s vote, but enabling her to live a life she has reason to value) 3. Two powers  —  developmental  (using one’s own capacities) vs  extractive  (living off another’s).  (A bonded labourer’s toil is extracted by the landlord; schooling, land and MGNREGA wages restore his developmental power) 4. The test of a democracy  — no one holds extractive power and all have equal developmental power; hence  social ownership  plus liberal institutions, and goods by  need not desert . 5. No Western monopoly  — three valid variants: liberal democracy ‘with a human touch’, communist systems with real intra-party democracy, and third-world systems legitimised by mass enthusiasm. 6. Critique & verdict  —  Norman Barry : he judges real liberalism against an ideal, never against real alternatives; still, he restores democracy’s  substantive  core. Model Answer 1. The target.  C.B. Macpherson , in  Democratic Theory: Essays in Retrieval , attacks the elitist-pluralist model of  Schumpeter  and  Dahl  — and behind them  Bentham’s  utilitarianism — for treating democracy as a  market equilibrium system . On that view politics is shopping: parties supply promises, voters spend their votes, and the transaction closes at the polling booth. Against it he insists that ‘democracy is not just a procedure; it is about the  empowerment of the masses ’. 2. The humanist vision.  Democracy’s essence for Macpherson is  creative freedom  — every individual ‘realising his creative faculties’. The test is therefore not whether a slum-dweller’s vote was counted but whether she is enabled to live a life she has reason to value. This is a deliberate return to the  developmental  tradition of  J.S. Mill  and  Green , now given a radical, egalitarian edge that the classical liberals never drew. 3. Two powers.  The vision rests on a distinction.  Developmental power  is a person’s capacity to use and extend her own faculties;  extractive power  is power over others, the ability to appropriate the fruits of their labour. A bonded labourer illustrates both at once: his creative energy exists, but it is extracted by the landlord. Schooling, land reform and guaranteed wages transfer power back from the extractive to the developmental column — which for Macpherson is what democratisation actually means. 4. The test of a democracy.  A genuinely democratic society is one ‘where  no one has extractive power over another and all have equal developmental power ’. Because extractive power flows from ownership, this requires combining  social ownership  of the means of production with the institutions of liberal democracy — rights, elections and opposition — and distributing goods by  need rather than desert . Macpherson thus refuses both the liberal’s procedural minimalism and the Marxist’s contempt for liberal institutions. 5. No Western monopoly.  Consistently with this, he denies the West any proprietary claim over democracy. He accepts three equally valid variants if their conditions are met: liberal democracy ‘with more human touch’, communist systems that practise full intra-party democracy, and third-world systems ‘legitimised by mass enthusiasm’ born of anti-colonial struggle. The criterion is always substantive — the actual distribution of developmental power — not the presence of a particular institutional form. 6. Critique and verdict.  Norman Barry  objects that Macpherson measures existing liberal democracy against an idealised standard rather than against the real alternatives on offer, which is an unfair benchmark; critics also doubt that social ownership can be married to liberal freedoms in practice. Even so, his radical theory restores the  substantive , emancipatory core that the empirical theories abandoned — democracy is finally about human self-development, not the counting of votes. Q — Distinguish the representative, participative and deliberative models of democracy, and explicate the features and criticisms of representative democracy. (UPSC 2016) What it’s asking:  First separate the three models cleanly, then do the heavy lifting on representative democracy — its merits and its standard criticisms. Gist — the spine to recall 1. The three models  — representative (we elect rulers), participative (we act ourselves), deliberative (we reason before deciding).  (One village road: an MLA sanctions it / villagers build and audit it / the Gram Sabha argues out where it should run) 2. Representative democracy  — indirect rule;  J.S. Mill  in  Considerations on Representative Government  called direct democracy best and representation ‘the second best’. 3. Delegate vs trustee  —  Locke/Bentham  bind the representative to a mandate;  Burke  gives him judgement.  (An MP under the anti-defection whip is a delegate; one voting his conscience on a social reform Bill is a trustee) 4. Why it is defended  — the only practicable form at scale, it spares citizens daily decision-making and gives government to those with education and expertise.  (No assembly can seat India’s 96-crore electorate) 5. Criticisms  — Mill’s  tyranny of the majority ;  Rousseau : ‘the English are free only once in five years’;  Schumpeter : popular sovereignty is a ‘mistaken belief’.  (Gandhi, M.N. Roy and JP therefore wanted party-less democracy) 6. Verdict  — indispensable for scale but merely  procedural ; hence the move to participative and deliberative models to make it  substantive . Model Answer 1. The three models.  The three mark a deepening of democracy — from choosing rulers, to acting oneself, to reasoning together. One village road shows all three: an elected MLA sanctions it (representative); the villagers execute and socially audit it (participative); the Gram Sabha argues out where it should run and whose land it crosses (deliberative). Each successive model treats the previous one as necessary but thin, supplying respectively legitimacy of authorisation, of involvement, and of reasoned justification. 2. Representative democracy.  This is indirect rule: citizens do not govern but elect those who do.  J.S. Mill , in  Considerations on Representative Government , conceded that direct democracy is ideally the best form, but held representative government to be ‘the second best’ and the only one available to a modern state. It is thus a device of necessity, converting the sovereign people into an electorate whose authority is exercised at one remove. 3. Delegate vs trustee.  Two theories of the representative follow. The  delegate  model of  Locke  and  Bentham  binds him to the electors’ mandate — ‘government is a trust’ and the representative merely a conduit. The  trustee or enlightened  model of  Edmund Burke  insists that ‘parliament is the assembly of the nation’, so the member owes his constituents his judgement, not obedience. Indian practice contains both: an MP bound by the anti-defection whip acts as a delegate, while one voting his conscience on a social reform Bill acts as a trustee. 4. Why it is defended.  Its merits are practical. It is the only form  practicable  in large, complex societies — no assembly can seat an electorate of ninety-six crore. It relieves ordinary citizens of the burden of continuous decision-making, leaving them free for productive life. And it places government in the hands of those with ‘education and expert knowledge’, which is precisely why the elitists, from  Burke  to  Schumpeter , prefer it to direct rule. 5. Criticisms.  Mill’s own anxiety was the  ‘tyranny of the majority’  — a numerical majority silencing minorities through the very machinery of representation.  Rousseau  mocked that ‘the English are free only once in five years’, sovereignty lapsing the moment the ballot is cast.  Schumpeter  went further, calling popular sovereignty a ‘mistaken belief’ since real power rests with representatives. In India  Gandhi ,  M.N. Roy  and  Jayaprakash Narayan  drew the radical conclusion and favoured a ‘party-less democracy’ of self-governing communities. 6. Verdict.  Representative democracy is indispensable for scale but insufficient for substance: it secures the  procedural  conditions — free elections, competition, accountability — without guaranteeing the  substantive  ones of equal and engaged citizenship. That gap is what drives theory onward to  participative  democracy ( Rousseau, Pateman ) and  deliberative  democracy ( Habermas ), each correcting the thinness of mere representation. Q — “Free and fair deliberation is the foundation of democracy.” Examine deliberative democracy and its critics. (UPSC 2019) What it’s asking:  Explain what deliberative democracy claims, who built it, and then test it against its critics and against real conditions. Gist — the spine to recall 1. The core claim  — legitimacy comes from reasoned public discussion, not from adding up votes.  (A Gram Sabha that argues out who the poorest beneficiary is legitimises the list; a show of hands without discussion merely records the dominant caste’s strength) 2. Habermas  — the  ideal speech situation  in the  public sphere : equal right and chance to speak, honest speech, and ‘no force except the force of the better argument’.  (Modelled on the 18th-century coffee house where rank was left at the door) 3. Joshua Cohen  — an ongoing association where deliberation is the sole route to policy, non-coercive, pluralism-accepting, and itself the  source of legitimacy . 4. Nancy Fraser  — the  ‘counter-public’  for subaltern voices excluded from the main sphere.  (Mahila Sabhas and SHG forums where women frame demands they could not voice before the men) 5. Critics  —  Waldron  defends majority rule among equals;  Dworkin : ‘the virtues of majoritarianism are exaggerated’, democracy rests on rights.  (And access is unequal — Gram Sabhas where the sarpanch-pati speaks for elected women) 6. Verdict  — it deepens democracy through public reason ( Sen : issues are addressed ‘only when they become matters of public debate’) but works only where free and equal speech is real. Model Answer 1. The core claim.  Deliberative democracy holds that a decision’s legitimacy flows not from the mere aggregation of preferences but from  reasoned public discussion  among those it affects. Democracy is ‘not the game of numbers but the right argument’, and as Pericles said, ‘discussion is an essential prerequisite for any wise action’. The contrast is visible in a Gram Sabha: a list of beneficiaries argued out in the open, with reasons given and challenged, binds the village — a bare show of hands merely records the dominant caste’s numbers. 2. Habermas.  Jurgen Habermas  supplies the foundation. Legitimate norms emerge only from  communicative action  in the  public sphere , whose historical model he finds in the coffee houses of eighteenth-century Europe, where rank was left at the door and only argument counted. His  ideal speech situation  sets four conditions: an equal right to speak, an equal chance to speak, honest speech, and ‘no force except the force of the better argument’. Power and status must be bracketed for reason to operate. 3. Joshua Cohen.  Cohen  translates the ideal into institutional features. Deliberative democracy is an ongoing association in which deliberation is the sole route to policy; the setting is free and non-coercive; pluralism of ends is accepted rather than suppressed; and deliberation is treated as the very  source of legitimacy , not a decorative preliminary to voting. In sum, the model gives ‘priority to voice over choice, debate over voting’. 4. Nancy Fraser.  Fraser  adds the feminist correction: a single public sphere is never neutral, because the terms of respectable speech are set by the dominant. She therefore proposes the  ‘counter-public’  — alternative arenas in which subaltern groups formulate their own interpretations of their needs. Mahila Sabhas and self-help-group forums illustrate this: women articulate demands there which they could not raise in a general body dominated by men. 5. Critics.  Jeremy Waldron  defends a  majoritarian  model — among political equals who disagree in good faith, counting heads is itself a form of respect, and endless deliberation privileges the articulate.  Ronald Dworkin  replies that ‘the virtues of majoritarianism are exaggerated’ because democracy ‘is based on rights’, which no discussion may bargain away. The practical objection is sharper still: access to the public sphere is unequal, as where an elected woman sarpanch is spoken for by her husband. 6. Verdict.  Deliberation deepens democracy by grounding it in public reason rather than raw numbers, and by converting preferences into justifications that can be publicly defended.  Amartya Sen  captures its practical force — issues are addressed ‘only when they become matters of public debate’. But it is a demanding ideal: it delivers only where the conditions of free, equal and informed speech are genuinely met, which is why it must be paired with the empowerment of participants, not merely with more forums. Q — “Deliberative democracy has no salience without participation, and participatory democracy no credence without deliberation.” Comment. (UPSC 2017) What it’s asking:  Show that participation and deliberation are mutually dependent — each is defective without the other — and say what the pair together produce. Gist — the spine to recall 1. The two terms  — participation is citizens acting; deliberation is citizens reasoning before deciding.  (A Gram Sabha with full attendance but no debate vs a well-argued meeting attended by twelve people) 2. Participation needs deliberation  — head-count without reasoning collapses into populism or tokenism.  (Quorum-filling Gram Sabhas where resolutions are read out and signed) 3. Deliberation needs participation  — debate confined to an elite excludes the very people whose consent legitimises it ( Habermas ,  Cohen ). 4. The progression  — representative  →  participative  →  deliberative: representation authorises, participation supplies the  base , deliberation the  quality . 5. The synthesis  —  Arendt’s  acting citizen ( zoon politikon ) plus  Habermas’  reasoning citizen yields  substantive , not merely procedural, democracy.  (Social audit under MGNREGA: villagers both attend and interrogate the muster roll) 6. Verdict  — numbers without reason are blind, reason without numbers is empty; a mature democracy fuses the two. Model Answer 1. The two terms.  The statement links the two moves that carry democracy beyond representation.  Participation  means citizens actively involved in decisions rather than voting once in five years;  deliberation  means reasoning together, publicly and with justification, before deciding. The contrast is easily seen: a Gram Sabha with full attendance but no debate, and a well-argued meeting attended by a dozen people, are defective in opposite ways — the first lacks quality, the second lacks base. 2. Participation needs deliberation.  Wider participation — of ‘tribals, Dalits, women and minorities’ — confers  legitimacy , and  Hannah Arendt  makes participation in the public realm the highest form of human action, man being  zoon politikon . But participation reduced to mere presence ‘has no credence’: quorum-filling Gram Sabhas where resolutions are read out and signed produce numbers without judgement, and such unreasoned mobilisation slides easily into populism or tokenism. 3. Deliberation needs participation.  Habermas’  ideal of communicative action and  Cohen’s  deliberative features both presuppose that those affected actually take part; otherwise the ‘ideal speech situation’ is satisfied only among those already admitted to the room. Deliberation confined to a narrow elite of experts and editorialists ‘has no salience’, because it excludes precisely the people whose consent is supposed to legitimise the outcome. 4. The progression.  The models therefore form a sequence rather than a menu: representative democracy authorises government but leaves the citizen passive; participative democracy supplies the democratic  base  by drawing the excluded in; deliberative democracy supplies its  quality  by subjecting decisions to public reason. Each stage presupposes the last — which is why ‘deliberation is the heart and soul of democracy’ only where participation has already been secured. 5. The synthesis.  Fused, the two produce  substantive  rather than merely procedural democracy:  Arendt’s  acting citizen supplies energy and inclusion,  Habermas’  reasoning citizen supplies discipline and justification. The social audit under MGNREGA is the working example — villagers must both attend in numbers and interrogate the muster roll line by line; either half alone leaves the audit worthless. 6. Verdict.  Participation and deliberation are thus two sides of one coin: numbers without reason are blind, and reason without numbers is empty. A mature democracy institutionalises both — forums that are genuinely open and genuinely argumentative — which is the standard against which India’s Panchayati Raj and its national debates alike must be judged. Q — Examine the democracy–development debate (Lee Kuan Yew vs Amartya Sen). Is democracy a ‘Western value’ incompatible with ‘Asian values’? What it’s asking:  Two linked questions — does democracy retard development, and is it culturally alien to Asia? State the Lee thesis, then demolish it with Sen. Gist — the spine to recall 1. The issue  — whether a poor country must choose between votes and growth, and whether democracy is a cultural import.  (The India-China growth comparison is the standard exhibit) 2. The Lee thesis  —  Lee Kuan Yew : democracy brings ‘populist policies and extraordinary delay in decision-making’; China grew faster ‘free from the bondages of democratic rule’.  (A land-acquisition project cleared in months there, litigated for years here) 3. The Asian-values claim  — democracy as a ‘Western obsession’; Asia prefers discipline, community and social solidarity, hence a ‘semi-authoritarian guided democracy’. 4. Sen’s rebuttal  — the two are ‘not mutually exclusive but interdependent’;  development as freedom , not mere GDP.  (Democratic Botswana grew fast; authoritarian regimes have grown and collapsed alike — the evidence is not there) 5. The famine argument  — no famine in India since 1947 because a  free press  forces corrective action; some 30 million died in China’s 1958–61 famine, unreported.  (Sen prefers the Kerala model to the Gujarat model) 6. Verdict  — democracy has  intrinsic, institutional and educational  value, and Indian roots ( The Argumentative Indian ): develop  through  democracy, not by suspending it. Model Answer 1. The issue.  The debate poses two questions at once: does democracy help or hinder development, and is it a value native only to the West? The standard exhibit is the India-China comparison — two continental economies starting from similar poverty in mid-century, one democratic and one not. Behind it lies a larger claim about whether poor societies must first accept discipline and postpone liberty, an argument with obvious appeal to every developmental autocrat. 2. The Lee thesis.  Lee Kuan Yew  argues that democracy obstructs development. He blames Indian democracy for ‘populist policies and extraordinary delay in decision-making’ — the project cleared in months in China but litigated and agitated for years here — and praises China’s faster growth as being ‘free from the bondages of democratic rule’. On this view the vote is a luxury good, affordable only after prosperity has been engineered from above. 3. The Asian-values claim.  Lee reinforces the economic argument with a cultural one: democracy is a  ‘Western obsession’  resting on individualism, whereas  Asian values  prize communitarianism, discipline, deference and social solidarity. He therefore prefers a ‘semi-authoritarian guided democracy’ which retains elections while insulating decision-making from popular pressure — authority tempered by consultation rather than constrained by opposition. 4. Sen’s rebuttal.  Amartya Sen  replies that democracy and development are ‘not mutually exclusive but interdependent’, and that ‘development cannot be equated merely to economic growth’: it is  ‘development as freedom’ , the expansion of capabilities of which political liberty is itself a part. The Lee thesis, he shows, rests on ‘questionable assumptions and insufficient evidence’ — democratic  Botswana  recorded some of the fastest growth in Africa, while many authoritarian regimes stagnated. Selecting two cases proves nothing. 5. The famine argument.  Sen’s decisive empirical point is the famine record: ‘India has suffered no famine since independence’, despite droughts and poverty, whereas around thirty million died in China’s 1958–61 famine. The mechanism is political, not agricultural — a  free press  and an opposition make hunger visible and force ‘corrective action’, while in China the failure went unreported and therefore uncorrected. Within India, Sen praises the  Kerala model  of literacy, health and public action over the growth-first Gujarat model. 6. Verdict.  Sen assigns democracy three values —  intrinsic  (participation is itself a source of self-worth),  institutional  (it makes government accountable and responsive) and  educational  (public debate forms informed, responsible citizens). Nor is it a Western import:  The Argumentative Indian  traces deliberation and tolerance from Ashoka and Akbar onwards. Development is best secured  through  democracy — the Lee thesis mistakes a short-run trade-off for a permanent law. Q — “Good governance is achievable only by strengthening grass-root democracy.” Discuss participatory democracy, the global democratic deficit, and why democracy survived in India. What it’s asking:  Argue that good governance is bottom-up: define participatory democracy, extend the logic globally, and explain India’s democratic durability. Gist — the spine to recall 1. The claim  — good governance (accountable, inclusive, responsive rule) depends on deepening democracy at the base, not on better rule from the top. 2. Rousseau, the pioneer  — ‘sovereignty cannot be represented’; participation is ‘a precondition for freedom’.  (Obeying a law you helped frame is freedom; obeying one framed for you is not) 3. Indian institutionalisation  — the  73rd/74th Amendments  made Panchayati Raj and the Gram Sabha constitutional.  (Plus RTI, social audit, citizens’ charters and reservation for women and SC/STs; non-institutional forms are social movements) 4. Pateman and Ostrom  — participation is  educative , realises the general will and makes democracy inclusive;  Ostrom  shows communities manage commons sustainably.  (Village forest and tank management) 5. The global democratic deficit  — states democratised, the world order did not ( Stiglitz );  Held’s   cosmopolitan democracy  would reform the UNSC, IMF and World Bank.  (India’s permanent-seat claim is this argument in practice) 6. Why India’s democracy survived  — elite commitment (Nehru), the national movement, British parliamentary institutions, the  argumentative tradition , a free press, judiciary and EC, sheer diversity, and civil-military separation. Model Answer 1. The claim.  Good governance — accountable, transparent, participatory and inclusive rule — cannot be manufactured at the top and delivered downwards; it depends on the density of democracy at the base. Where citizens decide, monitor and audit locally, administration becomes responsive because it is answerable to those it serves. Grass-root or  participatory democracy  is therefore not a supplement to good governance but its condition, converting beneficiaries into claim-making citizens. 2. Rousseau, the pioneer.  Rousseau  is the fountainhead of the participatory tradition. Holding that ‘sovereignty cannot be represented’, he made participation ‘a precondition for freedom’: to obey a law one has helped frame is liberty, to obey one framed for you is subjection, however benevolent the framer. His general will is thus not an aggregate of preferences but the product of citizens acting together, which is why he condemned representative government as a lapse from self-rule. 3. Indian institutionalisation.  India has given this the strongest constitutional expression among large democracies. The  73rd and 74th Amendments  made panchayats and municipalities constitutional bodies with regular elections, reservation for women and SC/STs, and the  Gram Sabha  as the deliberating assembly of all voters. Around it sit RTI, social audit and citizens’ charters, and beyond the state the  non-institutionalised  channel of social movements — Narmada, the right-to-food and MKSS campaigns — which participate by contesting. 4. Pateman and Ostrom.  Carole Pateman  identifies three benefits: participation is  educative , teaching citizens the discipline of public reasoning; it realises the general will rather than a bargained compromise; and it makes democracy inclusive by drawing in those whom representation leaves silent.  Elinor Ostrom  adds hard evidence that self-governing communities manage common-pool resources — village forests, tanks and pastures — sustainably, refuting the claim that only states or markets can. 5. The global democratic deficit.  Democracy has spread among states without the  world order  itself becoming democratic:  Stiglitz  notes the ‘democratic deficit’ of global institutions where weighted voting and veto power override numbers.  David Held’s   cosmopolitan model of democracy  answers it by proposing reform of the UN Security Council, IMF and World Bank, regional parliaments, entrenched cosmopolitan law and even global referenda. India’s claim to a permanent seat is this argument in practice. 6. Why India’s democracy survived.  Against the third-world trend, several factors held: the commitment of the political elite, above all  Nehru’s  scrupulous constitutionalism; the legacy of a mass national movement that had already taught mobilisation and debate; inherited British parliamentary institutions and a professional civil service; the  argumentative tradition   Sen  documents; enabling constitutional provisions — a free press, independent judiciary and Election Commission; the country’s very size and diversity, which made any single dominant bloc impossible; and a strict separation of civil and military authority. Good governance is thus finally bottom-up, and reforming global institutions merely extends the same logic beyond the nation-state. Revision Box — facts, keywords & quotes Herodotus  first used ‘democracy’ (5th c. BC);  Lincoln : ‘government of/by/for the people’. Plato  decried democracy;  Aristotle : a ‘perverted’ form, prefers a mixed constitution. Classical (normative):  protective (Locke/Bentham) + developmental (Mill/Green/Laski) models. Modern (empirical):  elitist (Pareto circulation of elites; Michels iron law of oligarchy) + pluralist. Schumpeter : democracy = ‘competitive struggle for the people’s vote’;  Dahl : ‘polyarchy’. Macpherson : ‘Dahl-Schumpeter axis’ reduces democracy to a ‘market equilibrium system’; developmental vs extractive power. Procedural  (institutions) vs  substantive  (equal, engaged citizens; welfare) democracy. Representation:  delegate model (Locke/Bentham) vs trustee model (Burke, Mill). Rousseau : ‘sovereignty cannot be represented’; ‘English free only once in five years’ — pioneer of participatory democracy. Habermas : ideal speech situation + communicative action + public sphere; ‘force of the better argument’. Joshua Cohen : features of deliberative democracy;  Nancy Fraser : ‘counter-public’. Carole Pateman : participation is educative, realises general will, makes democracy inclusive. Lee thesis  (Lee Kuan Yew): democracy slows development, a ‘Western obsession’;  Sen : development as freedom; free press prevents famine. Sen’s 3 values:  intrinsic, institutional, educational. David Held : cosmopolitan model of democracy for the global democratic deficit;  Huntington : three waves of democratisation. Why India’s democracy survived:  elite commitment, national movement, British institutions, argumentative tradition, diversity, civil-military separation. Last-Minute Revision Sheet (1 page) Classical vs modern (M1):  normative (protective/developmental) vs empirical (elitist + pluralist); Dahl-Schumpeter axis = market view. Macpherson (M2):  democracy = humanist empowerment; developmental vs extractive power; social ownership + liberal institutions; Norman Barry’s critique. Three models (M3):  representative (delegate/trustee; tyranny of majority) → participative (Rousseau/Pateman) → deliberative. Deliberative (M4):  Habermas ideal speech + public sphere; Cohen features; Fraser counter-public; voice over choice; Waldron vs Dworkin. Participation + deliberation (M5):  participation = base (Arendt), deliberation = quality (Habermas); each incomplete without the other. Democracy-development (M6):  Lee thesis (authoritarian growth) vs Sen (development as freedom; famine argument; 3 values); Asian values. Grass-root + global (M7):  participatory democracy (Rousseau/Pateman/Ostrom); Held’s cosmopolitan model; why India’s democracy survived. Killer quotes:  Schumpeter — ‘competitive struggle for the vote’; Macpherson — ‘market equilibrium system’; Rousseau — ‘free only once in five years’; Sen — ‘development as freedom’. Q — Distinguish between power and authority, and discuss the relationship between power, authority and legitimacy with reference to Weber and Beetham. (UPSC 2015/2018)

Define legitimacy, then explain WHY Habermas thinks capitalist democracies keep losing it — and why they nevertheless survive.

Legitimacy is the belief in the

of a government’s rule — the quality that converts naked power into accepted authority, so that citizens obey even measures they dislike because they regard the regime as their own. In modern liberal democracies its principal source is the democratic, electoral process: rulers are obeyed because they were chosen by a procedure the ruled accept as fair.

Competitive elections multiply promises — subsidised power, loan waivers, universal health care — that no exchequer dependent on private accumulation can fully honour. The chain therefore runs: democratic pressure → rising public spending and expanding state responsibilities → higher taxation, fiscal strain and inflation → a squeeze on capital accumulation, which in turn reduces the surplus available for welfare.

The legitimation-crisis thesis exposes the deep tension between
