contentText: Syllabus — Power, hegemony, ideology and legitimacy. (UPSC PSIR Paper-1A, Unit 7) Unit Snapshot What this unit covers:  the meaning, forms and dimensions of power (Lukes’ three faces; conventional vs constructive views); theories of power (elitist, pluralist, Marxist, feminist, Foucauldian); authority (Weber’s three types) and the power–authority–legitimacy relationship; Habermas’ legitimation crisis; the concept of ideology and the ‘end of ideology’ (Bell) and ‘end of history’ (Fukuyama) debates; and Gramsci’s concept of hegemony. Must-know thinkers:  Bertrand Russell, Robert Dahl, Hannah Arendt, Steven Lukes, Pareto, Mosca, Michels, C. Wright Mills, C.B. Macpherson, Michel Foucault, Max Weber, David Beetham, Habermas, Karl Marx, Mannheim, Daniel Bell, Fukuyama, Huntington, Antonio Gramsci. PYQ trend:  nature/meaning of power (2020), Arendt on power as group property (2014), power–authority–legitimacy (2018), power vs authority (2015), ideology & power (2021); Gramsci’s hegemony/organic intellectuals (2013/2015/2016/2019). Master Questions Q — Examine the nature, meaning and forms of power, and analyse the conventional versus constructive views (especially Hannah Arendt) and Lukes’ three dimensions. (UPSC 2020/2014) What it’s asking:  Define power → contrast the ‘power over’ and ‘power with’ views → show its three depths and its forms. Gist — the spine to recall 1. Meaning  — power is the capacity to secure compliance even against another’s will.  (A lockdown order is obeyed because disobedience invites arrest.)   Lasswell & Kaplan : politics is ‘the shaping and sharing of power’. 2. Conventional view — domination :  Russell  — ‘the production of intended effects’;  Dahl  — compliance won by ‘the prospect of severe sanctions’.  (Power is a thing rulers own and use downwards, like a fine or a jail term.) 3. Constructive view —  Arendt : power is ‘acting in concert’ and ‘belongs to a group’, never an individual.  (A satyagraha crowd has power only while it stays together; violence ‘can destroy power but never create it’.) 4. Lukes’ three faces  —  (i) an open decision: a Bill voted through Parliament; (ii) agenda-setting: a demand kept off the agenda so it is never debated; (iii) thought-control: a daughter who never even wants her share of ancestral land. 5. Forms  —  political  (offices and processes),  economic  (means of production),  ideological  —  Marx & Engels : ‘the ideas of the ruling class are in every epoch the ruling ideas’. 6. Conclusion  — power runs from open command to the silent shaping of desire; controlling ideas can outweigh controlling force. Model Answer 1. Meaning.  Power is the master concept of politics —  Lasswell and Kaplan  defined political science itself as ‘the study of the shaping and sharing of power’. In its simplest sense it is the capacity to secure compliance, if necessary against resistance: a lockdown order is obeyed because disobedience invites arrest. It is distinguished from  influence , which is mere external pressure or persuasion, in that power is  binding  on the one who obeys. 2. Conventional view — power as domination.  The conventional or  ‘power over’  view treats power as domination exercised downward.  Bertrand Russell  defined it as ‘the production of intended effects’;  Robert Dahl  as A’s ability to make B do what B would not otherwise do, compliance being secured ‘by creating the prospect of severe sanctions’. Power here is a  possession  — something rulers hold and deploy through fines, penalties and force. 3. Constructive view — Arendt.  Hannah Arendt  rejects this command–obedience model: power is not domination but  ‘acting in concert’ . Hence ‘power is never the property of an individual; it belongs to a group and exists only so long as the group holds together’ — a mass satyagraha has power precisely while it coheres, and none the moment it disperses. She therefore separates power from violence: ‘violence can destroy power but is utterly incapable of creating it’, and ‘only power, never violence, can create legitimate authority’. 4. Lukes’ three dimensions.  Steven Lukes  shows power operating at three depths. The  first face  is open  decision-making  — who prevails when a Bill is put to the vote, since ‘power lies in offices’. The  second face  is  agenda-setting  — the power of  non-decision : an inconvenient demand is simply kept off the order paper so that it is never debated at all. The  third face  is  thought-control  — shaping people’s very preferences, so that a daughter never even wants her legal share of ancestral property. This last is exemplified by  Gramsci’s  hegemony and  Foucault’s  power. 5. Forms of power.  Power takes  political  form (the organs and processes that resolve conflict — Alan Ball),  economic  form (control of the means of production) and  ideological  form; for  Marx and Engels , ‘the ideas of the ruling class are in every epoch the ruling ideas’. Power therefore runs through the whole of society and not merely through the state. 6. Conclusion.  Power is thus more than coercion: the conventional view captures domination,  Arendt  captures its collective and legitimating side, and  Lukes  shows it operating from open decisions down to the silent shaping of desire — which is why controlling ideas can be more powerful than controlling force. Q — Critically examine the major theories of power — elitist, pluralist, Marxist, feminist and Foucauldian. What it’s asking:  Take each school in turn and show WHERE it locates power — then judge which reading survives criticism. Gist — the spine to recall 1. The core question  — every theory answers ‘who really rules?’  (Is it a small elite, many competing groups, the owning class, men as a group, or nobody in particular?) 2. Elitist  — a minority always rules:  Pareto  (circulation of lions and foxes),  Mosca ,  Michels ’ iron law of oligarchy.  (Even a party founded to serve workers ends up run by a handful of leaders.) 3. Pluralist  — power is dispersed among competing groups, government an ‘honest broker’ ( Dahl’s  polyarchy).  (Farmer unions, industry bodies and trade unions each win some rounds and lose others.) 4. Marxist & feminist  — power is structural: it follows ownership of the means of production, and  patriarchy  (‘rule of the father’).  (Property in a man’s name, and the household head deciding for the household.) 5. Foucauldian  — ‘power is everywhere’,  productive , flowing through knowledge and discipline.  (The school timetable and the prison’s Panopticon: the watched, never knowing when they are watched, police themselves.) 6. Conclusion  — the theories move power outward and inward at once; power is both concentrated in structures and diffused through daily life. Model Answer 1. The core question.  Theories of power differ on  where power lies  and who actually holds it — a small elite, a plurality of competing groups, the class that owns productive property, men as a sex, or no one in particular. Each answer carries a verdict on democracy: whether popular rule is real, a facade, or beside the point. 2. Elitist theory.  Pareto, Mosca and Michels  hold that a  minority always rules . Pareto’s ‘circulation of elites’ sees history as the endless replacement of ‘lions’ (force) by ‘foxes’ (cunning); Mosca posits an organised ‘ruling class’ facing a disorganised majority; and Michels’  ‘iron law of oligarchy’  holds that every organisation, however democratic in intent, is reduced to oligarchy — even a party founded to serve workers ends up run by a handful of leaders.  C. Wright Mills  locates a  ‘power elite’  at the ‘strategic command posts’ of society. 3. Pluralist theory.  Robert Dahl  and  Lindblom  reply that power is  dispersed  among autonomous groups that check and balance one another, with government acting as an ‘honest broker’ — Dahl’s  polyarchy , rule by many minorities rather than by one majority. Farmer unions, industry chambers and trade unions each win some rounds and lose others. Critics note that it studies only visible decisions and ignores ‘non-decisions’;  Lindblom  himself conceded the ‘privileged position of business’. 4. Marxist and feminist theory.  For Marxists, political power is the product of  economic power : the class that owns the means of production rules, the state being its instrument, and power precedes and outlives the state ( Lenin ). Feminists relocate domination in sex: society is divided by gender and  patriarchy  — literally ‘rule of the father’ — is its deepest structure, seen wherever property stands in a man’s name and the ‘head of the household’ decides for all; Marxist-feminists add that capitalism reinforces it. 5. Foucauldian/postmodern theory.  Michel Foucault  dissolves the idea of power as a possession: ‘power is everywhere and comes from everywhere’, diffused through  discourse, knowledge and ‘regimes of truth’ . Crucially it is  productive  rather than merely repressive — ‘power produces reality’, manufacturing the very subjects it governs. It works as  disciplinary power  through the school timetable, the asylum and the prison: in Bentham’s  Panopticon  the inmate, never knowing when he is being watched, ends up policing himself. Hence ‘knowledge is power’.  Chomsky  objects that he ‘wildly exaggerates’ power’s reach in science. 6. Conclusion.  Together the theories move power outward and inward at once — from the ruling elite and competing groups, to the owning class and patriarchy, to the capillaries of everyday knowledge in Foucault — showing that power is at once concentrated in structures and pervasive in ordinary life. Q — Distinguish between power and authority, and discuss the relationship between power, authority and legitimacy with reference to Weber and Beetham. (UPSC 2015/2018) What it’s asking:  First separate power from authority, then show that legitimacy is the bridge between them. Gist — the spine to recall 1. Power vs authority  — power secures compliance by force; authority is the recognised  right  to be obeyed.  (A robber with a gun and a traffic constable both stop your car — you obey the first from fear, the second because he is entitled to stop you.) 2. Authority = power + legitimacy  — ‘if power is a naked sword, authority is the sword in its scabbard’.  (Obedience is given willingly, so the sword need never be drawn.) 3. Weber’s three authorities  —  traditional   (a hereditary maharaja obeyed because his ancestors ruled) ,  charismatic   (a mass leader obeyed for his ‘extraordinary’ gifts) ,  rational-legal   (an IAS officer obeyed because rules put him in that office) . 4. Legitimacy  — the belief that rule is  rightful ; it ‘lies in the eyes of the beholder’.  (A government that wins every election is legal; whether people accept it as rightful is a further question.) 5.  Beetham’s  three conditions — power exercised by  rules , justified by a  shared belief  in those rules, and validated by  expressed consent .  Tyler : fair  procedure  matters more than outcomes. 6. Conclusion  — Weber explains the  grounds  of rightfulness, Beetham its  conditions ; stable rule rests on legitimacy, not force. Model Answer 1. Power versus authority.  Power and authority are related but distinct.  Power  is the capacity to secure compliance, if necessary by force or sanction;  authority  is the  recognised right  to be obeyed, obedience being given willingly because it is thought rightful. A robber with a gun and a traffic constable can both stop your car: you obey the first out of fear and the second because he is entitled to stop you. Power compels; authority commands. 2. Authority = power + legitimacy.  The relationship is captured in the maxim that ‘if power is a naked sword, authority is the sword in its scabbard’. Legitimacy is what converts naked power into accepted authority: because subjects concede the right to rule, the coercive instrument may stay sheathed. Hence  authority = power + legitimacy , and a regime that must constantly draw the sword has power but no authority. 3. Weber’s three authorities.  Max Weber  (using the term  Herrschaft ) identifies three types of  legitimate authority .  Traditional  authority rests on the ‘sanctity of ancient traditions’ and inherited status — a hereditary maharaja obeyed because his ancestors ruled.  Charismatic  authority rests on belief in a leader’s ‘extraordinary’ or near-magical qualities, and is unstable because he must keep proving them.  Rational-legal  authority is vested not in persons but in offices governed by written rules, holders being appointed on achieved qualifications — an IAS officer commands only what his office permits — and is the basis of the modern bureaucratic state. 4. Legitimacy.  Legitimacy is the belief in the ‘rightfulness’ of rule — for  Weber , ‘a right to rule’ — and it ‘lies in the eyes of the beholder’, being a matter of what the ruled accept rather than of what the rulers assert. Legality and legitimacy are therefore not identical: a government may win every election and remain perfectly legal while large sections deny that it rightfully speaks for them. 5. Beetham’s three conditions.  David Beetham  specifies that power is legitimate when it is (1) exercised according to established  rules ; (2) justified by a  shared belief  of both dominant and subordinate in those rules; and (3) validated by the  expressed consent  of the subordinate.  Tom Tyler  adds that legitimacy rests less on favourable outcomes than on fair  procedure . Legitimacy is sustained through rights, a free press, an independent judiciary and fair elections — though  constitutionalism does not by itself guarantee legitimacy , as the Greek crisis showed. 6. Conclusion.  Power without legitimacy is naked coercion that must constantly compel; authority is power clothed in legitimacy and obeyed as of right.  Weber  explains the  grounds  of that rightfulness and  Beetham  its  conditions  — together showing why stable rule depends on legitimacy rather than force. Q — Discuss the concept of legitimacy and Habermas’ idea of the ‘legitimation crisis’ in liberal democracies. What it’s asking:  Define legitimacy, then explain WHY Habermas thinks capitalist democracies keep losing it — and why they nevertheless survive. Gist — the spine to recall 1. Legitimacy  — the belief that a government has the right to rule and be obeyed; in a democracy its main source is the ballot.  (A government people accept as ‘ours’ even when they dislike its policy.) 2. Crisis tendencies  —  Habermas ,  Legitimation Crisis : liberal capitalism carries built-in contradictions that erode that belief.  (A ‘legitimation crisis’ is the moment people stop believing the system deserves obedience.) 3. The contradiction  — democracy keeps raising demands for welfare while a profit-driven market cannot fund them all.  (Free power, loan waivers and universal health care promised at election time; the exchequer cannot meet them all.) 4. Government overload  — spending and taxes rise, capital accumulation is squeezed;  Anthony King ’s ‘government overload’.  (The state is asked to do more than any state can do.) 5. The safety valve  — elections let the system change policy and personnel, ‘retaining a high degree of legitimacy’.  (Voting a government out lets people reject rulers without rejecting the regime.) 6. Conclusion  — political equality raises claims economic inequality cannot meet; legitimacy must be re-earned continuously. Model Answer 1. Legitimacy.  Legitimacy is the belief in the  rightfulness  of a government’s rule — the quality that converts naked power into accepted authority, so that citizens obey even measures they dislike because they regard the regime as their own. In modern liberal democracies its principal source is the democratic, electoral process: rulers are obeyed because they were chosen by a procedure the ruled accept as fair. 2. Crisis tendencies.  Jurgen Habermas , in  Legitimation Crisis , argues that liberal-capitalist democracies contain  ‘crisis tendencies’  that steadily undermine this belief. A  legitimation crisis  is not a coup or a collapse but the point at which a system can no longer justify itself to its own citizens — they cease to believe it deserves their obedience. For Habermas the source of that erosion is structural, lying in the very combination of democracy with capitalism. 3. The contradiction.  The  democratic political system  continuously generates popular demands for welfare, security and equality, while the  capitalist economy  is driven by private profit and cannot indefinitely satisfy both. Competitive elections multiply promises — subsidised power, loan waivers, universal health care — that no exchequer dependent on private accumulation can fully honour. The state ‘cannot permanently satisfy both popular demands for social welfare and the requirements of a market economy based on private profit’. 4. Government overload.  The chain therefore runs: democratic pressure → rising public spending and expanding state responsibilities → higher taxation, fiscal strain and inflation → a squeeze on capital accumulation, which in turn reduces the surplus available for welfare.  Anthony King  names this condition  ‘government overload’  — the state is asked to deliver more than any state can deliver, and each unmet promise withdraws a little more consent. 5. The safety valve.  Habermas  notes that the  electoral mechanism  allows liberal democracies to adjust policy and replace personnel in response to these pressures, ‘enabling the system as a whole to retain a high degree of legitimacy’. Voting a government out lets citizens reject rulers without rejecting the regime, so the crisis remains a recurring tendency rather than an automatic collapse. 6. Conclusion.  The legitimation-crisis thesis exposes the deep tension between  democracy and capitalism : political equality keeps raising claims that economic inequality cannot meet. Legitimacy therefore has constantly to be re-earned — which is why welfare provision and democratic responsiveness are not luxuries but conditions of a capitalist democracy’s survival. Q — “Political ideology is primarily concerned with the allocation and utilisation of power.” Examine the concept of ideology and assess the ‘end of ideology’ (Bell) and ‘end of history’ (Fukuyama) debates. (UPSC 2021) What it’s asking:  Show that ideology is really about justifying power — then test the two claims that ideology is finished. Gist — the spine to recall 1. Meaning  — ideology is a systematic set of beliefs that  justifies a social order ; since every order is an order of power, it is about power.  Destutt de Tracy  coined it as ‘the science of ideas’. 2.  Marx  — ideology as  false consciousness : a class interest disguised as universal truth.  (Being taught that one’s station in life is ordained, so the order that impoverishes you looks natural and even sacred.) 3. Later Marxists  —  Gramsci’s   hegemony  vs counter-hegemony;  Mannheim  splits  ideology  (defends the order) from  utopia   (the aspiration of the oppressed to overturn it) . 4. End of ideology  —  Bell : after 1945 the great ideological battles exhausted themselves in a welfare-capitalist consensus;  Lipset  agreed.  (Left and right now argue over tax rates, not over the system.) 5. End of history  —  Fukuyama : the post-Cold War ‘worldwide triumph of liberal democracy’;  Huntington  replies with the ‘clash of civilizations’.  (Religion and ethnic loyalty, not ideology, drive later conflict.) 6. Conclusion  — both ‘ends’ mistook a passing consensus for a permanent one; the contest over power, and so over ideology, never ends. Model Answer 1. Meaning.  An ideology — a term coined by  Destutt de Tracy  as ‘the science of ideas’ — is a systematic set of beliefs that  justifies a social order , offering both a picture of existing society and a programme for it. Because every social order is at bottom an order of power, ideology is ultimately concerned with the  allocation and utilisation of power : it explains who ought to rule, on what terms, and why the ruled should accept it. 2. Marx: ideology as false consciousness.  Marx  treats ideology as  ‘false consciousness’  — part of the  superstructure  determined by the economic base, whereby ‘the ideas of the ruling class are the ruling ideas’ and a particular class interest is made to appear universal and natural. The exploited thus misperceive their own condition: taught that their station in life is ordained, they experience the very arrangement that impoverishes them as natural and even sacred, and so fail to recognise their real class interest. 3. Later Marxist refinements.  Gramsci  converts the idea into  hegemony  — the dominant ideas that secure consent — against which the subordinate class must build a  counter-hegemony .  Karl Mannheim  distinguishes  ideology , the thought of those defending the established order, from  utopia , the thought of the oppressed who aspire to overturn it — so that the same doctrine may be ideology in power and utopia in opposition. 4. The end of ideology.  Daniel Bell  argued that after the Second World War the great ideological battles had exhausted themselves — ‘economics triumphed over politics’ in a welfare-capitalist consensus in which parties quarrelled over tax rates rather than over the system itself.  Lipset  agreed that left–right differences were no longer profound. The thesis was criticised as being itself an ideology — the complacent self-image of Western liberalism at the height of the Cold War. 5. The end of history.  Francis Fukuyama  extended the claim after the Cold War: the ‘worldwide triumph of liberal democracy’ over fascism and communism marked the  ‘end of history’ , a Hegelian notion that ideological evolution had reached its terminus. Critics, above all  Samuel Huntington  with ‘the clash of civilizations’, replied that ethnic loyalty and religious fundamentalism, not ideology, would drive future conflict — hence the ‘end of the end of history’. 6. Conclusion.  Both ‘end’ theses mistook a temporary consensus or triumph for a permanent one; the persistence of nationalism, religion, identity politics and inequality shows ideology is far from dead. The statement therefore holds: to study ideology is to study the contest over the allocation and use of power — a contest that never ends. Q — Critically examine Gramsci’s concept of hegemony, his distinction between organic and traditional intellectuals, and his two-stage theory of revolution. (UPSC 2013/2015/2016/2019) What it’s asking:  Explain why revolution failed, how consent replaces force, and what strategy Gramsci therefore prescribes. Gist — the spine to recall 1. The problem  — why did workers not revolt? Gramsci ( Prison Notebooks ) answers by giving the  superstructure  autonomy, rescuing Marxism from crude economic determinism. 2. Hegemony  — ruling-class values live in subaltern minds as their own  common sense , so ‘the exploited find happiness in their exploitation’.  (Colonial rule accepted as benevolent despotism, a civilising mission doing India good.) 3. Integral state  =  political society   (police, courts, army — coercion)  +  civil society   (family, school, church, press — which manufacture consent and act as a ‘shock absorber’) . 4. Intellectuals  —  organic  ones rise with a class and voice its worldview  (managers, engineers, nationalist editors) ;  traditional  ones  (clergy, scholars)  look class-neutral while preserving continuity. 5. Two-stage revolution  —  war of position   (the ideological battle for minds, as in the Indian national movement)  must precede the  war of manoeuvre   (the physical seizure of power) . 6. Critique & significance  —  Althusser  (slights coercion),  Perry Anderson  (civil society pulls him from Marxism); yet he made culture a site of struggle. Model Answer 1. The problem.  Antonio Gramsci , an Italian Marxist writing from Mussolini’s prison ( Prison Notebooks ), set out to explain why Marx’s prediction of proletarian revolution had failed in advanced Western Europe. His answer rescued Marxism from ‘crude economic determinism’ by granting the  superstructure  — ideas, culture, institutions — real autonomy from the economic base; he is accordingly called the ‘theoretician of the superstructure’. 2. Hegemony.  The ruling class rules not by force alone but by  consent . Hegemony is ‘the ability of the ruling class to make its values live in the minds of the subaltern classes as their own common sense’ — ‘a kind of exploitation in which the exploited find happiness in their exploitation’. British rule in India illustrates it: colonialism was widely accepted as a benevolent despotism and civilising mission, so that domination appeared as tutelage. Hegemony ‘cannot be taken for granted; it must be produced continuously’. 3. Political versus civil society.  The  integral state  =  political society , the coercive apparatus of government, police and courts, plus  civil society , the consent-manufacturing institutions of family, school, church, press and associations. Civil society is the ‘first layer of protection’, a ‘shock absorber’ that cushions the state: where it is strong (an ‘opaque state’) exploitation is hidden and revolution difficult, unlike a ‘transparent state’ where naked coercion stands exposed. 4. Intellectuals.  ‘All men are intellectuals, but not all have the social function of intellectuals.’  Organic intellectuals  rise with a class and articulate its worldview — managers, engineers, civil servants and nationalist editors giving voice to an emerging class — and are therefore the agents who can build  counter-hegemony  for the subaltern.  Traditional intellectuals  — the clergy, the classical scholar — appear detached and class-neutral, but by claiming to stand above society they in fact maintain the continuity of the existing order. 5. Two-stage revolution.  Change requires first a  war of position  — an  ideological  struggle fought ‘at the level of the mind’, in which organic intellectuals assemble a  historic bloc  of classes and build counter-hegemony — followed by the  war of manoeuvre , the frontal, physical seizure of power ‘once the mind is shaped’.  Bipin Chandra  reads the Indian national movement as the classic case: decades of newspapers, associations and constructive work destroyed the moral legitimacy of the Raj before power was transferred. 6. Critique and significance.  Althusser  faults Gramsci for slighting the coercive apparatus, and  Perry Anderson  holds that his emphasis on ‘civil society’ pulls him away from Marxism towards liberalism. Yet by locating power in culture and consent he reshaped Marxism and inspired the Frankfurt School, subaltern studies and cultural theory — showing that the decisive battle is often fought over ideas rather than arms. Revision Box — facts, keywords & quotes Lasswell & Kaplan : politics = ‘the shaping and sharing of power’;  Russell : power = ‘production of intended effects’. Hannah Arendt : power is ‘acting in concert’, ‘belongs to a group’; ‘violence can destroy power but never create it’. Steven Lukes : 3 faces — decision-making, agenda-setting, thought-control. Forms of power:  political, economic, ideological (‘ruling ideas = ideas of ruling class’ — Marx & Engels). Elitists:  Pareto  (circulation of elites),  Michels  (iron law of oligarchy),  Mills  (power elite). Pluralist:  Dahl  (polyarchy, ‘honest broker’);  Foucault:  ‘power is everywhere’, productive, power/knowledge, Panopticon. Authority = Power + Legitimacy;  ‘naked sword’ vs ‘sword in scabbard’. Weber : 3 legitimate authorities — traditional, charismatic, rational-legal. David Beetham : legitimacy = rules + shared belief + expressed consent;  Tom Tyler : procedure matters most. Habermas ,  Legitimation Crisis : democracy’s welfare demands vs capitalism’s profit needs;  Anthony King : ‘government overload’. Marx : ideology = false consciousness;  Mannheim : ideology vs utopia;  Destutt de Tracy  coined ‘ideology’. Daniel Bell : ‘end of ideology’;  Fukuyama : ‘end of history’;  Huntington : clash of civilizations. Gramsci : hegemony = rule by consent; integral state = political + civil society. Intellectuals:  organic (rise with a class → counter-hegemony) vs traditional (appear neutral). Revolution:  war of position (ideological) → war of manoeuvre (physical); historic bloc; Indian national movement (Bipin Chandra). Gramsci critics:  Althusser  (ignores coercion),  Perry Anderson  (civil society pulls him from Marxism). Last-Minute Revision Sheet (1 page) Power (M1):  conventional = domination (Russell/Dahl) vs constructive = ‘acting in concert’ (Arendt); Lukes’ 3 faces; political/economic/ideological forms. Theories (M2):  elitist (Pareto/Michels/Mills) vs pluralist (Dahl polyarchy) vs Marxist (economic) vs feminist (patriarchy) vs Foucault (productive, everywhere). Power vs authority (M3):  authority = power + legitimacy; Weber’s 3 types (traditional/charismatic/rational-legal); Beetham’s 3 principles. Legitimation crisis (M4):  Habermas — democracy’s welfare demands vs capitalism’s profit; ‘government overload’; elections as safety valve. Ideology & the two ‘ends’ (M5):  ideology = false consciousness (Marx); end of ideology (Bell) & end of history (Fukuyama) vs Huntington. Gramsci (M6):  hegemony = rule by consent; political vs civil society; organic vs traditional intellectuals; war of position → war of manoeuvre. Killer quotes:  Arendt — ‘violence can destroy power but never create it’; Foucault — ‘power is everywhere’; Gramsci — the exploited ‘find happiness in their exploitation’; Marx — ‘ruling ideas are the ideas of the ruling class’. Previous Year Questions — coverage map 2021 — Political ideology & allocation/utilisation of power → M5. 2020 — Nature and meaning of power → M1 (+ M2). 2018 — Power, authority and legitimacy → M3 (+ M4). 2015 — Distinguish power and authority → M3. 2014 — Arendt: power belongs to a group → M1. 2016 — Gramsci’s concept of hegemony → M6. 2015 — Gramsci’s organic intellectuals → M6. 2019 — Hegemony as organisation of consent → M6. 2013 — Hegemony vs domination → M6.

title: 08 - Political Ideologies

content.text: Syllabus — Political Ideologies: Liberalism, Socialism, Marxism, Fascism, Gandhism, Feminism. (UPSC PSIR Paper-1A, Unit 8) [Gandhism is treated fully in Unit 9.]

the major political ideologies — Liberalism (classical, modern, neo-liberal), Socialism (utopian, revolutionary, evolutionary), Marxism (classical and neo-Marxism), Feminism (its waves and strands) and Fascism — together with Postmodernism and the ‘end of ideology’ and ‘end of history’ debates. Gandhism is covered in Unit 9.

Locke, Adam Smith, T.H. Green, Hayek, Nozick, Friedman, Rawls, Sen, Lyotard, Foucault, Robert Owen, Bernstein, G.B. Shaw (Fabians), Marx, Engels, Lenin, Mao, Gramsci, Marcuse, Althusser, Wollstonecraft, Beauvoir, Betty Friedan, Kate Millett, Mussolini, Hitler, Gentile.

liberalism as a revolutionary idea (2020), end of history (2017), pre-Marxist socialism (2015) & socialism as anti-capitalism (2014), relevance of Marxism (2019), liberal vs radical feminism (2012/2019) & eco-feminism (2017), fascist anti-rationalism, postmodernism (2017).
Q — Trace the evolution of liberalism from classical to modern to neo-liberalism. Was liberalism a revolutionary idea, and is neo-liberalism the ideology of globalization? (UPSC 2020)
Three tasks — define liberalism, prove it was revolutionary, then trace classical → modern → neo-liberal and test the globalization claim.
built on the individual: individualism, freedom, reason, justice, toleration.
(Toleration in practice: the state may not tell a citizen which god to worship or whom to marry.)
destroyed feudal privilege and the divine right of kings.
(Earlier birth fixed your station; liberalism made contract and merit fix it.)
(Like a night guard at a factory gate — he stops theft and violence but never enters the workshop; freedom = nobody interfering.)
: the state ‘hinders the hindrances’ to self-development.
(A starving, illiterate labourer is legally free but unable — hence free schooling and mid-day meals; freedom = ability, not merely absence of restraint.)
(India’s 1991 LPG reforms — licence-raj dismantled, tariffs cut, PSUs disinvested — on the Washington Consensus/WTO 1995 template.)
) revives positive liberty against neo-liberal excess.
Liberalism is best understood as a
— a broad ground on which rival doctrines contend — resting on a commitment to the individual and five core values:
individualism, freedom, reason, justice and toleration
. The individual, not the caste, class or community, is the basic unit of politics, and toleration means the state may not prescribe a citizen’s faith or spouse.
is acknowledged as its founding father.
In its own age liberalism was genuinely
. By grounding legitimate rule in the

rather than in birth or divinity, it overthrew feudal privilege and the divine right of kings, replacing a hierarchy of status with one of contract and merit. Constitutionalism, natural rights and limited government were the instruments with which it dismantled absolutism — which is why it began life as a doctrine of protest, not of order.
, that is freedom as the absence of interference: like a night guard at a factory gate, the state may prevent theft and violence but never enter the workshop.
: ‘that government is best which governs least’;
recast the state as a ‘source of virtue’ enabling

— the actual capacity for self-development. Green held that ‘will, not force, is the basis of the state’ and that it must ‘hinder the hindrances’ to self-realisation: a starving, illiterate labourer is legally free yet unable, so free schooling, mid-day meals and health care become conditions of freedom. This is the philosophical charter of the welfare state.
reverse the movement — ‘rolling back the state’ and ‘market fundamentalism’.
: ‘planning is the road to serfdom’ and ‘social justice is a mirage’;
: freedom is possible only through the market. It duly became globalization’s ideology — Thatcherism and Reaganism, shock therapy, the
and the WTO (1995) — and India’s 1991 liberalisation followed the same template.
Liberalism was a genuinely revolutionary force against absolutism, and it renews itself:

) revives positive liberty against neo-liberal excess by insisting that markets be judged by what they do to the worst-off. Its survival lies precisely in this capacity to travel from market-freedom to ‘humane governance’.
Q — Critically examine postmodernism’s ‘incredulity towards metanarratives’ alongside the ‘end of ideology’ and ‘end of history’ theses. (UPSC 2017)
Explain Lyotard’s attack on grand theories, then test the ‘end of ideology’ and ‘end of history’ claims against what actually happened.
— a revolt against Modernism, ‘emphasising the elusiveness of meaning and knowledge’;
is its father (‘God is dead’, ‘will to power’).
: disbelief in any grand universal theory, for ‘there is not one but many truths’.
(Marxism insists all history must end in communism, liberalism that every society must become a market democracy — one story told for everybody.)
(‘we do not discover truth, we invent truth’),
(The televised event, endlessly replayed, becomes more real to the viewer than the event itself.)
: the post-war welfare-capitalist consensus exhausted the great isms.
(Left and right stopped quarrelling over who owns the factories and quarrelled only over tax rates.)
: the worldwide triumph of liberal democracy after 1991;
— every ‘end’ was premature; and postmodern relativism leaves no ground on which to condemn injustice.

Postmodernism is a rejection of Modernism that ‘emphasises the elusiveness of meaning and knowledge’: reason, progress and objective truth — the Enlightenment’s promises — are treated as claims rather than facts.
is regarded as its father, his ‘God is dead’ and ‘will to power’ announcing a world without guaranteed foundations, in which knowledge is always somebody’s knowledge.
gave postmodernism its defining formula: it is

— disbelief in any grand, universal theory that explains everything, ‘for there is not one but many truths’. Marxism holds that all history must culminate in communism and liberalism that every society must end as a market democracy; postmodernism refuses both as single stories imposed on plural human experience.
holds that ‘we do not discover truth, we invent truth’ — what counts as knowledge is set by power.
dismantles the ‘metaphysics of presence’, denying any final meaning to a text.
‘hyper-reality’ describes a media world where the image outgrows the thing: the endlessly replayed broadcast becomes more real than the event.

) argued that after the Second World War the great ideological conflicts had exhausted themselves — ‘economics triumphed over politics’ in a welfare-capitalist consensus, and parties argued over tax rates rather than over ownership of the means of production. Critics such as
replied that ‘the end of ideology is itself an ideology’ — a defence of the status quo in neutral dress.
extended the thesis after the Cold War: the ‘worldwide triumph of liberal democracy’ over all rivals marked the end-point of mankind’s ideological evolution — a Hegelian idea.
countered with the ‘clash of civilizations’: future conflict would be driven by ethnic, religious and civilisational identity, not by ideology.

All three theses proclaim an ‘end’ — of universal truth, of ideology, of history — yet the resurgence of nationalism, religious politics and gross inequality refutes them. Postmodernism usefully warns against dogmatic metanarratives and recovers marginalised voices, but its own relativism risks leaving no firm ground from which injustice can be criticised at all.
Q — Distinguish revolutionary from evolutionary socialism; assess pre-Marxist (utopian) socialism and whether socialism may be reborn as anti-capitalism. (UPSC 2015/2014)
Three demands — separate utopian from scientific socialism, contrast the revolutionary and evolutionary roads, then ask what survives today.
— opposition to capitalism; its ‘defining value is equality, especially social equality’, and cooperation over competition.
: ‘a hat that has lost its shape because everyone wears it’.
(They painted the destination — a model village — but drew no road to it; Marx claimed to supply the laws of capitalism’s collapse, hence ‘scientific’.)
— the Marxist road: abolish capitalism ‘in a single stroke’, since the state is a class instrument that cannot be borrowed by the workers.
(Fabian gradualism reached India as Nehruvian socialism — a mixed economy built by Parliament and the Five-Year Plans, not by barricades.)
, Occupy Wall Street, the Yellow Vests,
— charged with being capitalism’s ‘safety valve’, socialism now survives less as a programme of power than as the moral vocabulary of the fight against inequality.

Socialism is defined by its opposition to capitalism: its ‘defining value is equality, especially social equality’, and it prefers cooperation to competition, holding human beings to be social creatures shaped by their conditions rather than self-seeking atoms. Because it has been claimed by so many,
quipped that ‘socialism is like a hat that has lost its shape because everyone wears it’.
, who first used the word ‘socialist’, proposed ‘villages of cooperation’;
favoured rule by scientific ‘luminaries’. Marx dismissed them as
because they painted an ideal destination without analysing capitalism or charting the road to it, appealing to the goodwill of the rich; his own socialism claimed to be
, deriving socialism from the laws of capitalist development itself.

The Marxist tradition holds that capitalism must be overthrown ‘in a single stroke’ and replaced by a classless society, since the existing state is an instrument of the propertied class and cannot simply be captured and used by the workers. Reform, on this view, only repairs the machine of exploitation; hence the dictatorship of the proletariat as a transitional necessity.
The democratic-socialist tradition proceeds gradually and parliamentarily.
— argued that workers armed with the vote need no revolution;
— preached the ‘inevitability of gradualness’ and inspired Nehruvian socialism, a mixed economy built through Parliament and the Five-Year Plans;
) sought workers’ control through unions and guilds rather than the state.
With inequality rising, socialism revives less as a state project than as an anti-capitalist critique:
, movements such as Occupy Wall Street and the Yellow Vests, and
stark alternative, ‘socialism or barbarism’, all attack concentrated wealth without promising a seizure of power.

Evolutionary socialism made socialism democratically respectable but stands charged with legitimising the bourgeois state — a ‘safety valve’ that releases pressure without changing ownership. Its twenty-first-century relevance therefore lies not in capturing power but in supplying the moral vocabulary of the struggle against inequality: socialism reborn as anti-capitalism.
Q — Explain the main tenets of Marxism (dialectical and historical materialism, class conflict, surplus value) and evaluate its contemporary relevance. (UPSC 2019)
Set out Marxism’s philosophical core — materialism, class conflict, exploitation — and then judge honestly what survives of it.
gave socialism a ‘scientific’ basis: history is the conflict of antagonistic classes over who owns production.
thesis–antithesis–synthesis, but matter not idea is the essence of reality.
(Hegel stood on his head: not ideas but the loom, the mill and the mine make history move.)
; stages run slave → feudal → capitalist → socialist → communist.
(Who owns the land and the factory decides whose law, morality and religion prevail.)
(A worker paid Rs 300 a day may add Rs 900 of value to the cloth: the unpaid Rs 600 is surplus value; and owning neither product nor pace of work, he is alienated from his own labour.)
— predictions failed and regimes collapsed, yet 2008,
— discredited as a blueprint for revolution, indispensable as a

, claims to place socialism on a ‘scientific’ footing by deriving it from the laws of social development rather than from moral aspiration. Its organising insight is that every society is divided by the ownership of the means of production into antagonistic classes, and that this conflict, not the deeds of great men, is the motor of history.

dialectic — thesis, antithesis, synthesis — with materialism: matter, not idea, is the essence of reality, so Hegel is famously stood on his head. Not philosophy but the loom, the mill and the mine make history move, and each social order generates within itself the contradiction that destroys it.
formalised its three laws, including the transformation of quantity into quality.
Applied to society, this yields the
(forces plus relations of production) determines the

of law, politics, religion and ideas — who owns the land and the factory decides whose law and whose morality prevail. History therefore advances through stages: primitive communism, slave, feudal, capitalist, socialist and finally communist society, each transition driven by a clash between new productive forces and old relations.
4. Class struggle, surplus value and alienation.
‘The history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggle’, and the proletariat is ‘the only really revolutionary class’. Exploitation is measured by
: labour alone creates value, so a worker paid Rs 300 a day who adds Rs 900 of value to the cloth surrenders Rs 600 unpaid to the capitalist.

Marxism’s specific predictions — imminent revolution in the advanced West, the progressive immiseration of the workers — largely failed, and the state-socialist regimes collapsed after 1989. Yet its

As a blueprint for revolution Marxism stands largely discredited; as a

for exploitation, alienation and structural inequality it remains strikingly relevant. That is why every crisis of capitalism sends readers back to Marx, even where nobody expects the proletarian revolution he foretold.

Feminist ideology rests on two beliefs — ‘that women are disadvantaged because of their sex, and that this disadvantage can and should be overthrown’. The first is descriptive and the second normative, which is why feminism is simultaneously a theory of society and a movement for its transformation, cutting across liberal, socialist and radical traditions rather than belonging to any one of them.

The sex/gender distinction is the theoretical foundation of every feminist strand because it turns women’s subordination from a fact of nature into a remediable injustice. What divides feminists is only the cure — equal rights, the end of capitalism, or the overthrow of patriarchy — not the diagnosis that gender is made, and therefore can be unmade.

Q — Is fascism a coherent ideology? Discuss its anti-rationalism and core tenets, its conception of the state, and whether it was merely an inter-war phenomenon.
