contentText: Syllabus — Political Ideologies: Liberalism, Socialism, Marxism, Fascism, Gandhism, Feminism. (UPSC PSIR Paper-1A, Unit 8) [Gandhism is treated fully in Unit 9.] Unit Snapshot What this unit covers:  the major political ideologies — Liberalism (classical, modern, neo-liberal), Socialism (utopian, revolutionary, evolutionary), Marxism (classical and neo-Marxism), Feminism (its waves and strands) and Fascism — together with Postmodernism and the ‘end of ideology’ and ‘end of history’ debates. Gandhism is covered in Unit 9. Must-know thinkers:  Locke, Adam Smith, T.H. Green, Hayek, Nozick, Friedman, Rawls, Sen, Lyotard, Foucault, Robert Owen, Bernstein, G.B. Shaw (Fabians), Marx, Engels, Lenin, Mao, Gramsci, Marcuse, Althusser, Wollstonecraft, Beauvoir, Betty Friedan, Kate Millett, Mussolini, Hitler, Gentile. PYQ trend:  liberalism as a revolutionary idea (2020), end of history (2017), pre-Marxist socialism (2015) & socialism as anti-capitalism (2014), relevance of Marxism (2019), liberal vs radical feminism (2012/2019) & eco-feminism (2017), fascist anti-rationalism, postmodernism (2017). Master Questions Q — Trace the evolution of liberalism from classical to modern to neo-liberalism. Was liberalism a revolutionary idea, and is neo-liberalism the ideology of globalization? (UPSC 2020) What it’s asking:  Three tasks — define liberalism, prove it was revolutionary, then trace classical → modern → neo-liberal and test the globalization claim. Gist — the spine to recall 1. Core  — a  meta-ideology  built on the individual: individualism, freedom, reason, justice, toleration.  (Toleration in practice: the state may not tell a citizen which god to worship or whom to marry.) 2. Revolutionary  — rule grounded in the  consent of the people  destroyed feudal privilege and the divine right of kings.  (Earlier birth fixed your station; liberalism made contract and merit fix it.) 3. Classical  —  Locke, Smith, Spencer : the  night-watchman state  and  negative liberty .  (Like a night guard at a factory gate — he stops theft and violence but never enters the workshop; freedom = nobody interfering.) 4. Modern / positive  —  Green, Hobhouse, Laski : the state ‘hinders the hindrances’ to self-development.  (A starving, illiterate labourer is legally free but unable — hence free schooling and mid-day meals; freedom = ability, not merely absence of restraint.) 5. Neo-liberalism  —  Hayek, Nozick, Friedman : ‘roll back the state’, market fundamentalism.  (India’s 1991 LPG reforms — licence-raj dismantled, tariffs cut, PSUs disinvested — on the Washington Consensus/WTO 1995 template.) 6. Conclusion  —  social liberalism  ( Rawls, Sen, Stiglitz ) revives positive liberty against neo-liberal excess. Model Answer 1. Core.  Liberalism is best understood as a  meta-ideology  — a broad ground on which rival doctrines contend — resting on a commitment to the individual and five core values:  individualism, freedom, reason, justice and toleration . The individual, not the caste, class or community, is the basic unit of politics, and toleration means the state may not prescribe a citizen’s faith or spouse.  Locke  is acknowledged as its founding father. 2. Revolutionary.  In its own age liberalism was genuinely  revolutionary . By grounding legitimate rule in the  consent of the people  rather than in birth or divinity, it overthrew feudal privilege and the divine right of kings, replacing a hierarchy of status with one of contract and merit. Constitutionalism, natural rights and limited government were the instruments with which it dismantled absolutism — which is why it began life as a doctrine of protest, not of order. 3. Classical liberalism.  Locke  — the ‘father of classical liberalism’ — with  Adam Smith  and  Herbert Spencer  champions the minimal ‘ night-watchman ’ state, laissez-faire, natural rights and  negative liberty , that is freedom as the absence of interference: like a night guard at a factory gate, the state may prevent theft and violence but never enter the workshop.  Jefferson : ‘that government is best which governs least’;  Macpherson  labels its individual ‘possessive’. 4. Modern / positive liberalism.  T.H. Green ,  Hobhouse  and  Laski  recast the state as a ‘source of virtue’ enabling  positive liberty  — the actual capacity for self-development. Green held that ‘will, not force, is the basis of the state’ and that it must ‘hinder the hindrances’ to self-realisation: a starving, illiterate labourer is legally free yet unable, so free schooling, mid-day meals and health care become conditions of freedom. This is the philosophical charter of the welfare state. 5. Neo-liberalism.  Hayek ,  Nozick  ( Anarchy, State and Utopia ) and  Friedman  reverse the movement — ‘rolling back the state’ and ‘market fundamentalism’.  Hayek : ‘planning is the road to serfdom’ and ‘social justice is a mirage’;  Friedman : freedom is possible only through the market. It duly became globalization’s ideology — Thatcherism and Reaganism, shock therapy, the  Washington Consensus  and the WTO (1995) — and India’s 1991 liberalisation followed the same template. 6. Conclusion.  Liberalism was a genuinely revolutionary force against absolutism, and it renews itself:  social liberalism  ( Rawls, Sen, Stiglitz ) revives positive liberty against neo-liberal excess by insisting that markets be judged by what they do to the worst-off. Its survival lies precisely in this capacity to travel from market-freedom to ‘humane governance’. Q — Critically examine postmodernism’s ‘incredulity towards metanarratives’ alongside the ‘end of ideology’ and ‘end of history’ theses. (UPSC 2017) What it’s asking:  Explain Lyotard’s attack on grand theories, then test the ‘end of ideology’ and ‘end of history’ claims against what actually happened. Gist — the spine to recall 1. What it is  — a revolt against Modernism, ‘emphasising the elusiveness of meaning and knowledge’;  Nietzsche  is its father (‘God is dead’, ‘will to power’). 2. Incredulity towards metanarratives  —  Lyotard : disbelief in any grand universal theory, for ‘there is not one but many truths’.  (Marxism insists all history must end in communism, liberalism that every society must become a market democracy — one story told for everybody.) 3. Key moves  —  Foucault  (‘we do not discover truth, we invent truth’),  Derrida  (deconstruction),  Baudrillard  (hyper-reality).  (The televised event, endlessly replayed, becomes more real to the viewer than the event itself.) 4. End of ideology  —  Bell : the post-war welfare-capitalist consensus exhausted the great isms.  (Left and right stopped quarrelling over who owns the factories and quarrelled only over tax rates.) 5. End of history  —  Fukuyama : the worldwide triumph of liberal democracy after 1991;  Huntington  replies with the ‘clash of civilizations’. 6. Conclusion  — every ‘end’ was premature; and postmodern relativism leaves no ground on which to condemn injustice. Model Answer 1. What it is.  Postmodernism is a rejection of Modernism that ‘emphasises the elusiveness of meaning and knowledge’: reason, progress and objective truth — the Enlightenment’s promises — are treated as claims rather than facts.  Nietzsche  is regarded as its father, his ‘God is dead’ and ‘will to power’ announcing a world without guaranteed foundations, in which knowledge is always somebody’s knowledge. 2. Incredulity towards metanarratives.  Jean-Francois Lyotard  gave postmodernism its defining formula: it is  ‘incredulity towards metanarratives’  — disbelief in any grand, universal theory that explains everything, ‘for there is not one but many truths’. Marxism holds that all history must culminate in communism and liberalism that every society must end as a market democracy; postmodernism refuses both as single stories imposed on plural human experience. 3. Key moves.  Foucault’s  power/knowledge  holds that ‘we do not discover truth, we invent truth’ — what counts as knowledge is set by power.  Derrida’s  deconstruction  dismantles the ‘metaphysics of presence’, denying any final meaning to a text.  Baudrillard’s  ‘hyper-reality’ describes a media world where the image outgrows the thing: the endlessly replayed broadcast becomes more real than the event. 4. End of ideology.  Daniel Bell  (with  Lipset  and  Dahrendorf ) argued that after the Second World War the great ideological conflicts had exhausted themselves — ‘economics triumphed over politics’ in a welfare-capitalist consensus, and parties argued over tax rates rather than over ownership of the means of production. Critics such as  Macpherson  and  MacIntyre  replied that ‘the end of ideology is itself an ideology’ — a defence of the status quo in neutral dress. 5. End of history.  Francis Fukuyama  extended the thesis after the Cold War: the ‘worldwide triumph of liberal democracy’ over all rivals marked the end-point of mankind’s ideological evolution — a Hegelian idea.  Samuel Huntington  countered with the ‘clash of civilizations’: future conflict would be driven by ethnic, religious and civilisational identity, not by ideology. 6. Conclusion.  All three theses proclaim an ‘end’ — of universal truth, of ideology, of history — yet the resurgence of nationalism, religious politics and gross inequality refutes them. Postmodernism usefully warns against dogmatic metanarratives and recovers marginalised voices, but its own relativism risks leaving no firm ground from which injustice can be criticised at all. Q — Distinguish revolutionary from evolutionary socialism; assess pre-Marxist (utopian) socialism and whether socialism may be reborn as anti-capitalism. (UPSC 2015/2014) What it’s asking:  Three demands — separate utopian from scientific socialism, contrast the revolutionary and evolutionary roads, then ask what survives today. Gist — the spine to recall 1. Core  — opposition to capitalism; its ‘defining value is equality, especially social equality’, and cooperation over competition.  Joad : ‘a hat that has lost its shape because everyone wears it’. 2. Utopian vs scientific  —  Owen  (‘villages of cooperation’),  Fourier ,  Saint-Simon .  (They painted the destination — a model village — but drew no road to it; Marx claimed to supply the laws of capitalism’s collapse, hence ‘scientific’.) 3. Revolutionary socialism  — the Marxist road: abolish capitalism ‘in a single stroke’, since the state is a class instrument that cannot be borrowed by the workers. 4. Evolutionary socialism  — revisionism ( Bernstein ), Fabianism ( Shaw, the Webbs ), syndicalism, guild socialism ( Cole ).  (Fabian gradualism reached India as Nehruvian socialism — a mixed economy built by Parliament and the Five-Year Plans, not by barricades.) 5. Rebirth as anti-capitalism  —  Miliband’s   Socialism for a Sceptical Age , Occupy Wall Street, the Yellow Vests,  Wallerstein’s  ‘socialism or barbarism’. 6. Conclusion  — charged with being capitalism’s ‘safety valve’, socialism now survives less as a programme of power than as the moral vocabulary of the fight against inequality. Model Answer 1. Core.  Socialism is defined by its opposition to capitalism: its ‘defining value is equality, especially social equality’, and it prefers cooperation to competition, holding human beings to be social creatures shaped by their conditions rather than self-seeking atoms. Because it has been claimed by so many,  C.E.M. Joad  quipped that ‘socialism is like a hat that has lost its shape because everyone wears it’. 2. Utopian versus scientific.  Robert Owen , who first used the word ‘socialist’, proposed ‘villages of cooperation’;  Charles Fourier  would make work pleasant;  Saint-Simon  favoured rule by scientific ‘luminaries’. Marx dismissed them as  ‘utopian’  because they painted an ideal destination without analysing capitalism or charting the road to it, appealing to the goodwill of the rich; his own socialism claimed to be  scientific , deriving socialism from the laws of capitalist development itself. 3. Revolutionary socialism.  The Marxist tradition holds that capitalism must be overthrown ‘in a single stroke’ and replaced by a classless society, since the existing state is an instrument of the propertied class and cannot simply be captured and used by the workers. Reform, on this view, only repairs the machine of exploitation; hence the dictatorship of the proletariat as a transitional necessity. 4. Evolutionary socialism.  The democratic-socialist tradition proceeds gradually and parliamentarily.  Revisionism  —  Eduard Bernstein  — argued that workers armed with the vote need no revolution;  Fabianism  —  G.B. Shaw  and  the Webbs  — preached the ‘inevitability of gradualness’ and inspired Nehruvian socialism, a mixed economy built through Parliament and the Five-Year Plans;  syndicalism  and  guild socialism  ( G.D.H. Cole ) sought workers’ control through unions and guilds rather than the state. 5. Rebirth as anti-capitalism.  With inequality rising, socialism revives less as a state project than as an anti-capitalist critique:  Ralph Miliband’s   Socialism for a Sceptical Age , movements such as Occupy Wall Street and the Yellow Vests, and  Wallerstein’s  stark alternative, ‘socialism or barbarism’, all attack concentrated wealth without promising a seizure of power. 6. Conclusion.  Evolutionary socialism made socialism democratically respectable but stands charged with legitimising the bourgeois state — a ‘safety valve’ that releases pressure without changing ownership. Its twenty-first-century relevance therefore lies not in capturing power but in supplying the moral vocabulary of the struggle against inequality: socialism reborn as anti-capitalism. Q — Explain the main tenets of Marxism (dialectical and historical materialism, class conflict, surplus value) and evaluate its contemporary relevance. (UPSC 2019) What it’s asking:  Set out Marxism’s philosophical core — materialism, class conflict, exploitation — and then judge honestly what survives of it. Gist — the spine to recall 1. Core  —  Marx  and  Engels  gave socialism a ‘scientific’ basis: history is the conflict of antagonistic classes over who owns production. 2. Dialectical materialism  —  Hegel’s  thesis–antithesis–synthesis, but matter not idea is the essence of reality.  (Hegel stood on his head: not ideas but the loom, the mill and the mine make history move.) 3. Historical materialism  — the economic  base  determines the  superstructure ; stages run slave → feudal → capitalist → socialist → communist.  (Who owns the land and the factory decides whose law, morality and religion prevail.) 4. Class struggle, surplus value, alienation  —  (A worker paid Rs 300 a day may add Rs 900 of value to the cloth: the unpaid Rs 600 is surplus value; and owning neither product nor pace of work, he is alienated from his own labour.) 5. Relevance  — predictions failed and regimes collapsed, yet 2008,  Piketty  and  Eagleton  revived the critique of capitalism. 6. Conclusion  — discredited as a blueprint for revolution, indispensable as a  diagnostic tool  for exploitation and inequality. Model Answer 1. Core.  Marxism, founded by  Karl Marx  and  Friedrich Engels , claims to place socialism on a ‘scientific’ footing by deriving it from the laws of social development rather than from moral aspiration. Its organising insight is that every society is divided by the ownership of the means of production into antagonistic classes, and that this conflict, not the deeds of great men, is the motor of history. 2. Dialectical materialism.  Marx fuses  Hegel’s  dialectic — thesis, antithesis, synthesis — with materialism: matter, not idea, is the essence of reality, so Hegel is famously stood on his head. Not philosophy but the loom, the mill and the mine make history move, and each social order generates within itself the contradiction that destroys it.  Engels  formalised its three laws, including the transformation of quantity into quality. 3. Historical materialism.  Applied to society, this yields the  base–superstructure  model: the economic  base  (forces plus relations of production) determines the  superstructure  of law, politics, religion and ideas — who owns the land and the factory decides whose law and whose morality prevail. History therefore advances through stages: primitive communism, slave, feudal, capitalist, socialist and finally communist society, each transition driven by a clash between new productive forces and old relations. 4. Class struggle, surplus value and alienation.  ‘The history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggle’, and the proletariat is ‘the only really revolutionary class’. Exploitation is measured by  surplus value : labour alone creates value, so a worker paid Rs 300 a day who adds Rs 900 of value to the cloth surrenders Rs 600 unpaid to the capitalist.  Alienation  is its human cost — owning neither the product nor the pace of his work, the worker is estranged from his labour, his fellows and himself. When the ‘class in itself’ becomes a ‘class for itself’, revolution follows. 5. Contemporary relevance.  Marxism’s specific predictions — imminent revolution in the advanced West, the progressive immiseration of the workers — largely failed, and the state-socialist regimes collapsed after 1989. Yet its  critique of capitalism  endures:  Thomas Piketty  ( Capital in the Twenty-First Century ) documents widening inequality,  Terry Eagleton  ( Why Marx Was Right ) defends its core, and the crash of 2008 and Occupy Wall Street echoed its concerns. 6. Conclusion.  As a blueprint for revolution Marxism stands largely discredited; as a  diagnostic tool  for exploitation, alienation and structural inequality it remains strikingly relevant. That is why every crisis of capitalism sends readers back to Marx, even where nobody expects the proletarian revolution he foretold. Q — How did neo-Marxism (Gramsci, the Frankfurt School, Althusser) reformulate the base–superstructure relationship? What it’s asking:  Explain why revolution never came in the West — and how Gramsci, the Frankfurt School and Althusser rebuilt Marxism around culture. Gist — the spine to recall 1. The problem  — classical Marxism made the superstructure a mere reflection of the economic base, yet the advanced West did not revolt; neo-Marxism rescues Marxism from this ‘crude economic determinism’. 2. Hegemony  —  Gramsci : the ruling class rules by consent manufactured in  civil society .  (School, temple, cinema and newspaper teach the poor that the existing order is natural ‘common sense’ — consent, not the police, keeps it standing.) 3. False consciousness & war of position  — the exploited think in their masters’ categories, so  organic intellectuals  must first win the battle of ideas.  (The worker who votes for his employer’s party has borrowed his employer’s worldview.) 4. Frankfurt School  — critical theory, the ‘culture industry’,  Marcuse’s  one-dimensional man and ‘false needs’.  (Capitalism sells the discontented a new phone instead of a new society.) 5. Althusser  —  ideological state apparatuses  and interpellation; the base determines only ‘in the last instance’. 6. Conclusion  — the battleground shifts from the economy to culture and consciousness, explaining capitalism’s durability. Model Answer 1. The problem.  Classical Marxism treated the  superstructure  — ideas, law, culture, the state — as a mere reflection of the economic  base , and expected revolution first in the most advanced capitalist societies. When it arrived instead in agrarian Russia and China while the Western worker grew reformist,  neo-Marxists  rescued Marxism from this ‘crude economic determinism’ by granting the superstructure a life and a power of its own. 2. Hegemony.  Antonio Gramsci , the ‘theoretician of the superstructure’, argued that the ruling class rules not by coercion alone but by  hegemony  — intellectual and moral leadership manufactured through  civil society : school, church, press and popular culture. Through them the existing distribution of property comes to look like natural ‘common sense’, so that consent rather than the policeman keeps the order standing. 3. False consciousness and the war of position.  The result is  false consciousness : the exploited understand their own condition in categories supplied by their exploiters — the worker who votes for his employer’s party has borrowed his employer’s worldview. Revolution therefore requires first a  war of position , a long ideological struggle in which  organic intellectuals  thrown up by the working class build a counter-hegemony, before any frontal ‘war of manoeuvre’ can succeed. 4. The Frankfurt School.  Horkheimer ,  Adorno  and  Marcuse  developed  critical theory  and the idea of the ‘culture industry’, which turns art and leisure into standardised commodities that pacify.  Marcuse’s   One-Dimensional Man  shows how advanced capitalism manufactures ‘false needs’ and absorbs dissent — selling the discontented a new phone instead of a new society — so that opposition itself becomes a commodity. 5. Althusser.  Louis Althusser , of the structuralist school, added the  ‘ideological state apparatuses’  — family, school, religion, media — which reproduce the relations of production more quietly than the repressive apparatus of army and police, and  interpellation , by which ideology ‘hails’ individuals into obedient subjects. His ‘multi-sectoral’ analysis allows each level relative autonomy, the economy being determinant only ‘in the last instance’. 6. Conclusion.  Neo-Marxism shifted the decisive battleground from the  economy to culture and consciousness . In doing so it explained capitalism’s remarkable durability and reshaped Marxism into a theory of ideology and hegemony rather than of inevitable economic collapse — the form in which Marxism still influences media studies, education and cultural politics today. Q — Why is the sex/gender distinction central to feminist analysis? Distinguish liberal, socialist and radical feminism and the waves of feminism. (UPSC 2012/2019) What it’s asking:  Two halves — why sex/gender is the foundation of feminist argument, and how the strands and the three waves differ. Gist — the spine to recall 1. Core  — feminism rests on two beliefs: ‘that women are disadvantaged because of their sex, and that this disadvantage can and should be overthrown’. 2. Sex vs gender  — sex is biological and fixed,  gender  a changeable social construct;  Beauvoir : ‘one is not born, but becomes, a woman’.  (Sex is who bears the child; gender is the rule that the daughter cooks while the son studies.) 3. Liberal feminism  —  Wollstonecraft, Mill, Friedan : equal legal and political rights within the system, since gender is ‘irrelevant to public life’.  (Equal education, the vote, equal pay for equal work.) 4. Socialist & radical  —  Engels  ties patriarchy to  capitalism  (women as a ‘reserve army of labour’);  Millett  locates it in  patriarchy  itself — ‘the personal is political’.  (The unpaid cooking and care that sends the wage-earner back to work each morning costs capital nothing.) 5. Three waves  — 1st: suffrage and legal rights; 2nd (1961–91): women’s liberation and the private sphere; 3rd (from the 1990s): difference — black, postcolonial, eco-feminism. 6. Conclusion  — the distinction converts subordination from a fact of nature into a remediable injustice; the strands differ only on the cure. Model Answer 1. Core.  Feminist ideology rests on two beliefs — ‘that women are disadvantaged because of their sex, and that this disadvantage can and should be overthrown’. The first is descriptive and the second normative, which is why feminism is simultaneously a theory of society and a movement for its transformation, cutting across liberal, socialist and radical traditions rather than belonging to any one of them. 2. Sex versus gender.  The  sex/gender distinction  is central because  sex  denotes ineradicable biological difference, whereas  gender  is a cultural construct of masculine and feminine roles that society imposes and can therefore unmake. As  Simone de Beauvoir  put it, ‘one is not born, but becomes, a woman’: sex is who bears the child, gender is the household rule that the daughter cooks while the son studies. This shatters the claim that ‘biology is destiny’ and converts subordination into a social wrong. 3. Liberal feminism.  Mary Wollstonecraft  ( A Vindication of the Rights of Woman ),  J.S. Mill  and  Betty Friedan  are reformist: gender is ‘irrelevant to public life’, so women need equal education, the vote, equal legal personality and equal pay within the existing order. Critics answer that formal equality leaves the unequal burdens of the home untouched, and that it speaks chiefly for educated middle-class women. 4. Socialist and radical feminism.  Socialist feminism  ( Engels ,  The Origin of the Family ;  Juliet Mitchell ) ties patriarchy to  capitalism : women form a ‘reserve army of labour’ and their unpaid domestic work reproduces labour power free of cost to capital.  Radical feminism  ( Kate Millett, Germaine Greer, Beauvoir ) replies that  patriarchy  is itself the root, prior to class — ‘the personal is political’ — so family, marriage and sexuality must be transformed, not merely property. 5. The three waves.  The  first wave  (to the 1960s) was the suffrage movement, winning legal and voting rights; the  second wave  (1961–91) was ‘women’s liberation’, which carried the struggle into the private sphere —  Friedan’s  ‘problem with no name’ named the discontent of the suburban housewife; the  third wave  (from the 1990s) embraces the politics of difference through black, postcolonial and eco-feminism. 6. Conclusion.  The sex/gender distinction is the theoretical foundation of every feminist strand because it turns women’s subordination from a fact of nature into a remediable injustice. What divides feminists is only the cure — equal rights, the end of capitalism, or the overthrow of patriarchy — not the diagnosis that gender is made, and therefore can be unmade. Q — “One is not born, but becomes, a woman.” Examine radical feminism and patriarchy, and evaluate eco-feminism and the newer strands (black, postcolonial). (UPSC 2017) What it’s asking:  Unpack Beauvoir’s line through radical feminism’s theory of patriarchy, then weigh the eco-, black and postcolonial challenges to it. Gist — the spine to recall 1. Patriarchy  —  Millett : a system in which ‘male shall dominate female, elder male shall dominate younger’, prior to class or race.  (Its unit is the family: property, surname and authority descend from father to son.) 2. The personal is political  — the private sphere is itself a structure of power.  (Who eats last, who does the unpaid housework, who decides a pregnancy — all are questions of politics, not of affection.) 3. Woman as the ‘Other’  —  Beauvoir ,  The Second Sex : woman is defined only against man, so she is made, not born;  Brownmiller : ‘rape is an institution of patriarchy’. 4. Eco-feminism  —  d’Eaubonne ,  Vandana Shiva ,  Mary Daly : woman and nature are both treated as passive resources.  (The Indian village woman who fetches the water and gathers the fuel is the first to suffer when the forest and the stream are destroyed.) 5. Black & postcolonial  —  bell hooks  and  Chandra Talpade Mohanty : mainstream feminism universalised the white middle-class woman and ignored race and class. 6. Conclusion  — feminism moves from sisterhood-as-sameness to a  politics of difference . Model Answer 1. Patriarchy.  Radical feminism, the defining strand of the  second wave , holds that  patriarchy  — literally ‘rule by the father’ — is the most fundamental and universal form of oppression, older and deeper than class or race.  Kate Millett  defines it as a system in which ‘male shall dominate female, elder male shall dominate younger’; its basic unit is the family, through which property, surname and authority descend from father to son. 2. The personal is political.  Its rallying idea,  ‘the personal is political’ , denies the liberal separation of public and private: the family, marriage, housework and sexuality are themselves structures of power. Who eats last, who performs the unpaid domestic labour and who decides a pregnancy are political questions, not matters of private affection — which is why domestic violence and marital rape became feminist causes rather than family secrets. 3. Woman as the ‘Other’.  Simone de Beauvoir  ( The Second Sex ) argues that man is posited as the norm and woman defined only in relation to him — the  ‘Other’  — so that ‘one is not born, but becomes, a woman’: femininity is manufactured by upbringing, not given by nature.  Susan Brownmiller  pressed the argument further, calling rape ‘an institution of patriarchy’, and some radicals advocate androgyny as the escape. 4. Eco-feminism.  Credited to  Francoise d’Eaubonne  and developed by  Vandana Shiva  and  Mary Daly , eco-feminism links the  domination of women  with the  domination of nature : a masculinist, exploitative order treats both as passive resources to be used up. For Shiva the Indian village woman who fetches the water and gathers the fuel is the first casualty when forest and stream are destroyed, which makes women the natural allies of ecology. 5. Black and postcolonial feminism.  Black feminism  ( bell hooks ) and  postcolonial feminism  ( Chandra Talpade Mohanty ) charge that mainstream white, middle-class feminism universalised one experience and ignored  race and class : the woman who must also fight poverty, caste and a colonial legacy does not share the suburban housewife’s agenda, and the ‘third-world woman’ cannot be spoken for by Western feminists. 6. Conclusion.  Radical feminism transformed the discipline by politicising the private sphere, but its assumption of a single ‘women’s experience’ — an ‘essential’ femininity — is exactly what eco-, black and postcolonial feminists contest. Feminism has accordingly moved from sisterhood-as-sameness to a  politics of difference . Q — Is fascism a coherent ideology? Discuss its anti-rationalism and core tenets, its conception of the state, and whether it was merely an inter-war phenomenon. What it’s asking:  Test whether fascism is an ideology at all — its anti-rational core, its state, and whether it died in 1945. Gist — the spine to recall 1. Core  — from  fasces , ‘strength through unity’: ‘the individual, in a literal sense, is nothing’; a ‘hodge-podge of ideologies’ rather than a system.  (No founding text answers to Marx’s Capital or Locke’s Treatises.) 2. Anti-rationalism  — a counter-Enlightenment cult of will, instinct and myth over reason:  Sorel’s  ‘political myths’, ‘action not talk’, ‘1789 is dead’.  (Torchlit parades, uniforms and the myth of national rebirth move the crowd where argument cannot.) 3. Struggle & leadership  — social Darwinism (‘war is to men what maternity is to women’), the Führerprinzip,  Nietzsche’s  Übermensch, chauvinistic ultranationalism. 4. The state  — totalitarian and  corporatist ;  Mussolini  and  Gentile : ‘nothing against the State, nothing over it, nothing beyond it’.  (State-licensed bodies of employers and workers replace free trade unions — class conflict abolished by decree.) 5. Merely inter-war?  —  Nolte  ties it to defeat, depression and fear of communism;  Fromm  to the ‘fear of freedom’ in human nature;  Laski : ‘capitalism defending itself’. 6. Conclusion  — not a coherent ideology but a reactive movement; its impulses recur wherever crisis breeds authoritarian nationalism. Model Answer 1. Core.  Fascism takes its name from the  fasces , the bundle of rods symbolising ‘strength through unity’, and subordinates the individual utterly to nation and state — ‘the individual, in a literal sense, is nothing’ — aiming to forge a ‘new man’ of duty and sacrifice. Having no founding text comparable to  Capital  or  Two Treatises of Government , it is commonly dismissed as a ‘ hodge-podge of ideologies ’ or a ‘political religion’ rather than a coherent doctrine. 2. Anti-rationalism.  Anti-rationalism  is its hallmark: a counter-Enlightenment cult of  will, instinct and myth  in place of reason.  Georges Sorel’s  ‘political myths’ supply the model — a belief is judged by its power to mobilise, not by its truth — and Mussolini preferred ‘action, not talk’, declaring that ‘1789 is dead’. Torchlit parades, uniforms and the myth of national rebirth were deliberately chosen to move crowds where argument could not. 3. Struggle and leadership.  Its other tenets follow:  struggle  as the law of life, a social Darwinism in which ‘war is to men what maternity is to women’;  leadership and elitism , the Führerprinzip by which the leader embodies the will of the people, drawing on  Nietzsche’s  Übermensch; the pseudo-radical appeal of ‘national socialism’; and a chauvinistic  ultranationalism  that ranks nations as organic and unequal wholes. 4. The state.  Fascism’s state is  totalitarian  and  corporatist . For  Mussolini  and  Giovanni Gentile  there is ‘nothing against the State, nothing over it, nothing beyond it’, an inheritance from Hegel’s worship of the state. Corporatism means that state-licensed bodies of employers and workers replace free trade unions, so class conflict is abolished by decree rather than resolved. Nazism added  racialism  — Aryan supremacy, anti-Semitism and the ‘final solution’. 5. Merely inter-war?  Ernst Nolte  treats fascism as the product of specific  inter-war circumstances  — military defeat, the Depression, wounded national pride and fear of communism — so that it died with its epoch.  Erich Fromm  locates it instead in human nature, in the ‘fear of freedom’ that tempts the insecure individual to surrender himself to an authority, which implies recurrence.  Laski  offers the Marxist reading: ‘a desperate attempt by capitalism to protect itself’. 6. Conclusion.  Fascism is best seen not as a coherent ideology but as a reactive, anti-rational movement of extreme nationalism and leader-worship, held together by enemies rather than by principles. Fromm’s ‘fear of freedom’ is the warning: it was no mere inter-war accident, and its impulses resurface wherever crisis breeds authoritarian nationalism. Revision Box — facts, keywords & quotes Liberalism = meta-ideology;  core values: individualism, freedom, reason, justice, toleration. Liberal phases:  classical (Locke/Smith, night-watchman) → modern (Green, positive liberty) → neo-liberal (Hayek/Nozick/Friedman). Green : ‘will, not force, is the basis of the state’; state ‘hinders the hindrances’. Lyotard : postmodernism = ‘incredulity towards metanarratives’;  Nietzsche  = father of postmodernism. Bell : ‘end of ideology’;  Fukuyama : ‘end of history’;  Huntington : clash of civilizations. Socialism:  Joad — ‘a hat that has lost its shape’; core value = social equality. Utopian socialists:  Owen  (villages of cooperation),  Fourier ,  Saint-Simon . Evolutionary socialism:  revisionism (Bernstein), Fabianism (Shaw/Webbs), syndicalism, guild socialism (Cole). Marxism:  dialectical + historical materialism; base→superstructure; class struggle; surplus value. Marx : ‘history of all society is the history of class struggle’; ‘workers have nothing to lose but their chains’. Neo-Marxism:  Gramsci  (hegemony, war of position), Frankfurt School (Marcuse ‘one-dimensional man’), Althusser (ISAs, interpellation). Feminism:  sex (biological) vs gender (social); Beauvoir — ‘one is not born but becomes a woman’. Feminist strands:  liberal (Wollstonecraft/Mill), socialist (Engels), radical (Millett/Greer); eco-feminism (d’Eaubonne, Shiva). Waves:  1st suffrage; 2nd women’s liberation (Friedan’s ‘problem with no name’); 3rd difference (black/postcolonial). Fascism:  fasces = strength through unity; anti-rationalism; ‘1789 is dead’; totalitarian corporatist state. Laski : fascism = ‘capitalism defending itself’;  Fromm : ‘fear of freedom’;  Nolte : inter-war product. Last-Minute Revision Sheet (1 page) Liberalism (MQ1):  revolutionary (vs feudalism); classical→modern→neo-liberal; neo-liberalism = globalization’s ideology; social-liberal revival. Postmodernism/ends (MQ2):  Lyotard ‘incredulity to metanarratives’; Bell (end of ideology), Fukuyama (end of history) vs Huntington. Socialism (MQ3):  utopian (Owen/Fourier/Saint-Simon); revolutionary vs evolutionary (Bernstein/Fabians); reborn as anti-capitalism. Marxism (MQ4):  dialectical+historical materialism; class struggle; surplus value; relevance (Piketty, Eagleton) despite failed predictions. Neo-Marxism (MQ5):  Gramsci hegemony/war of position; Frankfurt School culture industry; Althusser ISAs — culture over economy. Feminism (MQ6):  sex vs gender; liberal/socialist/radical; three waves (suffrage/liberation/difference). Radical & new feminism (MQ7):  patriarchy, personal is political, Beauvoir ‘Other’; eco-feminism (Shiva); black/postcolonial critique. Fascism (MQ8):  individual = nothing; anti-rationalism, struggle, leader, corporatist state; Nolte vs Fromm; Laski’s Marxist critique. Killer quotes:  Beauvoir — ‘one is not born but becomes a woman’; Hayek — ‘social justice is a mirage’; Mussolini — ‘nothing beyond the State’; Marx — ‘nothing to lose but chains’. Previous Year Questions — coverage map 2020 — Liberalism as a revolutionary idea → MQ1. 2017 — End of History debate / Postmodernism → MQ2. 2015 — Pre-Marxist socialist theory → MQ3. 2014 — Socialism reborn as anti-capitalism → MQ3. 2019 — Contemporary relevance of Marxism → MQ4 (+ MQ5). 2019/2012 — Liberal vs radical feminism → MQ6. Sex vs gender / differences within feminism → MQ6. 2017 — Eco-feminism; Beauvoir quote → MQ7. Fascist anti-rationalism / inter-war → MQ8; Mussolini ‘nothing beyond the State’ → MQ8. title: 09 - Indian Political Thought

content.text: Syllabus — Indian Political Thought: Dharmashastra, Arthashastra and Buddhist traditions; Sir Syed Ahmed Khan, Sri Aurobindo, M.K. Gandhi, B.R. Ambedkar, M.N. Roy. (UPSC PSIR Paper-1A, Unit 9)

the ancient traditions — Dharmashastra (Manu), Arthashastra (Kautilya) and Buddhist political thought — and the modern thinkers Sir Syed Ahmed Khan, Sri Aurobindo, M.K. Gandhi, B.R. Ambedkar and M.N. Roy.

Manu (dharma, varna), Kautilya (Saptanga, Mandala, Danda-niti, Matsyanyaya), Buddha (MahaSammat, Dhamma), Sir Syed (two-nation theory), Aurobindo (spiritual nationalism, Purna Swaraj), Gandhi (Satyagraha, Swaraj, Sarvodaya, Trusteeship), Ambedkar (annihilation of caste, social democracy), M.N. Roy (radical humanism).

Gandhi (2020/2019/2016/2015) and Ambedkar (2022/2020/2018/2016/2013) are the highest-yield; also Kautilya’s statecraft (2017/2012/2010/2007), Buddhist ethics (2021), Aurobindo (2017/2016/2014/2013), Sir Syed (2021/2013), Dharma (2020), M.N. Roy.

Q — Explicate the ideological components of Gandhism — Truth/Ahimsa, Satyagraha, Swaraj, Sarvodaya and Trusteeship — and evaluate his critique of modern Western civilization and his view of the state. (UPSC 2020/2019/2016/2015)
List the building blocks of Gandhi’s thought one by one, then judge his attack on modern civilization and on the state itself.

(Ahimsa is active love, not cowardly submission — the man who runs away from the blow is not practising it.)

(The satyagrahi breaks the unjust law openly, accepts the lathi-blow and the jail term without retaliating, so the opponent’s conscience — not his body — is defeated.)

(Not swapping a white ruler for a brown one: it is the village governing itself and the individual mastering his own appetites — ending in Ram Rajya, a near-stateless order of self-governing ‘oceanic circles’.)

(The mill-owner keeps the mill but holds its wealth in trust for his workers, drawing only what he needs — ‘there is enough for need but not for greed’.)
modern Western civilization is ‘satanic’ and materialist, and the state is ‘a soulless machine’ resting on coercion.
(Railways, lawyers and doctors spread disease, litigation and dependence rather than civilisation.)

(A freedom won by terror would itself have been an unfree India.)

In practice the satyagrahi disobeys the unjust law openly, invites arrest and absorbs the blow without returning it, converting the opponent by melting his conscience instead of crushing his body.

together — political, economic, social and cultural. Merely replacing English rulers by Indian ones would be English rule without the Englishman; genuine Swaraj means the village governing its own affairs through Panchayati Raj and the individual governing his own appetites. Its culmination is

His famous image guards this from parochialism: ‘I do not want my house to be walled in… I want the cultures of all lands to be blown about my house… but I refuse to be blown off my feet’.
— ‘the uplift of all’ rather than the greatest good of the greatest number — resting on

. Capitalists are ‘trustees, not owners’: the mill-owner retains the mill but holds its wealth in trust for his workers and for society, drawing only what he genuinely needs, since ‘there is enough for need but not for greed’. This substitutes class cooperation and a change of heart for the Marxist expropriation of the propertied class.

Gandhi condemns modern Western civilization as materialist and ‘satanic’ — it multiplies wants instead of mastering them, and its railways, lawyers and doctors spread disease, litigation and dependence rather than true civilisation, which he defines as that mode of conduct which points out to man the path of duty. The

is condemned on the same ground: it is ‘a soulless machine’ based on coercion, representing violence in a concentrated and organised form, and it stunts the self-reliance and moral growth of the individual. His ideal is therefore ‘enlightened anarchy’ — government reduced to the minimum as men learn to govern themselves.

Gandhism fuses ethics and politics through the ‘continuity of ends and means’ — ‘if we take care of the means, the end will take care of itself’, for a freedom won by terror would itself be unfree. Though Trusteeship and Ram Rajya are criticised as impractical and utopian, Gandhi’s non-violent Satyagraha remains his enduring contribution to world politics.
Q — Explain the sources and salient features of ancient Indian political thought, and examine the significance of Dharma in the Dharmashastra (Manu) tradition. (UPSC 2020)
Where ancient Indian thought comes from, what marks it out, and why Dharma is its master-concept.

(Politics is a chapter of ethics here, not the separate autonomous science it becomes in Machiavelli.)

Ancient Indian (‘Hindu’) political thought derives from

Four features stand out. It shows ‘enormous continuity’ of dharma and danda across centuries rather than sharp ruptures. It is
— the individual is always located within family, kula, jati and society, never posed against them as in Western individualism. It is
‘the entire world is a family’ captures the vasudhaiva kutumbakam spirit. But it is also

‘Dharma Shastras are books on law; Danda Shastras are books on politics’ — but they differ only in

The significance of dharma is shown negatively by what follows its absence:

Dharma is therefore the master concept of the ancient Indian polity — it simultaneously legitimises kingship and limits it, anticipating constitutionalism without a constitution. Yet the same tradition sanctified the varna hierarchy and graded punishment — ‘the lower the varna, the higher the punishment’ — which drew

Q — Discuss Kautilya’s theory of statecraft — the Saptanga (Sapta Prakriti), Mandala Siddhanta, Shadgunya-niti and the four Upayas — and his analysis of corruption. (UPSC 2017/2007)

Kautilya’s statecraft is remarkably systematic and practical — an ancient science of realpolitik, administration and geopolitics. Saptanga anticipates the organic theory of the state and the modern elements of statehood; the Mandala anticipates alliance theory and the

Q — Draw parallels and contrasts between Kautilya’s Arthashastra and the realist tradition of Machiavelli, and compare Dharmashastra and Arthashastra with reference to state power. (UPSC 2012/2010)

(The spies, poisoners and courtesan-agents of the Arthashastra have no parallel in The Prince.)

(Power is a means for Kautilya, an end for Machiavelli — and ‘Kautilya got his king, Machiavelli never got his prince’.)
(Manu’s king punishes to uphold the cosmic order; Kautilya’s punishes to keep the state strong, since artha is ‘supreme’ and dharma, kama and moksha depend on it.)

(Power is ruthless in operation yet answerable to a higher moral order.)

Both permit the ruler ‘all sorts of means’, both endorse an imperialist or expansionist foreign policy, and both in effect hold that the end justifies the means. Kautilya’s
— dividing the adversary — and Machiavelli’s counsel to keep rivals disunited are the same instrument under two different names.

The difference lies in ethics: ‘for Machiavelli the Prince is above religion; for Kautilya the king remains
’. Kautilya’s king is enjoined to be ‘generous and kind’, is bound by the welfare of his subjects, and treats power as a

; Machiavelli’s prince rules ‘with an iron hand’ and treats power as self-justifying. Machiavelli offers generic counsel, Kautilya precise administrative detail — and, as the contrast is often put, ‘Kautilya got his king, Machiavelli never got his prince’.
On state power the two Indian traditions differ in emphasis rather than in kind. The
: coercion exists to uphold the moral and cosmic order, and the king, bound by Raj Dharma, punishes in order to preserve varnashrama. The
and dharma peripheral: the king punishes to keep the state strong, because material well-being (‘artha’) is ‘supreme’, for ‘on it depend dharma, kama and moksha’.
Kautilya is a realist like Machiavelli but a

represents a distinctively Indian synthesis of statecraft and ethics: power is real, calculating and ruthless in operation, yet ultimately answerable to a higher moral order which the ruler did not create and cannot repeal.
Q — Examine the salient features of Buddhist political thought, assess whether it gave a greater ethical foundation to ancient Indian thought, and compare it with the Hindu tradition. (UPSC 2021)
Set out what is distinctive about Buddhist politics, then decide whether it is ethically superior to the Brahmanical tradition it broke from.

(This-worldly and deliberative against other-worldly and hierarchical.)
(Which is exactly why Ambedkar chose Buddhism in 1956 as the emancipatory alternative to caste Hinduism.)

tradition, the ‘Protestantism of the East’, which challenged caste, dispensed with the priestly intermediary and Vedic ritual, and preached in Pali rather than Sanskrit so that the message reached every varna.
accordingly treats the Buddha as a genuine political philosopher and not merely a religious teacher.
Where the Hindu tradition derives kingship from the need to end
ordained in the cosmic scheme, the Buddhist account is historical and moral: the state arises from the

of men. In an originally innocent society the growth of greed, property and theft made restraint necessary, and men themselves devised authority to supply it. Political power is therefore a human remedy for a human failing, not a divine institution.
It follows that the king is

— ‘the Great Elect’ — chosen by the people to keep order in return for a share of their produce, and remaining ‘only primus inter pares, by virtue of a social contract’. Authority is thus conditional upon consent and upon performance of the agreed function, giving Buddhism a theory of
decentralised democracy, equality and the social contract
many centuries before Hobbes, Locke and Rousseau — reflected institutionally in the ganasangha republics and in the deliberative procedure of the sangha itself.
— ethical persuasion — rather than by danda: the ideal ruler is the

who ‘wins others by the Dhamma Chakra’, conquering hearts instead of territory. Ashoka’s polity after Kalinga embodied this, yet he ‘never made Buddhism a state religion’ and enjoined respect for all sects — an implicit secularism.

The contrast is systematic: this-worldly against other-worldly;

; a king elected by the MahaSammat against a king of ‘divine personality’; the Chakravartin winning hearts against the vijigishu acquiring land; Dhamma and Panchsheel against Danda and Mandala; and, most consequentially, the
rejection of caste in favour of equality
against the Brahmanical hierarchy of varna. Where the Hindu tradition legitimises order through birth, the Buddhist legitimises it through consent and conduct.
Buddhist thought did lend a greater

Q — Assess Sir Syed Ahmed Khan as a social reformer and modernizer, tracing his transition from champion of Hindu-Muslim unity to originator of the two-nation theory. (UPSC 2021/2013)
Two halves — credit him as a reformer, then explain why the preacher of unity turned into the father of the two-nation theory.
— Muslim upliftment is ‘possible only with the modernization of Islam’, a faith ‘most compatible with science and rationality’.
(‘The Muslim youth should hold the book of science in one hand and the Quran in the other’.)
(MAO College grew into Aligarh Muslim University; his standing among Muslims is compared to Raja Ram Mohan Roy’s among Hindus.)
— a ‘champion of democratic ideals and freedom of speech’ who attacked religious intolerance.
(He denounced purdah, polygamy and easy divorce as social evils rather than sanctified custom.)
— a common Indian nationhood; by ‘qaum’ he meant both communities.
(‘Hindus and Muslims are the two eyes of the beautiful bride, India’ — sharing ‘the same soil… the same ruler… the hardships of a famine’.)
— fearing that under elections the Hindu majority would ‘totally override the interests of the smaller community’, he opposed representative government and the Congress.
(Counting heads where the majority is permanent means permanent minority subordination — hence the ‘Anglo-Muslim alliance’.)
— his educational and political legacies pull in opposite directions.
(AMU on one side, the ideological seed of Partition on the other.)

held that Muslim upliftment was ‘possible only with the modernization of Islam’, a faith he regarded as ‘most compatible with science and rationality’. Writing after 1857, when the community had turned inward and boycotted English education, his central message was the reconciliation of revelation with reason: ‘the Muslim youth should hold the book of science in one hand and the Quran in the other’. Faith and modern knowledge, he insisted, cannot contradict each other because both proceed from the same source.
He acted on this creed institutionally. He launched the journal
to reform Muslim manners and opinion, founded a scientific society to translate Western works into Urdu, and established the
and became the seedbed of a modern Muslim professional class. His status among Muslims is fairly compared to
He was, in the textbook’s phrase, a ‘champion of democratic ideals and freedom of speech’ who attacked religious intolerance and irrational custom wherever he found them. He denounced
as social evils rather than sanctified practice, and urged that scripture be interpreted in the light of reason and changing circumstance — a position that drew the hostility of the orthodox ulema.

In his earlier phase he was an unambiguous exponent of a common Indian nationhood. Hindus and Muslims are ‘the two eyes of the beautiful bride, India’ — injure one and the bride is disfigured — for they share ‘the same soil… the same ruler… the hardships of a famine’. By
(nation) he expressly meant ‘both Hindus and Muslims’, and he worked closely with Hindu leaders in educational and civic causes.
The shift came with the prospect of

. Sir Syed feared that where elections turn on counting heads in a society of permanent majorities and minorities, the Hindu majority would ‘totally override the interests of the smaller community’, reducing Muslims to permanent subordination. He therefore turned against parliamentary self-government, opposed the Congress, and sought an ‘Anglo-Muslim alliance’, becoming the originator of the

— the doctrine that Hindus and Muslims form two distinct nations. The Urdu-Hindi controversy, his dependence on government funding for the Aligarh college, and rising Hindu revivalism all accelerated the transition.

Sir Syed was a genuine modernizer who dragged a defeated and conservative community toward science, English education and social reform. But his later communal politics laid the ideological seed of Partition, so that his educational legacy at Aligarh and his political legacy in the two-nation theory pull in exactly opposite directions.
Q — Analyse Sri Aurobindo’s theory of cultural/spiritual nationalism, his conception of Swaraj and his idea of freedom. (UPSC 2017/2016/2014/2013)
Three linked ideas — the nation as spirit, Swaraj as complete independence, and freedom as inner self-realisation.

(Nationalism is not a political programme but a way of life like religion — the patriot is a devotee, not a party worker.)

nation is a faith, a religion, the nation has a spirit

(Swadeshi, boycott and non-cooperation — the doctrinal ground on which Gandhi’s Satyagraha was later built.)

(‘Political freedom is the life-breath of a nation’; to attempt social reform ‘without aiming first at political freedom is the height of ignorance’.)

(‘Obeying the law of our own existence’ — swadharma — so a man free of foreign rule but enslaved to his appetites is not free.)
— he raised nationalism from programme to vocation, though critics call it reactionary and idealistic.
(By rooting it in an ‘open and universal’ Sanatana Dharma he radicalised the freedom movement.)

saw in him ‘the highest synthesis of the genius of Asia and of Europe’. For him nationalism was not a mere political programme but a way of life like religion: the patriot approaches the nation as a devotee approaches the divine, with faith and self-surrender rather than a calculation of interest. This converted the freedom struggle from a constitutional claim into a spiritual vocation.
claim that ‘the nation is natural and has a spirit’ — and drawing on
Neo-Vedanta, Aurobindo held that ‘the nation is not a piece of land… the
nation is a faith, the nation is a religion, the nation has a spirit
’. India is not a territory but a living Mother with a
— to give spirituality to a materialist world — so her subjection is a spiritual and not merely a political wrong.
In his extremist phase Aurobindo dismissed the Moderates’ constitutional petitioning as futile and pioneered a systematic theory of

— organised non-cooperation with an alien administration, backed by swadeshi, boycott and national education, to be abandoned only if repression made resistance impossible. This body of doctrine prepared the ground on which
Satyagraha would be built a decade later.
He was the first Indian leader to interpret Swaraj as

— complete independence rather than colonial self-government within the Empire — to be won through swadeshi, boycott, national education and passive resistance. ‘Political freedom is the life-breath of a nation’, he wrote, and to attempt social reform ‘without aiming first at political freedom is the height of ignorance’. Swaraj is thus the ‘necessary condition for India to accomplish its destined goal’ — the political shell within which the spiritual mission can be realised.

Aurobindo found the liberal, near-anarchic conception of liberty ‘mechanical’ — an absence of external restraint that says nothing about what the free man becomes — and the socialist conception neglectful of the individual. Real freedom is
: ‘obeying the law of our own existence’, that is, swadharma. A man released from foreign rule but enslaved to his own appetites has not become free. His later thought —
Sacchidananda, the Supermind and Integral Yoga
— accordingly makes national self-realisation one stage in the spiritual evolution of humanity as a whole.

Aurobindo raised nationalism from a political programme to a spiritual vocation. Critics call his spiritual nationalism reactionary, idealistic and open to majoritarian appropriation; yet by rooting freedom in an ‘open and universal’ Sanatana Dharma rather than a narrow creed, and by demanding Purna Swaraj when others asked only for reform, he decisively radicalised the Indian freedom movement.

Q — Evaluate Ambedkar’s idea of social justice — annihilation of caste, critique of Hinduism and of Marxism, and his conception of social/economic/political democracy — comparing his egalitarian justice with Rawls. (UPSC 2022/2020/2018/2016/2013)
Build Ambedkar’s theory of justice upward from caste, then measure it against Rawls’ procedural justice.

(A guild you may leave; a caste you are born into and must marry within — so inter-caste marriage, not ritual reform, is the real solvent.)
— ‘Hinduism is nothing but Brahmanism’, sanctified by the Vedas and the Manusmriti.
(He would ‘put dynamite’ on the Manusmriti, and finding reform impossible from within, converted to Buddhism in 1956: ‘I reject the religion which treats me as inferior’.)
— democracy is ‘a way of life’ on the ‘inseparable trinity of liberty, equality and fraternity’; political democracy must be completed by
(One man one vote is worthless if the same man may not draw water from the village well.)
(Not merely obeying the text but internalising its spirit — self-restraint, due process, respect for dissent — in a soil he called ‘essentially undemocratic’.)
— religion is not mere ‘opium’, and ‘society is more exploitative than the state’.
(Buddhism, built on karuna, samata and prajna, liberates; and the untouchable is humiliated by his neighbours, so the state must be his instrument of emancipation, not his enemy.)
(Rawls reasons from a hypothetical veil of ignorance; Ambedkar starts from a real history of humiliation and demands safeguards to undo it.)
— ‘chief architect of the Constitution’ and himself born a Mahar — made the
he argues that caste is ‘not the division of labour but the
’: a guild divides work and may be left, whereas caste divides human beings themselves into fixed, graded compartments one is born into. Its steel frame is
, which is why he held that inter-caste marriage and inter-dining, not the reform of ritual, are the real solvents of the system.
Caste for Ambedkar is not an excrescence but the essence: ‘Hinduism is nothing but Brahmanism’, a graded inequality sanctified by the Vedas and above all by the

, on which he said he would ‘put dynamite’ and which he publicly burnt in 1927. Because the sanction is scriptural, reform from within is impossible — destroy belief in the sanctity of the shastras and caste collapses. Finding no such reform forthcoming, he
in 1956: ‘I reject the religion which treats me as inferior’.

For Ambedkar democracy is not a form of government but ‘a way of life’, resting on the ‘inseparable trinity of liberty, equality and fraternity’, which he traced to the Buddha rather than to the French Revolution. Hence his warning that India was entering a life of contradictions: political equality of one man one vote alongside social and economic inequality. Political democracy must therefore be completed by
, for ‘political democracy cannot last unless there lies at its base social democracy’ — the vote is empty if the voter may not draw water from the village well.
The instruments of that completion are

and ‘state socialism’. Borrowing the phrase from Grote, Ambedkar meant not mere obedience to the constitutional text but internalisation of its spirit — self-restraint by those in power, respect for forms and for dissent, and the settling of conflict by due process rather than agitation — a habit he thought had to be deliberately cultivated because Indian soil was ‘essentially undemocratic’. Alongside it he urged state ownership of key industries and of land, so that concentrated economic power could not defeat formal equality.

Ambedkar rejected two Marxist claims. First, that religion is mere ‘opium’: Buddhism, resting on karuna, samata and prajna, is a liberating morality and not a narcotic. Second, that the state is the chief instrument of oppression — for Ambedkar ‘society is more exploitative than the state’, since the untouchable is humiliated by his own neighbours and not primarily by officials, so the state must be strengthened as an instrument of emancipation. He also rejected violent revolution and the dictatorship of the proletariat in favour of constitutional methods.
— the active uplift of the depressed classes through state action, reservation and constitutional safeguards — whereas

, derived from a hypothetical original position behind a veil of ignorance. Ambedkar begins not from an abstraction but from a documented history of humiliation. He thus transformed justice in India from a matter of procedure into one of
, making the annihilation of caste and the completion of democracy his enduring legacy.
Q — Trace M.N. Roy’s ideational journey from Marxism to Radical Humanism, and identify the major components of Modern Indian Political Thought with reference to Gandhi and Roy.
Follow Roy’s three phases and his two breaks, then use Gandhi and Roy together to name what modern Indian thought is made of.
(A revolutionary who founded the CPI abroad and ended by dissolving his own party for the sake of the individual.)

(Lenin wanted communists to ally with bourgeois-nationalists like the Congress; Roy insisted they lead the colonial proletariat directly — ‘for socialism to win in the West it must first win in the East’.)
in ‘the collective ego of the proletariat’; historical materialism is ‘economic determinism’; the sanction against exploitation is ‘not economic but
(Man, not class or party, is the measure — freedom is ‘the progressive removal of restrictions on the unfolding of the potentialities of individuals… not as cogs in a mechanized social organism’.)
— parties ‘bred social and political immorality’ and reduce sovereignty to a ‘legal fiction’.
(He dissolved his own party in 1948 for ‘people’s committees’ and ‘miniature republics’ — candidates chosen for merit, not for a party ticket.)
— spiritual against rationalist, yet both converge on
decentralisation, the individual, and morality in politics
(Bidyut Chakraborty thinks Roy never fully escaped Marxism, yet his is the most individual-centred voice in modern Indian thought.)
intellectual life moved through three distinct phases —

. Beginning as a revolutionary nationalist in Bengal, he became a founder of the Communist Party of India and one of the very few Asians to hold a leading position in the Comintern, and ended by dissolving his own party in the name of the individual — a trajectory from collective revolution to personal freedom.
The first break came at the Second Congress of the Comintern (1920), where Roy clashed with
. Lenin’s colonial theses proposed a two-stage strategy in which communists would first ally with bourgeois-nationalist movements such as the Congress; Roy’s

replied that such movements were led by classes with a stake in the existing order, and that communists must organise and lead the colonial proletariat and peasantry directly. His larger claim was that imperial profit sustained European capitalism, so that ‘for socialism to win in the West it must first win in the East’.
Disillusioned, Roy came to regard ‘Marxism as more method than dogma’ and criticised it on three counts. It

, dissolving the person into ‘the collective ego of the proletariat’ and then into the party. Its historical materialism is mere ‘economic determinism’, denying the creative role of ideas and of human will in history. And the true sanction for ending exploitation is ‘not economic but
’ — a revolution begun in immorality cannot end in freedom.
— man is essentially rational, and blind faith, whether religious or ideological, must be rejected.
— secular and rational, rooted in man’s own rationality rather than in divine command. And

, defined as ‘the progressive removal of all restrictions on the unfolding of the potentialities of individuals… not as cogs in a mechanized social organism’. Man, not class or party, is the measure of every social arrangement, and the goal is a cosmopolitan ‘commonwealth of spiritually free men’.

Holding that the party system ‘bred social and political immorality’ — subordinating conscience to the whip and reducing popular sovereignty to a ‘legal fiction’ exercised for a moment at the ballot box — Roy dissolved his own party in 1948 in favour of ‘organized democracy’: decentralised ‘people’s committees’ and ‘miniature republics’ in which candidates are chosen for personal merit rather than a party ticket, and power is exercised continuously from below with primacy given to the individual.
The major components of modern Indian political thought are visible in the contrast between the two.

decentralisation, the primacy of the individual and the community, and the insistence on morality in politics
— the recurring signature of modern Indian thought. Though

(UPSC PSIR Paper-1A, Unit 9) Unit Snapshot What this unit covers:  the ancient traditions — Dharmashastra (Manu), Arthashastra (Kautilya) and Buddhist political thought — and the modern thinkers Sir Syed Ahmed Khan, Sri Aurobindo, M.K. Gandhi, B.R. Ambedkar and M.N. Roy. Must-know thinkers & concepts:  Manu (dharma, varna), Kautilya (Saptanga, Mandala, Danda-niti, Matsyanyaya), Buddha (MahaSammat, Dhamma), Sir Syed (two-nation theory), Aurobindo (spiritual nationalism, Purna Swaraj), Gandhi (Satyagraha, Swaraj, Sarvodaya, Trusteeship), Ambedkar (annihilation of caste, social democracy), M.N. Roy (radical humanism).
