Master Questions Q — Explicate the ideological components of Gandhism — Truth/Ahimsa, Satyagraha, Swaraj, Sarvodaya and Trusteeship — and evaluate his critique of modern Western civilization and his view of the state. (UPSC 2020/2019/2016/2015) What it’s asking:  List the building blocks of Gandhi’s thought one by one, then judge his attack on modern civilization and on the state itself. Gist — the spine to recall 1. Truth & Ahimsa  — the twin foundation: ‘God and truth are inseparable’ and non-violence is ‘not the resort of the weak but the power of the strong’.  (Ahimsa is active love, not cowardly submission — the man who runs away from the blow is not practising it.) 2. Satyagraha  — satya + agraha = ‘soul-force over brute-force through self-suffering’, aimed ‘against the evil, not the evil-doer’.  (The satyagrahi breaks the unjust law openly, accepts the lathi-blow and the jail term without retaliating, so the opponent’s conscience — not his body — is defeated.)   Martin Luther King : ‘Christ furnished the spirit, Gandhi furnished the method’. 3. Swaraj & Ram Rajya  — liberty as  self-rule plus self-control , political, economic, social and cultural.  (Not swapping a white ruler for a brown one: it is the village governing itself and the individual mastering his own appetites — ending in Ram Rajya, a near-stateless order of self-governing ‘oceanic circles’.) 4. Sarvodaya & Trusteeship  — from Ruskin’s  Unto This Last , ‘the uplift of all’ through bread labour, with the rich as ‘trustees, not owners’.  (The mill-owner keeps the mill but holds its wealth in trust for his workers, drawing only what he needs — ‘there is enough for need but not for greed’.) 5. Critique of modernity & the state  — in  Hind Swaraj  modern Western civilization is ‘satanic’ and materialist, and the state is ‘a soulless machine’ resting on coercion.  (Railways, lawyers and doctors spread disease, litigation and dependence rather than civilisation.) 6. Conclusion  — ends and means are continuous: ‘if we take care of the means, the end will take care of itself’.  (A freedom won by terror would itself have been an unfree India.) Model Answer 1. Truth & Ahimsa.  Gandhi denied there was any ‘Gandhism’;  Humayun Kabir  called him ‘not a philosopher but a strategist… a psychologist’, and his ideas — set out in  Hind Swaraj  and  My Experiments with Truth , drawing on the Gita, Tolstoy and Ruskin — rest on two inseparable foundations. ‘God and truth are inseparable’, and  Ahimsa  is the only means of realising truth: it is ‘not the resort of the weak but the power of the strong’, active love rather than the cowardice of the man who simply runs away from the blow. 2. Satyagraha.  From truth and non-violence flows  Satyagraha  (satya + agraha) — ‘soul-force over brute-force through self-suffering’, directed ‘against the evil, not the evil-doer’, and therefore quite distinct from mere passive resistance, which is the weapon of the weak. In practice the satyagrahi disobeys the unjust law openly, invites arrest and absorbs the blow without returning it, converting the opponent by melting his conscience instead of crushing his body.  Martin Luther King  acknowledged the debt: ‘Christ furnished the spirit, Gandhi furnished the method’. 3. Swaraj & Ram Rajya.  Gandhi’s idea of liberty is  self-rule and self-control  together — political, economic, social and cultural. Merely replacing English rulers by Indian ones would be English rule without the Englishman; genuine Swaraj means the village governing its own affairs through Panchayati Raj and the individual governing his own appetites. Its culmination is  Ram Rajya , a stateless society of ‘oceanic circles’ in which the individual is the centre and no circle dominates another. His famous image guards this from parochialism: ‘I do not want my house to be walled in… I want the cultures of all lands to be blown about my house… but I refuse to be blown off my feet’. 4. Sarvodaya & Trusteeship.  From Ruskin’s  Unto This Last  Gandhi drew  Sarvodaya  — ‘the uplift of all’ rather than the greatest good of the greatest number — resting on  bread labour  and on  Trusteeship . Capitalists are ‘trustees, not owners’: the mill-owner retains the mill but holds its wealth in trust for his workers and for society, drawing only what he genuinely needs, since ‘there is enough for need but not for greed’. This substitutes class cooperation and a change of heart for the Marxist expropriation of the propertied class. 5. Critique of modernity & the state.  In  Hind Swaraj  Gandhi condemns modern Western civilization as materialist and ‘satanic’ — it multiplies wants instead of mastering them, and its railways, lawyers and doctors spread disease, litigation and dependence rather than true civilisation, which he defines as that mode of conduct which points out to man the path of duty. The  state  is condemned on the same ground: it is ‘a soulless machine’ based on coercion, representing violence in a concentrated and organised form, and it stunts the self-reliance and moral growth of the individual. His ideal is therefore ‘enlightened anarchy’ — government reduced to the minimum as men learn to govern themselves. 6. Conclusion.  Gandhism fuses ethics and politics through the ‘continuity of ends and means’ — ‘if we take care of the means, the end will take care of itself’, for a freedom won by terror would itself be unfree. Though Trusteeship and Ram Rajya are criticised as impractical and utopian, Gandhi’s non-violent Satyagraha remains his enduring contribution to world politics. Q — Explain the sources and salient features of ancient Indian political thought, and examine the significance of Dharma in the Dharmashastra (Manu) tradition. (UPSC 2020) What it’s asking:  Where ancient Indian thought comes from, what marks it out, and why Dharma is its master-concept. Gist — the spine to recall 1. Sources & riti  — thought derives from  riti , the cosmic order known through spiritual experience, and from the shrutis and smritis (the  Manusmriti ).  (Riti does for India what natural law does for the West — a higher order the ruler did not make and cannot unmake.) 2. Salient features  — ‘enormous continuity’,  communitarian, pluralistic and cosmopolitan , but non-critical and regressive about history.  (Sant Tukaram: ‘the entire world is a family’ — the individual sits inside kula, jati and society, never against them.) 3. Dharma & Danda in continuum  — ‘Dharma Shastras are books on law; Danda Shastras are books on politics’, differing in degree, not in kind.  (Politics is a chapter of ethics here, not the separate autonomous science it becomes in Machiavelli.) 4. Manu & the significance of Dharma  —  Manu , the ‘first law-giver’: ‘ Prithvim Dharma Dhritam ’, dharma is that which holds life on earth.  (It is social cement — each varna and ashrama performing its own svadharma keeps the whole edifice standing.) 5. Matsyanyaya & the king under law  — dharma’s absence brings  arajakta  and  Matsya Nyaya .  (‘The big fish eats the small fish’ — anarchy, where strength alone decides.)  Hence the king has ‘divine personality’ but  no divine rights . 6. Conclusion  — dharma both legitimises and limits kingship, yet sanctifies varna hierarchy —  Ambedkar’s  target.  (‘The lower the varna, the higher the punishment’.) Model Answer 1. Sources & riti.  Ancient Indian (‘Hindu’) political thought derives from  riti  — the all-pervading cosmic order, discoverable through spiritual experience, which orders nature and society alike. It performs the same office as the Western concept of  natural law : a standard the ruler neither creates nor can abolish, and against which his commands are measured. Its textual sources are the  Vedic corpus  — the shrutis (the Vedas, ‘that which is heard’) and the smritis (‘that which is remembered’), above all the  Manusmriti . 2. Salient features.  Four features stand out. It shows ‘enormous continuity’ of dharma and danda across centuries rather than sharp ruptures. It is  communitarian  — the individual is always located within family, kula, jati and society, never posed against them as in Western individualism. It is  pluralistic and cosmopolitan ;  Sant Tukaram’s  ‘the entire world is a family’ captures the vasudhaiva kutumbakam spirit. But it is also  non-critical , taking a regressive rather than a progressive view of history — the golden age lies behind, in Satya Yuga, and the present is a fall from it. 3. Dharma & Danda in continuum.  ‘Dharma Shastras are books on law; Danda Shastras are books on politics’ — but they differ only in  degree , for Indian thought treats them not ‘in silos but in a continuum’. Politics is thus a chapter of ethics rather than an autonomous science, unlike the Machiavellian separation of the two. Within the  Dharmashastra  tradition dharma is the core and danda the periphery; in the Arthashastra the emphasis is exactly reversed. 4. Manu & the significance of Dharma.  Manu , the ‘first law-giver’ and Manasputra of Brahma, is the chief exponent of this tradition.  Dharma  — at once moral, natural and social order — is its master concept: ‘ Prithvim Dharma Dhritam ’, dharma is that which holds life on earth. It works as social cement, each varna and each ashrama discharging its own svadharma so that the whole edifice stands; and it is also the source of the king’s obligations, since Raj Dharma binds him as tightly as it binds the subject. 5. Matsyanyaya & the king under law.  The significance of dharma is shown negatively by what follows its absence:  arajakta  (anarchy) and  Matsya Nyaya  — literally the law of the fish, where ‘the big fish eats the small fish’ and strength alone decides, the Indian equivalent of the Hobbesian state of nature. Kingship exists precisely to prevent this. Yet although the king possesses a ‘divine personality’, he has  no divine rights  of the European kind: he is bound by Raj Dharma and stands  under the law , and a king who violates dharma forfeits his claim to obedience. 6. Conclusion.  Dharma is therefore the master concept of the ancient Indian polity — it simultaneously legitimises kingship and limits it, anticipating constitutionalism without a constitution. Yet the same tradition sanctified the varna hierarchy and graded punishment — ‘the lower the varna, the higher the punishment’ — which drew  Ambedkar’s  sharp critique and exposed the tension between order and equality lying at its heart. Q — Discuss Kautilya’s theory of statecraft — the Saptanga (Sapta Prakriti), Mandala Siddhanta, Shadgunya-niti and the four Upayas — and his analysis of corruption. (UPSC 2017/2007) What it’s asking:  Take Kautilya’s toolkit in order — the parts of the state, the map of neighbours, the six policies and four devices — and end with his diagnosis of corruption. Gist — the spine to recall 1. The text & Danda-niti  — the  Arthashastra  is a manual of administration, and  danda-niti , the science of the rod, is what holds society together.  (Withdraw the rod and you get Matsyanyaya, ‘big fish eats small fish’ — punishment is the price of order.) 2. Saptanga  — the seven limbs: Swami, Amatya, Janapada, Durga, Kosha, Danda/Bala, Mitra.  (An organic body — the king is the ‘Nabhi’ or navel, ministers its eyes, the treasury its blood; ‘one wheel alone does not turn the chariot’.) 3. Mandala Siddhanta  — concentric rings of natural enemy (Ari) and natural friend (Mitra) around the  vijigishu .  (Your neighbour is your enemy and his neighbour your friend; a state lying between two powers — as Nepal lies between India and China — is the Madhyama or buffer.) 4. Shadgunya-niti & four Upayas  — six policies (Sandhi, Vigraha, Asana, Yana, Samshraya, Dvaidhibhava) and Sama, Dama, Danda, Bheda.  (Persuade → buy off → punish → divide: escalate only when the cheaper device fails.) 5. Corruption  — ‘inevitable yet not desirable’; he lists ‘forty ways of embezzlement’.  (‘As it is impossible not to taste honey on the tongue’, and ‘a fish moving in water cannot be detected drinking it’.)  Remedies: transfers, whistle-blowers, rewards. 6. Conclusion  — an ancient science of realpolitik anticipating the organic theory of the state and the  balance of power .  (Saptanga prefigures the modern elements of statehood; Mandala prefigures alliance theory.) Model Answer 1. The text & Danda-niti.  Kautilya’s   Arthashastra  is essentially ‘a book on the art of administration’ and the first Indian text of  statecraft  and geopolitics. Its normative anchor is the maxim that ‘in the happiness of the subjects lies the happiness of the king’, but the means are hard-headed.  Danda-niti  — the science of the rod — is for Kautilya the decisive branch of knowledge, because coercive authority alone prevents  Matsyanyaya , the condition in which ‘the big fish eats the small fish’. Punishment wrongly used terrifies, left unused invites anarchy; used justly it upholds dharma, artha and kama alike. 2. Saptanga (Sapta Prakriti).  The state is presented as an organism of  seven limbs , exactly as a body has limbs:  Swami  (the king, the ‘Nabhi’ or navel around which all else turns),  Amatya  (ministers, its eyes and ears),  Janapada  (territory with its population),  Durga  (the fort),  Kosha  (the treasury — ‘all undertakings depend upon Kosha’, its blood),  Danda or Bala  (the army, its arms) and  Mitra  (the ally). No limb is dispensable and none suffices alone: ‘one wheel alone does not turn the chariot’. This organic conception strikingly anticipates the modern enumeration of the elements of statehood. 3. Mandala Siddhanta.  Foreign policy is mapped as a  mandala  — concentric circles drawn around the  vijigishu , ‘the one who aspires to victory’. The immediate neighbour is the natural enemy ( Ari ), the neighbour beyond him the natural friend ( Mitra ), and so outward in alternating rings; a strong state situated between two rivals is the  Madhyama  or buffer — the position Nepal occupies between India and China — while a state outside the system altogether is the  Udasina  or neutral. Enmity is therefore structural, a function of geography rather than sentiment, which is why the theory is read as an early doctrine of the  balance of power . 4. Shadgunya-niti & the four Upayas.  Within the mandala the vijigishu chooses among six measures —  Shadgunya-niti : Sandhi (a peace treaty), Vigraha (hostility), Asana (keeping quiet or neutrality), Yana (marching to war), Samshraya (seeking shelter with a stronger king) and Dvaidhibhava (the double policy of peace with one and war with another). To achieve any of these he applies the four  Upayas  in ascending order of cost:  Sama  (conciliation),  Dama  (gifts or bribery),  Danda  (force) and  Bheda  (sowing division) — escalating only when the cheaper instrument has failed. 5. Corruption.  Kautilya thought corruption ‘inevitable yet not desirable’, and his realism about it is unmatched in ancient literature: ‘just as it is impossible not to taste honey on the tongue, so it is impossible for one dealing with government funds not to taste the king’s wealth’, and ‘a fish moving in water cannot be detected drinking it’. He catalogues  forty ways of embezzlement  and prescribes institutional rather than merely moral remedies — frequent transfers of officials, protection and reward for informers and whistle-blowers, rewards for the honest, and punishment of ‘the entire chain’ rather than of the lowest offender alone. 6. Conclusion.  Kautilya’s statecraft is remarkably systematic and practical — an ancient science of realpolitik, administration and geopolitics. Saptanga anticipates the organic theory of the state and the modern elements of statehood; the Mandala anticipates alliance theory and the  balance of power ; and his treatment of corruption reads like a modern manual of administrative vigilance. Q — Draw parallels and contrasts between Kautilya’s Arthashastra and the realist tradition of Machiavelli, and compare Dharmashastra and Arthashastra with reference to state power. (UPSC 2012/2010) What it’s asking:  A two-part comparison — first Kautilya against Machiavelli, then Dharmashastra against Arthashastra on where power stands relative to morality. Gist — the spine to recall 1. Chronology first  — the  Arthashastra  precedes  The Prince  by about  1800 years .  ( Upinder Singh : it is more accurate to call Machiavelli the ‘Italian Kautilya’ than Kautilya the ‘Indian Machiavelli’, as Nehru did.) 2. Parallels  — both are  realists  writing for a fragmented motherland, permitting ‘all sorts of means’ and an expansionist policy.  (Kautilya’s Bheda and Machiavelli’s advice to keep rivals disunited are the same device under two names.) 3. Weber’s verdict  —  Max Weber : ‘Kautilya is more Machiavelli than Machiavelli — Machiavelli’s Prince is harmless compared to Kautilya’s vijigishu’.  (The spies, poisoners and courtesan-agents of the Arthashastra have no parallel in The Prince.) 4. The decisive contrast  — ‘for Machiavelli the Prince is above religion; for Kautilya the king remains  under dharma ’.  (Power is a means for Kautilya, an end for Machiavelli — and ‘Kautilya got his king, Machiavelli never got his prince’.) 5. Dharmashastra vs Arthashastra  — Manu subordinates  danda to dharma ; Kautilya makes  danda central .  (Manu’s king punishes to uphold the cosmic order; Kautilya’s punishes to keep the state strong, since artha is ‘supreme’ and dharma, kama and moksha depend on it.) 6. Conclusion  — Kautilya is a  dharma-bounded realist , a distinctively Indian synthesis of statecraft and ethics.  (Power is ruthless in operation yet answerable to a higher moral order.) Model Answer 1. Chronology first.  Nehru called Kautilya the ‘Indian Machiavelli’ and the label has stuck; but since the  Arthashastra  predates  The Prince  by roughly  1800 years ,  Upinder Singh  rightly notes that it would be more accurate to call Machiavelli the ‘Italian Kautilya’. The comparison must therefore run forward from Kautilya, not backward, and any suggestion of influence is chronologically impossible. 2. Parallels.  Both are  realists  of the first rank, writing amid political fragmentation for a motherland under threat — Kautilya for a Magadha facing invasion, Machiavelli for a divided Italy — and both make consolidation the supreme object. Both permit the ruler ‘all sorts of means’, both endorse an imperialist or expansionist foreign policy, and both in effect hold that the end justifies the means. Kautilya’s  Bheda  — dividing the adversary — and Machiavelli’s counsel to keep rivals disunited are the same instrument under two different names. 3. Weber’s verdict.  Max Weber  judged that ‘Kautilya is more Machiavelli than Machiavelli — Machiavelli’s Prince is harmless compared to Kautilya’s vijigishu’. The judgment is defensible on detail: the  Arthashastra  prescribes an elaborate machinery of spies, informers, poisoners and courtesan-agents, and a whole calculus of subversion, for which  The Prince  offers no equivalent. Kautilya is thus the more thorough realist precisely because he is the more administrative one. 4. The decisive contrast.  The difference lies in ethics: ‘for Machiavelli the Prince is above religion; for Kautilya the king remains  under dharma ’. Kautilya’s king is enjoined to be ‘generous and kind’, is bound by the welfare of his subjects, and treats power as a  means, not an end ; Machiavelli’s prince rules ‘with an iron hand’ and treats power as self-justifying. Machiavelli offers generic counsel, Kautilya precise administrative detail — and, as the contrast is often put, ‘Kautilya got his king, Machiavelli never got his prince’. 5. Dharmashastra vs Arthashastra.  On state power the two Indian traditions differ in emphasis rather than in kind. The  Dharmashastra  of  Manu  subordinates  danda to dharma : coercion exists to uphold the moral and cosmic order, and the king, bound by Raj Dharma, punishes in order to preserve varnashrama. The  Arthashastra  of  Kautilya  makes  danda central  and dharma peripheral: the king punishes to keep the state strong, because material well-being (‘artha’) is ‘supreme’, for ‘on it depend dharma, kama and moksha’. 6. Conclusion.  Kautilya is a realist like Machiavelli but a  dharma-bounded  one, which is why the  Arthashastra  represents a distinctively Indian synthesis of statecraft and ethics: power is real, calculating and ruthless in operation, yet ultimately answerable to a higher moral order which the ruler did not create and cannot repeal. Q — Examine the salient features of Buddhist political thought, assess whether it gave a greater ethical foundation to ancient Indian thought, and compare it with the Hindu tradition. (UPSC 2021) What it’s asking:  Set out what is distinctive about Buddhist politics, then decide whether it is ethically superior to the Brahmanical tradition it broke from. Gist — the spine to recall 1. The rebel child  —  Bhikhu Parekh : Buddhism is ‘the rebel child of Hinduism’, egalitarian, rationalist and republican.  (The ‘Protestantism of the East’ — it bypassed the priest and the Sanskrit text, preaching in Pali to every varna.) 2. Origin of the state  — the state arises from the  moral fall  of men, not from a divine scheme.  (Once greed and theft appeared in an innocent society, men had to invent authority to restrain themselves.) 3. MahaSammat  — the king is  elected  by consensus, ‘only primus inter pares, by virtue of a social contract’.  (‘The Great Elect’ — the people choose one man and pay him a share of the grain to keep order: a social contract centuries before Hobbes and Locke.) 4. Rule by Dhamma  — government by ethical persuasion, not danda; the  Chakravartin  ‘wins others by the Dhamma Chakra’.  (Ashoka conquers hearts rather than land, and pointedly never made Buddhism a state religion — an implicit secularism.)   Amartya Sen  praises its commitment to public discussion. 5. Buddhist vs Hindu  — republican vs monarchical, elected king vs divine personality, Dhamma vs Danda, and  rejection of caste  vs Brahmanical hierarchy.  (This-worldly and deliberative against other-worldly and hierarchical.) 6. Conclusion  — a genuinely stronger  ethical and deliberative  foundation.  (Which is exactly why Ambedkar chose Buddhism in 1956 as the emancipatory alternative to caste Hinduism.) Model Answer 1. The rebel child.  Bhikhu Parekh  calls Buddhism ‘the rebel child of Hinduism’ — an  egalitarian, rationalist and republican  tradition, the ‘Protestantism of the East’, which challenged caste, dispensed with the priestly intermediary and Vedic ritual, and preached in Pali rather than Sanskrit so that the message reached every varna.  Gail Omvedt  accordingly treats the Buddha as a genuine political philosopher and not merely a religious teacher. 2. Origin of the state.  Where the Hindu tradition derives kingship from the need to end  arajakta  ordained in the cosmic scheme, the Buddhist account is historical and moral: the state arises from the  moral fall or corruption  of men. In an originally innocent society the growth of greed, property and theft made restraint necessary, and men themselves devised authority to supply it. Political power is therefore a human remedy for a human failing, not a divine institution. 3. MahaSammat.  It follows that the king is  elected  by consensus in the  MahaSammat  — ‘the Great Elect’ — chosen by the people to keep order in return for a share of their produce, and remaining ‘only primus inter pares, by virtue of a social contract’. Authority is thus conditional upon consent and upon performance of the agreed function, giving Buddhism a theory of  decentralised democracy, equality and the social contract  many centuries before Hobbes, Locke and Rousseau — reflected institutionally in the ganasangha republics and in the deliberative procedure of the sangha itself. 4. Rule by Dhamma.  Government is by  Dhamma  — ethical persuasion — rather than by danda: the ideal ruler is the  Chakravartin  who ‘wins others by the Dhamma Chakra’, conquering hearts instead of territory. Ashoka’s polity after Kalinga embodied this, yet he ‘never made Buddhism a state religion’ and enjoined respect for all sects — an implicit secularism.  Amartya Sen  praises the tradition’s ‘foundational commitment to public communication and discussion’, tracing India’s argumentative and deliberative ethos to the Buddhist councils. 5. Buddhist vs Hindu.  The contrast is systematic: this-worldly against other-worldly;  republican against monarchical ; a king elected by the MahaSammat against a king of ‘divine personality’; the Chakravartin winning hearts against the vijigishu acquiring land; Dhamma and Panchsheel against Danda and Mandala; and, most consequentially, the  rejection of caste in favour of equality  against the Brahmanical hierarchy of varna. Where the Hindu tradition legitimises order through birth, the Buddhist legitimises it through consent and conduct. 6. Conclusion.  Buddhist thought did lend a greater  ethical and deliberative  foundation to ancient Indian political thought — egalitarian, rational and consent-based — anticipating ideas the West reached only much later. That is precisely why  Ambedkar  chose it in 1956 as the emancipatory alternative to caste Hinduism, converting at Nagpur with lakhs of followers. Q — Assess Sir Syed Ahmed Khan as a social reformer and modernizer, tracing his transition from champion of Hindu-Muslim unity to originator of the two-nation theory. (UPSC 2021/2013) What it’s asking:  Two halves — credit him as a reformer, then explain why the preacher of unity turned into the father of the two-nation theory. Gist — the spine to recall 1. Core creed  — Muslim upliftment is ‘possible only with the modernization of Islam’, a faith ‘most compatible with science and rationality’.  (‘The Muslim youth should hold the book of science in one hand and the Quran in the other’.) 2. Educational modernizer  — the journal  Tehzeeb-ul-Akhlaq , a scientific society and  MAO College .  (MAO College grew into Aligarh Muslim University; his standing among Muslims is compared to Raja Ram Mohan Roy’s among Hindus.) 3. Social reformer  — a ‘champion of democratic ideals and freedom of speech’ who attacked religious intolerance.  (He denounced purdah, polygamy and easy divorce as social evils rather than sanctified custom.) 4. Phase 1 — Hindu-Muslim unity  — a common Indian nationhood; by ‘qaum’ he meant both communities.  (‘Hindus and Muslims are the two eyes of the beautiful bride, India’ — sharing ‘the same soil… the same ruler… the hardships of a famine’.) 5. Phase 2 — the two-nation theory  — fearing that under elections the Hindu majority would ‘totally override the interests of the smaller community’, he opposed representative government and the Congress.  (Counting heads where the majority is permanent means permanent minority subordination — hence the ‘Anglo-Muslim alliance’.) 6. Conclusion  — his educational and political legacies pull in opposite directions.  (AMU on one side, the ideological seed of Partition on the other.) Model Answer 1. Core creed.  Sir Syed Ahmed Khan  held that Muslim upliftment was ‘possible only with the modernization of Islam’, a faith he regarded as ‘most compatible with science and rationality’. Writing after 1857, when the community had turned inward and boycotted English education, his central message was the reconciliation of revelation with reason: ‘the Muslim youth should hold the book of science in one hand and the Quran in the other’. Faith and modern knowledge, he insisted, cannot contradict each other because both proceed from the same source. 2. Educational modernizer.  He acted on this creed institutionally. He launched the journal  Tehzeeb-ul-Akhlaq  to reform Muslim manners and opinion, founded a scientific society to translate Western works into Urdu, and established the  Mohammedan Anglo-Oriental College  at Aligarh, which grew into  Aligarh Muslim University  and became the seedbed of a modern Muslim professional class. His status among Muslims is fairly compared to  Raja Ram Mohan Roy’s  among Hindus. 3. Social reformer.  He was, in the textbook’s phrase, a ‘champion of democratic ideals and freedom of speech’ who attacked religious intolerance and irrational custom wherever he found them. He denounced  purdah, polygamy and easy divorce  as social evils rather than sanctified practice, and urged that scripture be interpreted in the light of reason and changing circumstance — a position that drew the hostility of the orthodox ulema. 4. Phase 1 — Hindu-Muslim unity.  In his earlier phase he was an unambiguous exponent of a common Indian nationhood. Hindus and Muslims are ‘the two eyes of the beautiful bride, India’ — injure one and the bride is disfigured — for they share ‘the same soil… the same ruler… the hardships of a famine’. By  qaum  (nation) he expressly meant ‘both Hindus and Muslims’, and he worked closely with Hindu leaders in educational and civic causes. 5. Phase 2 — the two-nation theory.  The shift came with the prospect of  representative government . Sir Syed feared that where elections turn on counting heads in a society of permanent majorities and minorities, the Hindu majority would ‘totally override the interests of the smaller community’, reducing Muslims to permanent subordination. He therefore turned against parliamentary self-government, opposed the Congress, and sought an ‘Anglo-Muslim alliance’, becoming the originator of the  two-nation theory  — the doctrine that Hindus and Muslims form two distinct nations. The Urdu-Hindi controversy, his dependence on government funding for the Aligarh college, and rising Hindu revivalism all accelerated the transition. 6. Conclusion.  Sir Syed was a genuine modernizer who dragged a defeated and conservative community toward science, English education and social reform. But his later communal politics laid the ideological seed of Partition, so that his educational legacy at Aligarh and his political legacy in the two-nation theory pull in exactly opposite directions. Q — Analyse Sri Aurobindo’s theory of cultural/spiritual nationalism, his conception of Swaraj and his idea of freedom. (UPSC 2017/2016/2014/2013) What it’s asking:  Three linked ideas — the nation as spirit, Swaraj as complete independence, and freedom as inner self-realisation. Gist — the spine to recall 1. Nationalism as spirituality  — he ‘connected nationalism with spirituality’;  Romain Rolland  saw in him ‘the highest synthesis of the genius of Asia and of Europe’.  (Nationalism is not a political programme but a way of life like religion — the patriot is a devotee, not a party worker.) 2. Cultural/spiritual nationalism  — ‘the nation is not a piece of land… the  nation is a faith, a religion, the nation has a spirit ’.  (Herder’s national spirit + Bankim’s Mother India as Goddess + Vivekananda’s Neo-Vedanta — India’s ‘divine mission’ is to give spirituality to the world.) 3. Passive resistance  — in his extremist phase he rejected Moderate constitutionalism and theorised organised resistance.  (Swadeshi, boycott and non-cooperation — the doctrinal ground on which Gandhi’s Satyagraha was later built.) 4. Swaraj as Purna Swaraj  — the first to read Swaraj as  complete independence .  (‘Political freedom is the life-breath of a nation’; to attempt social reform ‘without aiming first at political freedom is the height of ignorance’.) 5. Inner freedom  — the liberal view is ‘mechanical’ and the socialist neglects the individual; true freedom is  inner freedom .  (‘Obeying the law of our own existence’ — swadharma — so a man free of foreign rule but enslaved to his appetites is not free.) 6. Conclusion  — he raised nationalism from programme to vocation, though critics call it reactionary and idealistic.  (By rooting it in an ‘open and universal’ Sanatana Dharma he radicalised the freedom movement.) Model Answer 1. Nationalism as spirituality.  Sri Aurobindo  ‘connected nationalism with spirituality’, and  Romain Rolland  saw in him ‘the highest synthesis of the genius of Asia and of Europe’. For him nationalism was not a mere political programme but a way of life like religion: the patriot approaches the nation as a devotee approaches the divine, with faith and self-surrender rather than a calculation of interest. This converted the freedom struggle from a constitutional claim into a spiritual vocation. 2. Cultural / spiritual nationalism.  Applying the German romantic idea —  Herder’s  claim that ‘the nation is natural and has a spirit’ — and drawing on  Bankim’s  vision of  Mother India as Goddess  and  Vivekananda’s  Neo-Vedanta, Aurobindo held that ‘the nation is not a piece of land… the  nation is a faith, the nation is a religion, the nation has a spirit ’. India is not a territory but a living Mother with a  divine mission  — to give spirituality to a materialist world — so her subjection is a spiritual and not merely a political wrong. 3. Passive resistance.  In his extremist phase Aurobindo dismissed the Moderates’ constitutional petitioning as futile and pioneered a systematic theory of  passive resistance  — organised non-cooperation with an alien administration, backed by swadeshi, boycott and national education, to be abandoned only if repression made resistance impossible. This body of doctrine prepared the ground on which  Gandhi’s  Satyagraha would be built a decade later. 4. Swaraj as Purna Swaraj.  He was the first Indian leader to interpret Swaraj as  Purna Swaraj  — complete independence rather than colonial self-government within the Empire — to be won through swadeshi, boycott, national education and passive resistance. ‘Political freedom is the life-breath of a nation’, he wrote, and to attempt social reform ‘without aiming first at political freedom is the height of ignorance’. Swaraj is thus the ‘necessary condition for India to accomplish its destined goal’ — the political shell within which the spiritual mission can be realised. 5. Inner freedom.  Aurobindo found the liberal, near-anarchic conception of liberty ‘mechanical’ — an absence of external restraint that says nothing about what the free man becomes — and the socialist conception neglectful of the individual. Real freedom is  inner freedom : ‘obeying the law of our own existence’, that is, swadharma. A man released from foreign rule but enslaved to his own appetites has not become free. His later thought —  Sacchidananda, the Supermind and Integral Yoga  — accordingly makes national self-realisation one stage in the spiritual evolution of humanity as a whole. 6. Conclusion.  Aurobindo raised nationalism from a political programme to a spiritual vocation. Critics call his spiritual nationalism reactionary, idealistic and open to majoritarian appropriation; yet by rooting freedom in an ‘open and universal’ Sanatana Dharma rather than a narrow creed, and by demanding Purna Swaraj when others asked only for reform, he decisively radicalised the Indian freedom movement. Q — Evaluate Ambedkar’s idea of social justice — annihilation of caste, critique of Hinduism and of Marxism, and his conception of social/economic/political democracy — comparing his egalitarian justice with Rawls. (UPSC 2022/2020/2018/2016/2013) What it’s asking:  Build Ambedkar’s theory of justice upward from caste, then measure it against Rawls’ procedural justice. Gist — the spine to recall 1. Annihilation of caste  — caste is ‘not the division of labour but the  division of labourers ’, held together by  endogamy .  (A guild you may leave; a caste you are born into and must marry within — so inter-caste marriage, not ritual reform, is the real solvent.) 2. Critique of Hinduism  — ‘Hinduism is nothing but Brahmanism’, sanctified by the Vedas and the Manusmriti.  (He would ‘put dynamite’ on the Manusmriti, and finding reform impossible from within, converted to Buddhism in 1956: ‘I reject the religion which treats me as inferior’.) 3. The three democracies  — democracy is ‘a way of life’ on the ‘inseparable trinity of liberty, equality and fraternity’; political democracy must be completed by  social and economic democracy .  (One man one vote is worthless if the same man may not draw water from the village well.) 4. Constitutional morality  — the safeguard, alongside ‘state socialism’.  (Not merely obeying the text but internalising its spirit — self-restraint, due process, respect for dissent — in a soil he called ‘essentially undemocratic’.) 5. Critique of Marxism  — religion is not mere ‘opium’, and ‘society is more exploitative than the state’.  (Buddhism, built on karuna, samata and prajna, liberates; and the untouchable is humiliated by his neighbours, so the state must be his instrument of emancipation, not his enemy.) 6. Ambedkar vs Rawls & conclusion  — his justice is  egalitarian and outcome-oriented ; Rawls’ is  procedural .  (Rawls reasons from a hypothetical veil of ignorance; Ambedkar starts from a real history of humiliation and demands safeguards to undo it.) Model Answer 1. Annihilation of caste.  Ambedkar  — ‘chief architect of the Constitution’ and himself born a Mahar — made the  annihilation of caste  his central concern. In  Annihilation of Caste  he argues that caste is ‘not the division of labour but the  division of labourers ’: a guild divides work and may be left, whereas caste divides human beings themselves into fixed, graded compartments one is born into. Its steel frame is  endogamy , which is why he held that inter-caste marriage and inter-dining, not the reform of ritual, are the real solvents of the system. 2. Critique of Hinduism.  Caste for Ambedkar is not an excrescence but the essence: ‘Hinduism is nothing but Brahmanism’, a graded inequality sanctified by the Vedas and above all by the  Manusmriti , on which he said he would ‘put dynamite’ and which he publicly burnt in 1927. Because the sanction is scriptural, reform from within is impossible — destroy belief in the sanctity of the shastras and caste collapses. Finding no such reform forthcoming, he  converted to Buddhism  in 1956: ‘I reject the religion which treats me as inferior’. 3. The three democracies.  For Ambedkar democracy is not a form of government but ‘a way of life’, resting on the ‘inseparable trinity of liberty, equality and fraternity’, which he traced to the Buddha rather than to the French Revolution. Hence his warning that India was entering a life of contradictions: political equality of one man one vote alongside social and economic inequality. Political democracy must therefore be completed by  social and economic democracy , for ‘political democracy cannot last unless there lies at its base social democracy’ — the vote is empty if the voter may not draw water from the village well. 4. Constitutional morality.  The instruments of that completion are  constitutional morality  and ‘state socialism’. Borrowing the phrase from Grote, Ambedkar meant not mere obedience to the constitutional text but internalisation of its spirit — self-restraint by those in power, respect for forms and for dissent, and the settling of conflict by due process rather than agitation — a habit he thought had to be deliberately cultivated because Indian soil was ‘essentially undemocratic’. Alongside it he urged state ownership of key industries and of land, so that concentrated economic power could not defeat formal equality. 5. Critique of Marxism.  Ambedkar rejected two Marxist claims. First, that religion is mere ‘opium’: Buddhism, resting on karuna, samata and prajna, is a liberating morality and not a narcotic. Second, that the state is the chief instrument of oppression — for Ambedkar ‘society is more exploitative than the state’, since the untouchable is humiliated by his own neighbours and not primarily by officials, so the state must be strengthened as an instrument of emancipation. He also rejected violent revolution and the dictatorship of the proletariat in favour of constitutional methods. 6. Ambedkar vs Rawls & conclusion.  Ambedkar’s social justice is  egalitarian and outcome-oriented  — the active uplift of the depressed classes through state action, reservation and constitutional safeguards — whereas  Rawls’  ‘justice as fairness’ is  procedural , derived from a hypothetical original position behind a veil of ignorance. Ambedkar begins not from an abstraction but from a documented history of humiliation. He thus transformed justice in India from a matter of procedure into one of  substantive social emancipation , making the annihilation of caste and the completion of democracy his enduring legacy. Q — Trace M.N. Roy’s ideational journey from Marxism to Radical Humanism, and identify the major components of Modern Indian Political Thought with reference to Gandhi and Roy. What it’s asking:  Follow Roy’s three phases and his two breaks, then use Gandhi and Roy together to name what modern Indian thought is made of. Gist — the spine to recall 1. Three phases  —  nationalism → communism → radical humanism .  (A revolutionary who founded the CPI abroad and ended by dissolving his own party for the sake of the individual.) 2. Break with Lenin  — at the Comintern (1920) his  Supplementary Theses  opposed Lenin’s two-stage strategy.  (Lenin wanted communists to ally with bourgeois-nationalists like the Congress; Roy insisted they lead the colonial proletariat directly — ‘for socialism to win in the West it must first win in the East’.) 3. Critique of Marxism  — it  subdues individualism  in ‘the collective ego of the proletariat’; historical materialism is ‘economic determinism’; the sanction against exploitation is ‘not economic but  moral ’.  (Marxism is ‘more method than dogma’.) 4. Radical Humanism  —  New Humanism: A Manifesto  rests on  Reason, Morality and Freedom .  (Man, not class or party, is the measure — freedom is ‘the progressive removal of restrictions on the unfolding of the potentialities of individuals… not as cogs in a mechanized social organism’.) 5. Party-less radical democracy  — parties ‘bred social and political immorality’ and reduce sovereignty to a ‘legal fiction’.  (He dissolved his own party in 1948 for ‘people’s committees’ and ‘miniature republics’ — candidates chosen for merit, not for a party ticket.) 6. Gandhi & Roy — and conclusion  — spiritual against rationalist, yet both converge on  decentralisation, the individual, and morality in politics .  (Bidyut Chakraborty thinks Roy never fully escaped Marxism, yet his is the most individual-centred voice in modern Indian thought.) Model Answer 1. Three phases.  M.N. Roy’s  intellectual life moved through three distinct phases —  nationalism → communism → radical humanism . Beginning as a revolutionary nationalist in Bengal, he became a founder of the Communist Party of India and one of the very few Asians to hold a leading position in the Comintern, and ended by dissolving his own party in the name of the individual — a trajectory from collective revolution to personal freedom. 2. Break with Lenin.  The first break came at the Second Congress of the Comintern (1920), where Roy clashed with  Lenin . Lenin’s colonial theses proposed a two-stage strategy in which communists would first ally with bourgeois-nationalist movements such as the Congress; Roy’s  Supplementary Theses  replied that such movements were led by classes with a stake in the existing order, and that communists must organise and lead the colonial proletariat and peasantry directly. His larger claim was that imperial profit sustained European capitalism, so that ‘for socialism to win in the West it must first win in the East’. 3. Critique of Marxism.  Disillusioned, Roy came to regard ‘Marxism as more method than dogma’ and criticised it on three counts. It  subdues individualism , dissolving the person into ‘the collective ego of the proletariat’ and then into the party. Its historical materialism is mere ‘economic determinism’, denying the creative role of ideas and of human will in history. And the true sanction for ending exploitation is ‘not economic but  moral ’ — a revolution begun in immorality cannot end in freedom. 4. Radical Humanism.  His alternative, set out in  New Humanism: A Manifesto  and the  Twenty-Two Theses , rests on three elements.  Reason  — man is essentially rational, and blind faith, whether religious or ideological, must be rejected.  Morality  — secular and rational, rooted in man’s own rationality rather than in divine command. And  Freedom , defined as ‘the progressive removal of all restrictions on the unfolding of the potentialities of individuals… not as cogs in a mechanized social organism’. Man, not class or party, is the measure of every social arrangement, and the goal is a cosmopolitan ‘commonwealth of spiritually free men’. 5. Party-less radical democracy.  Holding that the party system ‘bred social and political immorality’ — subordinating conscience to the whip and reducing popular sovereignty to a ‘legal fiction’ exercised for a moment at the ballot box — Roy dissolved his own party in 1948 in favour of ‘organized democracy’: decentralised ‘people’s committees’ and ‘miniature republics’ in which candidates are chosen for personal merit rather than a party ticket, and power is exercised continuously from below with primacy given to the individual. 6. Gandhi & Roy — and conclusion.  The major components of modern Indian political thought are visible in the contrast between the two.  Gandhi  is spiritual, treats religion as a moralising force, and looks to a decentralised Ram Rajya secured by non-violence;  Roy  is rationalist and humanist, militantly secular, individual-centred and party-less. Yet both converge on  decentralisation, the primacy of the individual and the community, and the insistence on morality in politics  — the recurring signature of modern Indian thought. Though  Bidyut Chakraborty  judged Roy ‘unable to free himself entirely from Marxism’, his radical humanism remains its most genuinely individual-centred and cosmopolitan voice. Revision Box — facts, keywords & quotes Ancient thought =  riti (cosmic order) ≈ natural law; dharma & danda in continuum; Sant Tukaram — ‘the world is a family’. Manu : first law-giver; ‘Prithvim Dharma Dhritam’; king = divine personality but NO divine rights, bound by Raj Dharma. Kautilya : Saptanga (7 organs), Mandala Siddhanta, Shadgunya-niti, 4 Upayas (Sama/Dama/Danda/Bheda); ‘forty ways of embezzlement’. Weber : ‘Kautilya is more Machiavelli than Machiavelli’; Kautilya under dharma, Machiavelli’s prince above religion; Kautilya predates him ~1800 yrs. Buddhist:  ‘rebel child of Hinduism’; king elected by MahaSammat (social contract); rule by Dhamma; Chakravartin wins hearts; rejects caste. Gandhi : Satyagraha (soul-force, self-suffering), Swaraj (self-rule → Ram Rajya), Sarvodaya/Trusteeship; state = ‘soulless machine’. Gandhi : ‘I want the cultures of all lands blown about my house… but refuse to be blown off my feet’; ends-means continuity. Sir Syed : modernizer (MAO College/AMU); ‘two eyes of the beautiful bride, India’ → later originator of the two-nation theory. Aurobindo : spiritual/cultural nationalism — ‘nation is a faith, a religion’; first to define Purna Swaraj; ‘inner freedom’. Ambedkar : annihilation of caste — ‘division of labourers, not labour’; ‘Hinduism = Brahmanism’; converted to Buddhism (1956). Ambedkar : ‘political democracy cannot last without social democracy’; liberty-equality-fraternity trinity; constitutional morality. Ambedkar vs Rawls:  egalitarian/outcome justice vs procedural ‘justice as fairness’. M.N. Roy : nationalism → communism → radical humanism; broke with Lenin (Supplementary Theses); reason + morality + freedom. Roy : party-less radical democracy — ‘people’s committees’, ‘miniature republics’, primacy of the individual. Gandhi vs Marx:  spiritualist vs materialist; class cooperation (trusteeship) vs class conflict; state redundant vs state withers away. Salient features of Indian thought:  continuity, communitarian, pluralistic, cosmopolitan, non-critical/regressive. Last-Minute Revision Sheet (1 page) Gandhi (MQ1):  Truth/Ahimsa → Satyagraha; Swaraj/Ram Rajya; Sarvodaya/Trusteeship; critique of modern civilization; state = soulless machine. Dharmashastra/Manu (MQ2):  riti ≈ natural law; dharma holds society; king under dharma, no divine rights; varna hierarchy (Ambedkar’s critique). Kautilya statecraft (MQ3):  Saptanga; Mandala; Shadgunya; 4 Upayas; corruption ‘forty ways’. Kautilya vs Machiavelli (MQ4):  both realists; Kautilya under dharma, predates Machiavelli; Dharmashastra (dharma>danda) vs Arthashastra (danda>dharma). Buddhist (MQ5):  rebel child of Hinduism; MahaSammat election/social contract; rule by Dhamma; rejects caste; greater ethical/deliberative foundation. Sir Syed (MQ6):  modernizer (science + Quran, AMU); Hindu-Muslim unity → two-nation theory. Aurobindo (MQ7):  spiritual/cultural nationalism (‘nation is a religion’); Purna Swaraj; inner freedom. Ambedkar (MQ8):  annihilation of caste; Hinduism=Brahmanism; social + economic democracy; critique of Marxism; egalitarian vs Rawls’ procedural justice. M.N. Roy (MQ9):  Marxism → radical humanism; Lenin break; reason/morality/freedom; party-less democracy. title: 10 - Western Political Thought

content.text: Syllabus — Western Political Thought: Plato, Aristotle, Machiavelli, Hobbes, Locke, John S. Mill, Marx, Gramsci, Hannah Arendt. (UPSC PSIR Paper-1A, Unit 10)

the canon of Western political thinkers — Plato, Aristotle, Machiavelli, Hobbes, Locke, J.S. Mill, Marx, Gramsci and Hannah Arendt — their central ideas, the comparisons the syllabus draws (Plato vs Aristotle, Hobbes vs Locke, Marx vs Gramsci) and their critiques.

Plato (justice, philosopher-king, Popper critique), Aristotle (constitutions, revolution), Machiavelli (realism, virtu-fortuna), Hobbes (Leviathan, sovereignty), Locke (natural rights, limited state), Mill (liberty, harm principle), Marx (materialism, alienation, surplus value), Gramsci (hegemony), Arendt (vita activa, banality of evil).
Q — Examine Plato’s conception of justice, education, communism and the philosopher-king, and evaluate Popper’s charge that ‘Plato was an enemy of the open society’. (UPSC 2015)
Build Plato’s ideal state — justice, education, philosopher-king, communism — and then judge whether it really amounts to totalitarianism.
— functional harmony, ‘one man, one job’: each class does its own task and no other.
(The doctor heals, the soldier guards, the farmer farms; injustice is the farmer trying to command the army.)
2. Soul and the myth of metals
(Gold, silver and bronze souls — yet a bronze father may have a gold son, so birth is not destiny.)
‘The state is the individual writ large’.
— a lifelong sieve ending at 50 in rule by the wise.

(Allegory of the cave: prisoners mistake shadows on the wall for reality; only he who has left the cave and seen the sun may rule — as one wants the trained navigator at the helm, not the loudest sailor.)
— no private property or family for the two ruling classes only.
(A judge who owns no shares in the company before him, and no son to favour, cannot be bought.)
(Censorship of poets and state-arranged breeding — the closed society in miniature.)
: all Western philosophy is ‘footnotes to Plato’.
defines justice as ‘each element in society doing its appropriate task, doing it well and doing it only’ — a

rather than a legal rule. On this ‘one man, one job’ principle the doctor heals, the soldier guards and the farmer produces; injustice is meddling, the farmer presuming to command the army. Justice is thus ‘the architectonic principle’ that holds the whole polis together.
2. Soul and the myth of metals.
The state mirrors the soul: its three parts —
— correspond to rulers, guardians and producers, since ‘the state is the individual writ large’. The

legitimises this order as a ‘noble lie’: men are born with gold, silver or bronze in their souls. Crucially the scheme is not hereditary caste — a bronze artisan’s gifted son may be promoted to gold, so function, not birth, fixes rank.
, a lifelong sieve culminating at fifty in the rule of the
— ‘until philosophers are rulers or rulers learn philosophy, there is no end to the ills of states’. The

supplies the justification: chained prisoners take flickering shadows for reality, and only the philosopher who has climbed out and seen the sun knows the Form of the Good. Hence ‘it is foolish to limit an expert physician with the book of medicine’ — the philosopher-king rules by wisdom, not by law.
To free the rulers from private temptation, Plato prescribes
communism of property and of wives

— but only for the two upper classes, the producers keeping both. The logic is the modern conflict-of-interest rule: a judge who owns no shares in the company before him, and has no son to promote, cannot be bought. It is therefore an ‘economic solution to a political ailment’, unlike
The Open Society and Its Enemies
, holds that ‘Plato was an enemy of the open society’: a rigid class order, censorship of poets and music, state-arranged breeding, and rule by an unaccountable elite add up to
. Above all Plato sought to ‘arrest all political change’ — ‘change is evil, rest divine’ — which is the mark of the closed society.
The charge is powerful but arguably anachronistic, reading twentieth-century fascism back into a fourth-century BC moral treatise;

replies that ‘fascism and Platonism are incomparable’, for Plato’s rulers hold no property and seek no glory. Whatever the verdict, his linkage of knowledge, virtue and rule remains the founding statement of political philosophy — all Western philosophy, said
Q — Analyse Aristotle’s critique of Plato’s idealism, and contrast their theories of justice and the state. (UPSC 2019)
Show how the pupil demolished the teacher — on Forms, on ‘one man, one job’ and communism — and then set their justice and state side by side.
— idealism gives way to empirical realism.
(Plato designs the state he wishes existed; Aristotle collects 158 constitutions that actually exist.)
‘Plato is my friend, but truth is a greater friend’.
— a separate ‘world of ideas’ is unreal; the essence lies inside the thing.
(There is no perfect Chair in heaven — only chairs, studied and classified.)
3. Against ‘one man, one job’ and communism
(‘What is common to the greatest number gets the least care’ — like a shared hostel kitchen nobody cleans.)
— Plato: inner, moral, duty-based; Aristotle: external, legal,
(Equal pay for equal work, but higher office for higher merit — the seed of reservation debates.)
— both make it the school of the good life, but Plato perfects an ideal, Aristotle improves the actual.
(Philosopher-king vs rule of law and a middle-class polity.)
— realism corrects idealism; hence Aristotle, not Plato, is the ‘father of political science’.
was Plato’s pupil for twenty years and ‘rectified the limitations of Plato’s ideas’ by replacing idealism with

. Where Plato deduces the state he wishes existed from the Form of the Good, Aristotle collects and dissects 158 actual constitutions. The method is captured in ‘Plato is my friend, but truth is a greater friend’ — or, as
puts it, ‘as Brutus loved Rome more, so for Aristotle dear is Plato, but dearer is truth’.

— the claim that a separate, changeless ‘world of ideas’ is more real than the world we inhabit. For him the essence of a thing lies within the thing itself: there is no perfect Chair in heaven, only chairs to be observed, compared and classified. Politics accordingly becomes a practical science of what is attainable for men as they are, not a contemplation of an unrealisable ideal.
3. Against ‘one man, one job’ and communism.
Plato’s functional justice is faulted as
, too subjective and moral rather than legal, and as stressing duties while ignoring rights. His

fares worse: ‘what is common to the greatest number gets the least care’ — everyone’s property is no one’s responsibility, as in a shared hostel kitchen nobody cleans. Aristotle defends private property as the spur to effort and the family as a ‘time-tested institution’ of emotional stability.
— the harmony of the soul, a matter of performing duties. For Aristotle it is

: ‘it is unjust to treat equals unequally and unequals equally’. Equal work earns equal pay, but greater merit earns greater office — the ancestor of every modern argument over merit and compensatory discrimination. He splits it into

Both hold the state essential to the good life — Plato aims at ‘the greatest happiness of the whole’, Aristotle declares ‘man is by nature a political animal’ and the state exists ‘for the sake of the good life’. But Plato is the
who designs an ideal polis ruled by philosopher-kings above the law, while Aristotle is the
who prefers the rule of law and a middle-class ‘polity’ as the most stable attainable form.

Aristotle’s realism corrects Plato’s idealism — the shift is from an ideal to be constructed to institutions to be observed, compared and improved — which is why he, and not Plato, is called the ‘father of political science’. Yet the correction is internal to a shared Socratic conviction: the state exists not for mere life but for human excellence.
Q — Explain Aristotle’s classification of constitutions, his theory of proportionate equality and revolution, and assess his contribution to modern constitutional democracy. (UPSC 2021/2017)
Give the two criteria and the six forms, defend polity, then link proportionate equality and the causes of revolution to modern constitutionalism.
— how many rule, and for whose benefit.
(A single ruler serving the people is a king; the same man serving himself is a tyrant.)
(For Aristotle ‘democracy’ is the perverted form — rule by the poor in their own interest.)
— the middle class buffers rich and poor.
(A society of billionaires and beggars flips between oligarchy and mob rule; a large middle class steadies it.)
— equals equally, unequals unequally in proportion.
(Distributive: offices by merit; corrective: the court restores what was taken, whoever the parties are.)
— ‘the feeling of inequality, real or imagined, is the cause of revolution’.
(Perception is enough: a group that merely believes it is being denied its due will rebel.)
— rule of law, mixed government and stability seed modern constitutionalism, though his exclusions must go.
, the ‘father of comparative politics’, who with his students examined 158 constitutions, classifies governments on two axes: the
— one, few or many — and the

, whether the common good or the rulers’ own interest. The second is decisive: one man ruling for his people is a king, the same man ruling for himself is a tyrant. Form alone never settles legitimacy.
The cross-classification yields three correct forms and their perversions: rule by one —
. The last pair surprises modern readers: for Aristotle ‘democracy’ is the debased form, rule by the poor majority in their own class interest, whereas polity is the many ruling for the common good.
Polity is the ‘golden mean’ between oligarchy and democracy, and Aristotle identifies it with the

. Neither so rich as to be arrogant nor so poor as to be servile, it is the class most amenable to reason and to law. A society polarised between billionaires and beggars oscillates between oligarchy and mob rule; a broad middle stratum moderates the conflict and makes the constitution both stable and practicable — the best form for most states most of the time.
Justice requires ‘treating equals equally and unequals unequally in proportion to their inequalities’ —
, which allots honours and offices according to merit and contribution to the polis, and
, which simply restores what has been wrongly taken, treating the parties as arithmetically equal. The distinction remains the backbone of every argument about equity versus formal equality.

‘The feeling of inequality, real or imagined, is the cause of revolution’, and ‘poverty is the parent of revolution and crime’. The insight is psychological rather than economic: perception suffices, so a group that merely believes it is denied its due will revolt. Aristotle catalogues general and regime-specific causes and cures, counselling moderation, obedience to law, and enlargement of the middle class — a conservative concern for

over the rule of persons — ‘law is reason without passion’ — his mixed, middle-class polity and his focus on constitutional stability directly anticipate modern constitutional democracy, and reach India through the basic-structure idea of a government limited by law. His exclusion of women, workers and slaves from citizenship is ‘unacceptable in modern times’; democratise the citizen body and the framework survives intact.
Q — Critically examine Machiavelli’s separation of politics from ethics and religion, and his place in the evolution of political science. (UPSC 2018/2014)
Explain why he cuts politics loose from morality and the Church, then judge what that did for the discipline.
— men are selfish and fickle, so theorise them as they are.
(‘Men sooner forget the death of their father than the loss of their patrimony’.)
2. Politics vs ethics — the lion and the fox
— the prince ‘needs to know how to be bad’.
(The lion frightens off wolves but walks into traps; the fox sees the trap but cannot fight wolves — a ruler needs force and cunning together.)
(Fortuna is a river in flood: dykes built in calm weather — virtu — decide whether it drowns you.)
— religion is a tool of civic discipline: ‘use religion, don’t get used by it’.
(An oath binds a soldier where a wage will not.)
— the empirical method applied to states ‘as they are, not as they ought to be’;
amid the chaos of Renaissance Italy,

on a bleak reading of human nature: men are ungrateful, fickle and acquisitive, and ‘sooner forget the death of their father than the loss of their patrimony’. Political theory must therefore be built on men as they are, not as scripture wishes them to be — the first premise of every subsequent realist, from Hobbes to Morgenthau.
2. Politics vs ethics — the lion and the fox.
rather than morality, he holds that the prince ‘needs to know how to be bad rather than good’ and must combine ‘the courage of the

’, changing colours ‘like a chameleon’. The image is exact: the lion frightens off wolves but blunders into traps, the fox spots the trap but cannot fight wolves — force without guile, or guile without force, both fail. Hence, on the safer bet, ‘it is better for a prince to be
— not Christian virtue but energy, foresight and manly skill — contending with

, the element of chance in politics. Machiavelli likens fortuna to a river in flood: it cannot be abolished, but embankments raised in calm weather decide whether it drowns you. Roughly half of human affairs is thus governed by fortune and half left to our own control — a rejection of both divine providence and fatalism.

: not as truth to be obeyed but as a unifying, disciplining force to be managed, so that the ruler should ‘use religion rather than get used by it’. An oath binds a soldier where a wage will not, and Roman civic religion made citizens brave, whereas Christian otherworldliness had, he thought, made Italians weak. This subordination of Church to state makes him the ‘father of European secularism’.

to human affairs — studying states ‘as they are, not as they ought to be’ and reasoning from Roman and Italian example — Machiavelli breaks decisively with medieval theology and makes politics an autonomous, observable domain.

was the Galileo of political theory.
He is condemned as ‘the most universally reprobated figure’ (
), an amoral cynic who licenses cruelty;

saw the divorce of ethics from politics as a ‘death trap’. Yet the realism endures because it describes practice: as
observed, ‘everyone practises Machiavellism without confessing it’.
Q — Discuss Hobbes’ derivation of the state from human nature and the state of nature, his theory of absolute sovereignty and political obligation, and compare him with Machiavelli. (UPSC 2017)
Trace the chain — human nature to state of nature to contract to absolute sovereign — then say how this differs from Machiavelli’s realism.
— ‘an endless desire for power after power that ceases only in death’, driven by fear.
(‘Fear and I were born twins’ — Hobbes was born as the Armada approached.)
— a ‘war of every man against every man’; life ‘solitary, poor, nasty, brutish and short’.
(Not a jungle but a blackout riot: no police, so even the peaceable arm themselves first.)
— all with all, surrendering every right at once; society and state are born together.
(The sovereign is not a party, so he can breach nothing.)

(A conscript may flee the battlefield; if the state cannot protect you, it cannot command you.)

Using the ‘resolutive-compositive’ method borrowed from Galileo — break society into its parts, then rebuild it —

Absent a common power to keep men in awe, natural equality of ability breeds equality of hope, and hope breeds conflict: the result is a

Escape comes through reason — the laws of nature counselling peace — executed by a

Since the covenant binds subjects to one another, obligation to obey is

Q — Evaluate Locke as the father of liberalism through his two contracts, natural rights, labour theory of property and toleration; and contrast with Hobbes on how each legitimizes state authority.

(A trustee who loots the estate is dismissed — hence the right of revolution.)
— ‘property is the product of one’s labour’, limited by spoilage and ‘enough and as good’ left for others.
(The apple is mine because I picked it, not because the king granted it.)

(But not for atheists, whose oaths he thought worthless.)

, the ‘father of liberalism’, begins from a

The separation matters constitutionally: because society precedes government, the fall of a government does not dissolve the community — a nation outlives a dissolved Parliament — and a people may replace its rulers without returning to anarchy.
3. Natural rights and the trust state.
are inalienable and are carried into civil society, not surrendered to it. The state therefore holds

, never original power: a ‘night-watchman’ state whose ‘sole purpose is the protection of property’, organised through separated legislative, executive and federative powers with the legislature supreme. A trustee who loots the estate is dismissed — which is precisely Locke’s

Property is pre-political and moral: ‘every man has a property in his own person’, so by mixing his labour with nature he makes a thing his own. The apple is mine because I picked it, not because the sovereign granted it. Two limits apply — no accumulation beyond what one can use without

The principle is the seed of the modern secular state and of freedom of conscience — though he notoriously excludes atheists, whose oaths he thought worthless, and Catholics, as owing allegiance abroad.
Both argue from contract, but from opposite premises:

Q — Assess Mill’s harm principle and defence of free expression, his status as a ‘reluctant democrat’, and his case for the equality of women, within his revision of utilitarianism. (UPSC 2014/2018/2021)

— pleasures differ in kind, not only in quantity.
(‘Better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied’ — poetry outranks pushpin, rescuing Bentham from the ‘pig’s philosophy’.)

(Drinking alone is self-regarding and free; drunk driving harms others and may be punished.)

(Even one dissenter must be heard: the silenced opinion may be true, or hold part of the truth.)

Mill gives liberty priority: ‘over himself, over his own body and mind, the individual is sovereign’. The

Drinking alone is self-regarding and free; drunk driving is other-regarding and punishable. Liberty ends exactly where it harms another.

Mill’s defence of discussion is absolute: ‘all silencing of discussion is an assumption of infallibility’, and if all mankind minus one held an opinion, mankind would be no more justified in silencing that one than he in silencing mankind. The silenced view may be true; if false, truth held unchallenged decays into ‘dead dogma’; usually each side holds part of the truth. Hence his defence of the eccentric ‘crank’, whose rare genius benefits mankind.

influence, Mill attacks the legal subordination of women as ‘one of the chief hindrances to human improvement’ and observes that ‘there remains no legal slave save the mistress of every house’. Equality would end the family as ‘a school of despotism’, make it instead a school of sympathy, and ‘double the mass of mental faculties available for the higher service of humanity’. He moved the first parliamentary amendment for women’s suffrage.
Mill is the ‘first serious liberal democrat’ (

Q — Discuss Marx’s base-superstructure model, class and class struggle, and alienation; and how Gramsci’s concepts of hegemony, the integral state and organic intellectuals rescued Marxism from economic determinism. (UPSC 2015/2016/2020 + Gramsci 2013/2016/2019)

History advances by contradiction between forces and relations, through slave, feudal, capitalist and communist stages.

4. Class in itself to class for itself.
Classes are defined by relation to the means of production, and ‘the history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggle’. But a

Gramsci relocates the decisive struggle from economics to

Q — Critically examine Arendt’s conceptual triad of labour, work and action, her distinction between power and violence, and her conception of ‘the political’ as the antidote to totalitarianism. (UPSC 2019)

5. Totalitarianism and the banality of evil.
